# Data Proxy

> Data Proxy serves BigQuery data through PostgreSQL, DuckLake and an OpenResty proxy. This file has the documentation pages as plain text, in reading order. Each page starts after a line of three hyphens, with its source path.

## Data Proxy

Data Proxy copies tables from a source, such as BigQuery, into PostgreSQL and serves them as a REST API. Each caller reads only the rows that its token and the access policy allow. This wiki explains how it works, how to use it and how to run it. The Glossary defines the terms.

```mermaid
%% System context
flowchart LR
  apps["API clients<br/>apps and scripts"]
  people["People<br/>in a browser"]
  idp["Identity provider<br/>Keycloak"]
  subgraph dp["Data Proxy"]
    api["API<br/>proxy and PostgREST"]
    console["Console<br/>web app and notebooks"]
    sync["Sync service"]
    store["Data<br/>PostgreSQL and DuckLake"]
  end
  source["Source<br/>BigQuery"]
  apps -->|"(1) get a token"| idp
  apps -->|"(2) query with the token"| api
  people -->|"sign in"| console
  people -->|"sign in"| idp
  api -->|"read the rows<br/>that the token allows"| store
  console -->|"views and actions"| api
  console -->|"start and control runs"| sync
  sync -->|"copy tables"| source
  sync -->|"write and publish"| store
```

## Architecture

This page shows the parts of Data Proxy and how they depend on each other. Data Proxy serves source data from PostgreSQL through DuckLake catalogs, and a sync service keeps those catalogs up to date. The Glossary defines the terms, and its Tools table says what each tool does.

### Components

```mermaid
%% System components
flowchart TD
  subgraph clients["Clients"]
    api_client["API client"]
    browser["Browser"]
  end
  idp["Identity provider"]
  gateway["Istio gateway"]
  subgraph serving["Serving layer"]
    proxy["Proxy (OpenResty)"]
    redis["Redis cache"]
    postgrest["PostgREST"]
    pgdog["PgDog"]
  end
  subgraph pg["PostgreSQL"]
    appdb["Application database"]
    catalog["ducklake database"]
  end
  s3["SeaweedFS (S3): Parquet files"]
  subgraph sync["Sync layer"]
    workers["Sync workers (DBOS)"] --> duckdb["DuckDB (ducklake extension)"]
  end
  source["Source"]
  subgraph console["Console layer"]
    app["Console server"]
    notebooks["Notebook"]
  end
  api_client --> gateway
  browser --> console
  gateway --> proxy
  gateway -->|"signing keys (JWKS)"| idp
  proxy --> redis
  proxy --> postgrest
  postgrest -->|"signing keys (JWKS)"| idp
  postgrest --> pgdog
  pgdog -->|"reads to standbys, writes to primary"| appdb
  pg -->|"pg_duckdb reads Parquet"| s3
  workers -->|"DBOS state"| appdb
  duckdb -->|"commits snapshots"| catalog
  duckdb -->|"writes Parquet"| s3
  workers --> source
  workers -->|"new generation"| redis
  app --> postgrest
  app -->|"sign in (OpenID Connect)"| idp
  app -->|"file lists"| catalog
  app -->|"storage identities"| s3
  notebooks -->|"signed links"| s3
```

### Layers

| Layer   | What it does                                                                                                   | Page                        |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Serving | Answers API reads. It checks the token, uses the cache, and reads only the rows that the access policy allows. | Serving layer |
| Sync    | Copies source tables into DuckLake and keeps the PostgreSQL views in step.                                     | Sync layer     |
| Console | Shows the system to people and changes the configuration. It starts and controls sync runs.                    | Console layer |

PostgreSQL stores metadata only:

- Roles and grants
- `access_policy` and `access_log`
- PostgreSQL views and `SECURITY DEFINER` functions
- DBOS workflow state

The table data is in DuckLake. PostgreSQL doesn't contain application data rows.

### Authentication

Each boundary has its own credential. The table lists who proves what, and where the details are.

| Boundary                    | Credential and check                                                                                                                         | Details                                        |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| API client to gateway       | A bearer JSON Web Token (JWT). The gateway checks the signature with the JWKS of the identity provider, and the issuer, audience and expiry. | Identity provider   |
| Browser to console          | The OpenID Connect authorization code flow with PKCE. The console keeps the tokens in an encrypted `httpOnly` cookie.                        | Application               |
| Console server to PostgREST | The access token of the user. The browser never calls PostgREST.                                                                             | Application               |
| PostgREST to PostgreSQL     | PostgREST validates the signature with `postgrest.jwksUri`. It connects as the `serving` login.                                              | Authorization flow      |
| Sync workers to PostgreSQL  | The `ops` login.                                                                                                                             | Database Schema          |
| PostgreSQL to SeaweedFS     | The DuckDB S3 secret, which `configure-db` writes.                                                                                           | Serving layer |
| Sync workers to the source  | The credentials of the source, such as `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` for BigQuery or Workload Identity.                                   | Environment    |
| Notebook to SeaweedFS       | A signed link for one object, for `GET` only, valid for 5 minutes.                                                                           | Query tab               |

The token proves who the caller is. A token lives 5 minutes, and a role change takes effect with the next token. See Identity provider and Tokens.

### Authorization

The database decides what the caller may do, so no layer above it calculates permissions. The table lists each decision and what makes it.

| Decision                   | What decides it                                                                                           | Details                                                      |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| The role                   | PostgREST switches to the database role of the `role` claim. `rbac.toml` gives that role its permissions. | Roles                                |
| The schemas                | The `schemas` claim limits the schemas that a token reaches.                                              | Permissions                    |
| The rows                   | The access policy matches the subject and the unit. The table function passes the predicate to DuckDB.    | Schema and row authorization |
| A console action           | The database function checks the permission, the schemas and the status.                                  | Control a run and a schedule           |
| The files of the query tab | `read_files`, the schema, a catalog role and a signed link.                                               | Query tab                       |

The cache key includes the role, so a token with another role never reads an answer that another token cached.

### DuckLake pieces

DuckLake has six pieces. Each piece lives in one place, and one layer writes it.

| Piece                 | Where it lives                                                            | Written by                                  | Read by                                                                                  |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Catalog               | The `ducklake` database, with one metadata schema for each source schema. | The sync workers, as `ops`, on the primary. | `pg_duckdb` in every PostgreSQL instance, as `duckdb`. The console reads the file lists. |
| Data files            | SeaweedFS, under `s3://<bucket>/ducklake/<schema>/`.                      | The sync workers.                           | `pg_duckdb`. The notebooks read them through signed links.                               |
| `pg_duckdb`           | An extension inside every PostgreSQL instance.                            | The image installs it.                      | The table functions of PostgREST views.                                                  |
| DuckDB in the workers | The sync worker process, with the DuckLake extension.                     | None.                                       | The publish step uses it to commit snapshots.                                            |
| DuckDB secrets        | The shared volume `<release>-duckdb`, in `/duckdb/secrets`.               | The `configure-db` Job, on the primary.     | Every PostgreSQL instance.                                                               |
| Signer keys           | The table `signer.keys` in the `ducklake` database.                       | The console.                                | The console, to sign file links.                                                         |

See Data model for the tables.

### Kubernetes

The chart deploys one CloudNativePG (CNPG) cluster with a primary and at least one standby, one PgDog workload, one PostgREST workload and one proxy workload. See Topology.

---

Source: architecture/serving.md

## Serving layer

The serving layer answers API reads. It checks the token, uses the cache and reads only the rows that the access policy allows.

### Parts

| Part | Work |
| --- | --- |
| Istio gateway | Checks the JSON Web Token (JWT) signature, issuer and audience. |
| Proxy | Looks up the cache, sends the filter to the database, and retries a failed read. See Proxy. |
| Redis | Stores the cached answers. Redis is a cache and never a source of truth. |
| PostgREST | Switches to the database role of the token, runs `pre_request`, and reads one view for each table. |
| PgDog | Pools the connections and routes each transaction. See What PgDog does. |
| PostgreSQL standby | Runs the table views and the `SECURITY DEFINER` functions. |
| `pg_duckdb` | Runs DuckDB inside PostgreSQL. It reads the DuckLake catalog and the Parquet files. |

### Request sequence

The diagram shows one API read, from the JWT check at the gateway to the cached answer. It covers the cache, the role switch, the row-level security checks, the DuckLake scan and the fallback to the source.

```mermaid
%% API read sequence
sequenceDiagram
  participant c as Client
  participant gw as Istio gateway
  participant n as Proxy
  participant r as Redis
  participant api as PostgREST
  participant db as PostgreSQL standby
  participant s3 as SeaweedFS
  participant src as Source
  c->>gw: GET with Bearer JWT
  gw->>gw: check the JWT
  alt JWT not valid
    gw-->>c: 401
  else JWT valid
    gw->>n: forward the request
    n->>r: look up the cache key
    alt cache hit
      r-->>n: cached answer
      n-->>c: response (HIT)
    else cache miss
      n->>api: forward the JWT
      api->>api: switch to the role
      api->>db: read-only transaction (PgDog)
      db->>db: pre_request, checks
      alt not allowed
        db-->>c: 403
      else no policy match
        db-->>api: empty list
      else allowed
        db->>s3: scan Parquet (RLS)
        s3-->>db: rows
        opt fallback
          db->>src: read other partitions
          src-->>db: rows
        end
        db-->>api: rows
      end
      api-->>n: rows, X-Source
      n->>r: store if not empty
      n-->>c: response (MISS)
    end
  end
```

The table view calls a function that checks the access policy. The function plans DuckLake and the optional partition fallback from `data_proxy.state`, and it reads them in order. It passes the access policy predicate to DuckDB, so the Parquet scan returns only authorized rows. PostgREST filters aren't pushed into DuckDB. PostgreSQL applies them after the function returns the authorized rows.

An aggregate select is the exception: the proxy calls the aggregate function of the table, and DuckDB runs the `GROUP BY`. See Query pushdown.

### What PgDog does

PgDog is a connection pooler between PostgREST and PostgreSQL. It runs `pgdog.replicas` pods (two by default) and has no scaler.

| Traffic | Goes to | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A read-only transaction (each `GET`) | A standby, through the `-ro` Service | Reads spread over the standbys. |
| Any other transaction (a write or a function call) | The primary, through the `-rw` Service | Only the primary accepts writes. |
| The `LISTEN` connection of PostgREST | The primary | PgDog never gives a read/write session, so PostgREST connects to the `-rw` Service itself. |
| A read while no standby can serve | The primary | The read still succeeds. |

PgDog pools transactions, so many PostgREST connections share a few PostgreSQL backends. The pool uses the `serving` login. PgDog reads the log position of each standby and sends no read to a standby that's more than 16 MiB behind. CNPG removes the same standby from the `-ro` Service. See Topology for the failure behavior.

### DuckLake read path

Each PostgreSQL schema has one DuckLake catalog. The catalog is a metadata schema with the same name, in the `ducklake` database of the CNPG cluster. Two roles use the database:

| Role | Used by | Access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ops` | The sync workers, through the `-rw` Service. | Owns the database and creates the metadata schemas. |
| `duckdb` | `pg_duckdb` in every PostgreSQL instance. | Reads every metadata schema. Can't write. |

A catalog reaches the readers in this order:

1. The writer (a sync worker) commits a snapshot to the primary.
2. CNPG streaming replication copies the catalog to every standby.
3. A `pg_duckdb` backend attaches the catalog of its own instance through `localhost`.

A backend that attached earlier sees a new snapshot at the start of its next query. Nothing refreshes the readers, and nothing restarts PgDog.

The DuckDB secrets `ducklake_catalog_pg` (the PostgreSQL login of the catalog) and `ducklake_catalog` (the catalog itself) contain the address and the credentials. The `configure-db` Job writes them as persistent secrets to the shared volume. The same Job sets default privileges, so `duckdb` can read every metadata schema that `ops` creates later.

The writer writes the Parquet files before it commits the snapshot, so a catalog never points at a missing file. A standby can be a few seconds behind the primary. Snapshot expiration keeps the files that an older snapshot uses. See Sync layer.

---

Source: architecture/sync.md

## Sync layer

The sync layer copies the tables of the source into DuckLake. It also keeps the PostgreSQL views, the cache and the proxy settings in step with the data. The layer is a set of DBOS workflows. Sync describes its configuration.

### Workflows

Each row of the table names one workflow or step, its work and its result.

| Component | Work | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `run_sync` | Plans changed tables and partitions. | Enqueues dump and publish workflows. |
| `dump_task` | Extracts source data. | Writes independent scratch Parquet files. |
| `seed_schemas` | Reconciles the PostgreSQL functions and views of every table in a planned schema, and rebuilds the tables whose stored signature changed. | Returns whether the view set changed. |
| `reconcile_idle_schemas` | Reconciles the PostgreSQL functions and views of the scope when the plan has no change. | Returns whether the view set changed. |
| `publish_schema` | Inserts scratch Parquet into the schema catalog. | The commit creates a snapshot that every instance sees after replication. |
| `apply_ducklake_maintenance` | Runs inside `publish_schema` after a publication. | Expires old snapshots, merges files, and removes old and orphaned Parquet files. |
| `finalize_run` | Clears the scratch objects and the cache. | Keeps the DuckLake data prefix intact. |

A run without a data change still reconciles the views of its scope. Each view stores the signature of its generated definition, so the step rebuilds only a table whose definition changed. This is how a new release reaches a table that didn't change. A run that dumps some tables does the same for every table of its planned schemas, so one run applies a release. The step reads the column types of each table from the source, so each run costs one lookup for each table of the schema. It doesn't dump, publish or clear the cache.

Seed and publish run concurrently. When a view is added or removed, the workflow tells PostgREST to reload its schema after every publisher finishes. The database first waits until every standby replayed the change. A new snapshot alone reloads nothing.

### Run log

Each workflow writes its log lines to a DBOS stream, and the console shows the lines of every workflow of a run in one list. A line carries the schema and the table of its workflow, so the console filters by table.

A dump task writes these lines:

| Line | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `Dump started` | `task_id` |
| `Extraction started` | `task_id`, `paths` |
| `Source described` | `task_id`, `columns` |
| `Partition written` | `task_id`, `path`, `partition_number`, `partition_count`, `rows`, `bytes`, `seconds` |
| `Extraction attempt failed` | `task_id`, `error`. It's a warning, and each retry of the step writes one. |
| `Extraction completed`, `Dump completed` | `task_id`, and `status` for the second line. |

A publish writes `Publish started`, `DuckLake commit started`, one `Table published` for each table and `DuckLake commit completed` with `published_tables`, `failed_paths` and `snapshot_id`.

### Scaling and access

KEDA reads the length of the DBOS queues in the application database and scales the sync workers. The sync ServiceAccount can read pods and CronJobs, and it can create and watch Jobs, in its namespace. When the Swagger UI is on, it can also read and patch one ConfigMap, the schema list of that page. It has no other rights. The workflow recovery needs the pod list, the provision step needs the CronJob and the Jobs, and the step `publish_swagger_schemas` needs the ConfigMap.

### Release and recovery

The chart keeps `DBOS_APPLICATION_VERSION` (`sync.dbos.applicationVersion`) at `0.1.0` for every release. The recovery Deployment then lets any new pod continue the workflows of a dead pod. A new release replays the saved steps of a workflow that was running. Drain the queues before a release that adds, removes or reorders steps of a workflow, or change `sync.dbos.applicationVersion` for that release. A new version leaves the queued workflows of the old version to the old pods.

### Sync sequence

The diagram shows one sync run, from the start to the cleanup. It covers provisioning, planning, the dump tasks, the views, publication and the reload of PostgREST.

```mermaid
%% Sync run sequence
sequenceDiagram
  participant t as Trigger
  participant run as run_sync
  participant prov as Provision Job
  participant pg as PostgreSQL
  participant wk as Workers
  participant src as Source
  participant s3 as SeaweedFS
  participant api as PostgREST
  participant r as Redis
  t->>run: start a run
  run->>prov: run Job, wait
  run->>pg: read configuration
  run->>src: plan changed tables
  run->>wk: enqueue dump tasks
  par dump tasks
    wk->>src: extract rows
  and
    wk->>s3: write scratch Parquet
  end
  wk-->>run: results
  run->>pg: record scope
  run->>pg: seed views, functions
  run->>wk: enqueue publish tasks
  rect rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.15)
    Note over t,r: For each schema (in parallel)
    wk->>s3: read scratch, write data
    wk->>pg: commit snapshot
    wk->>pg: commit table state
    wk->>pg: maintenance
    pg->>pg: replicate to standbys
  end
  opt views changed
    run->>pg: wait for standbys
    pg-->>api: NOTIFY: reload
  end
  run->>s3: remove scratch objects
  run->>r: count up the cache generation of each schema
```

### DuckLake write path

A publish worker commits one schema at a time. It uses DuckDB with the DuckLake extension.

```mermaid
%% DuckLake publication sequence
sequenceDiagram
  participant wk as Publish worker
  participant dd as DuckDB (ducklake)
  participant s3 as SeaweedFS
  participant cat as ducklake database
  participant app as Application database
  participant sb as Standby
  rect rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.15)
    Note over wk,sb: Commit the snapshot
    wk->>dd: attach the catalog
    dd->>cat: read the metadata
    wk->>dd: create tables, set partitions and sort
    dd->>s3: read scratch Parquet
    dd->>s3: write DuckLake data files
    dd->>cat: commit one snapshot
  end
  rect rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.15)
    Note over wk,sb: Record the state
    wk->>app: write data_proxy.state
  end
  rect rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.15)
    Note over wk,sb: Reach the readers
    cat->>sb: WAL replication
    sb->>sb: next query sees the snapshot
  end
  opt a snapshot was committed
    wk->>dd: run maintenance
    dd->>cat: expire snapshots
    dd->>s3: merge files, remove old files
  end
```

- **One writer for each schema:** publishing is parallel across schemas and sequential within each schema. One `publish` queue serves all schemas, and the schema name is its partition key. A new schema needs no new queue.
- **Files first:** the writer writes the Parquet files before it commits the snapshot.
- **State after each table:** the writer saves the signature of a table right after the commit of that table. A failed publish keeps the tables that committed, and the next run skips them.
- **Retry:** a commit retries while the catalog is locked. `DUCKLAKE_COMMIT_MAX_ATTEMPTS` and `DUCKLAKE_COMMIT_RETRY_SECONDS` set the limit.
- **Maintenance:** it runs only after a commit made a snapshot. A maintenance error is logged and doesn't stop the sync run.
- **Retention:** `DUCKLAKE_SNAPSHOT_EXPIRATION` (7 days by default) keeps the files that an older snapshot uses. The CNPG backups cover the catalogs.

See DuckLake read path for how a catalog reaches the readers.

---

Source: architecture/console.md

## Console layer

The console shows the system to people and changes its configuration. It's a web app with a database as its API. The browser never calls PostgREST, and the SvelteKit server calls it with the token of the user.

### Parts

| Part | Work |
| --- | --- |
| Console server | Signs people in, keeps the session, and calls PostgREST. It also signs the file links of the query tab. |
| Notebook site | A static site on its own origin. It runs the notebook of the query tab in the browser. |
| Identity provider | Signs people in and issues the tokens. |
| PostgREST | Serves the `console` schema as an API. |
| `console` schema | The views, the functions and the configuration tables. The database checks every permission. |
| Sync worker | Takes the workflows that the console queues. A worker that listens to the `control` queue runs the control actions. |
| `ducklake` database | The console reads the file lists, and it stores the sealed storage secrets in `signer.keys`. |
| SeaweedFS | Stores the Parquet files. The console creates one storage identity for each schema. |

### Requests

The diagram shows how the console loads a page, starts a sync run and edits the configuration. Application shows the sign-in, and Query tab shows the query tab.

```mermaid
%% Console requests
sequenceDiagram
  participant u as Browser
  participant app as Console server
  participant api as PostgREST
  participant db as PostgreSQL
  participant w as Sync worker
  rect rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.15)
    Note over u,w: Load a page
    u->>app: GET /sync
    app->>api: views, with the user token
    api->>db: switch role, check rights
    db-->>api: rows
    api-->>app: rows
    app-->>u: page
  end
  rect rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.15)
    Note over u,w: Start a run
    u->>app: press Start run
    app->>api: POST /rpc/start_sync
    api->>db: enqueue run_sync
    w->>db: take the run
  end
  rect rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.15)
    Note over u,w: Edit the configuration
    u->>app: save a change
    app->>api: write a row
    api->>db: check schemas, run triggers
    w->>db: take queued workflows
  end
```

See Console for the pages of the app and its database views.

### Run control

A console user can cancel a sync run. The same path serves resume and the schedule actions. The console never changes a workflow itself. The database function checks the permission, the schemas and the status, and then it queues a workflow in the `control` queue. A sync worker runs that workflow with the DBOS API.

```mermaid
%% Run control sequence
sequenceDiagram
  participant u as Console user
  participant app as Console server
  participant api as PostgREST
  participant db as PostgreSQL
  participant w as Sync worker (control queue)
  u->>app: cancel a sync run
  app->>api: POST /rpc/cancel_run
  api->>db: check permission, scope and status
  alt refused
    db-->>api: 403, 404 or 409
  else allowed
    db->>db: enqueue cancel_run in control
    db-->>api: done
  end
  api-->>app: answer
  app-->>u: page
  w->>db: take the workflow
  w->>db: cancel the run and its tasks
```

See Control a run and a schedule for the allowed statuses and the error codes.

---

Source: sync.md

## Sync

This page is the reference for the sync configuration. The sync configuration is a JSON document that declares PostgreSQL schemas, their ingestion sources and source tables. The field `source.type` names the source adapter, and `bigquery` is the only adapter today. Each sync run loads the document once, at its start, so a change never reaches a sync run that already started.

The tables of the `console` schema contain the configuration (Console), and the engine reads it with `console.sync_config()`. An empty configuration means there is nothing to sync.

```json
{
  "schemas": {
    "my_schema": {
      "source": { "type": "bigquery" },
      "claim": "preferred_username",
      "ducklake": { "encrypted": false },
      "tables": [
        {
          "name": "project.dataset.events",
          "strategy": "partitioned",
          "n": 7,
          "ducklake": { "sort": ["event_time", "unit_id"] },
          "rls": [{ "column": "unit_id", "unit_type": "unit" }]
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

### Schema fields

| Field      | Required                | Meaning                                                                                   |
| ---------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `source`   | No                      | One external source for every table in this schema. Defaults to `{ "type": "bigquery" }`. |
| `claim`    | When a table uses `rls` | JSON Web Token (JWT) claim matched against `access_policy.subject`.                       |
| `tables`   | No                      | Tables in this PostgreSQL schema. Defaults to `[]`.                                       |
| `ducklake` | No                      | Schema-level DuckLake settings, including `encrypted`.                                    |

The schema key is the target PostgreSQL schema. Don't add a schema field to a table entry.

The console exports and imports the same document grouped by project, and the schema key is then the short name. The import also reads the form above, and puts those schemas in the project `default`.

```json
{ "projects": { "sales": { "schemas": { "orders": { "tables": [] } } } } }
```

This document makes the schema `sales_orders`. The engine reads `sync_config()`, which lists each schema by its physical name.

### Table fields

These fields describe one table of a schema in `sync.json`. The table says which fields are required.

| Field       | Required         | Meaning                                                                                                    |
| ----------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`      | Yes              | Reference validated by the schema source. BigQuery uses `project.dataset.table`.                           |
| `strategy`  | Yes              | `full` replaces the DuckLake table, and `partitioned` updates physical partitions.                         |
| `n`         | No               | Keep the newest `n` time partitions.                                                                       |
| `fallback`  | Partitioned only | Allow the configured source to serve uncovered partitions when it has fallback metadata. Default: `false`. |
| `cache_ttl` | No               | Proxy cache lifetime in seconds.                                                                           |
| `rls`       | No               | Unit column and unit type pairs. See Security.                                        |
| `ducklake`  | No               | Table-level DuckLake settings, including `sort` and `partitioning`.                                        |
| `ducklake`  | No               | Table-level DuckLake settings, including custom partition transforms.                                      |

### Pipeline

The scheduled `run_sync` workflow plans the changed tables and partitions, dumps them as scratch Parquet files and publishes each schema to its DuckLake catalog. Publishing runs in parallel across schemas and in sequence within a schema, so each catalog has one writer. After a publication, the workflow expires old snapshots, merges and rewrites files and cleans orphaned files. A maintenance error is logged and doesn't stop the sync run. Sync layer lists the workflows and shows the sequence.

### DuckLake partitioning and encryption

DuckLake partitioning follows the source partition column by default only for a time partitioned source. An integer range source gives the table no partitioning. The column can have a different value in every row, and DuckLake makes one partition for each value. A table can set its own partitioning with transforms such as:

```json
"ducklake": {
  "partitioning": [
    { "column": "event_time", "transform": "month" },
    { "column": "unit_id", "transform": "bucket", "buckets": 16 }
  ]
}
```

An integer range table of a few gigabytes needs no partition key, because the batches of a run are contiguous key ranges. Set a `bucket` transform only for a table with hundreds of files. Never use `identity` on a column with a different value in each row. See the measured layouts.

Changing a table transform triggers a full table rewrite before the writer publishes the new layout. Configure encryption only under the schema-level `ducklake.encrypted` setting. The engine rejects table-level encryption, because DuckLake encryption is catalog scoped.

### Schema evolution

Before publication, the writer compares each incoming Parquet schema with the existing DuckLake table. It adds new nullable columns and applies only lossless type promotions.

It rejects removed columns, renames and incompatible type changes before changing the table. Inserts use column names, not column positions. Existing Parquet files aren't rewritten for these schema changes.

### Catalog lifecycle

The sync workers write the catalog as `ops` through the primary, and every PostgreSQL pod reads it as `duckdb` from its own instance. The Parquet files are at `s3://<bucket>/ducklake/<schema>/<table>/`. See Serving layer.

### Partition fallback

Set `fallback: true` on a partitioned table to let its configured schema source serve data that DuckLake doesn't store. For a BigQuery schema, the table function reads published partitions from DuckLake and every other partition from BigQuery.

```json
{
  "name": "project.dataset.events",
  "strategy": "partitioned",
  "fallback": true
}
```

`fallback` is invalid on full tables. It's also invalid when the configured source has no fallback metadata. Without it, the table function reads DuckLake only. See Proxy.

### Adding a source

A source is responsible for synchronization ingestion. It validates references, creates DuckDB scan expressions, reports modification and partition state, caches external clients and declares DuckDB extensions.

Register the source in `sync/src/sync/sources/registry.py`.

Each PostgreSQL schema has exactly one source. Add `source.settings` only when a source requires non-secret settings. Put credentials in environment variables or Kubernetes Secrets, not in `sync.json`.

DuckLake is the fixed local primary source. The configured schema source is the only possible partition fallback.

### Partitions

A `full` table creates one dump task. A partitioned table creates one extraction task for each batch of contiguous changed partitions. Each batch writes one Parquet file. See Dump batches.

| Source type       | `n`       | `__NULL__`                        |
| ----------------- | --------- | --------------------------------- |
| Time partitioned  | Supported | Ignored                           |
| Range partitioned | Rejected  | Synced as the remainder partition |

`__UNPARTITIONED__` is unsupported and stops planning.

### Schema initialization

The provision job creates configured schemas, `access_policy`, `access_log`, row policies and triggers. It doesn't create application data tables in PostgreSQL. The sync workflow creates the views.

Application table names are PostgreSQL views over DuckLake functions.

---

---

Source: using.md

## Using the API

Data Proxy exposes synced tables through [PostgREST](https://docs.postgrest.org/). Use a JSON Web Token (JWT) and select the target schema with `Accept-Profile`.

```bash
curl \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}" \
  --header "Accept-Profile: my_schema" \
  "${BASE_URL}/participants?select=region_id,name&limit=20"
```

### Request routing

The proxy sends every request to the `postgrest` Deployment, which connects through PgDog. PgDog sends a `GET` to a standby and every write to the primary. See Topology.

Sync tells PostgREST to reload its schema once when generated serving PostgreSQL objects change. The database waits until every standby replayed the change, then sends a `NOTIFY` on the `pgrst` channel. No pod restarts. The workflow requires its sync metric checkpoints. A failure to record a metric fails the related workflow, so operators never treat an unobserved run as successful.

### OpenAPI

When `swaggerUi.enabled` is true, the OpenAPI page is available at:

```text
${BASE_URL}/docs
```

The page can list table and column names without exposing data. Use its Authorize control with the token value only. The page adds `Bearer `.

The schema selector lists the schemas of the console. A sync worker updates the list after each schema change and at the start of every sync run. Reload the page to see the change, which takes about a minute.

### Querying

| Need           | Example                                     |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Columns        | `?select=id,name`                           |
| Equality       | `?id=eq.1`                                  |
| Range          | `?updated_at=gte.2025-01-01`                |
| List           | `?id=in.(1,2,3)`                            |
| Order and page | `?order=updated_at.desc&limit=20&offset=40` |

Combine filters with `&`. PostgREST applies them with AND. row-level security (RLS) filters rows in the DuckDB scan. The proxy also pushes the filters, the selected columns and the `limit` into the scan, so they reduce the data that DuckDB reads. See Query pushdown.

A `select` with `sum()`, `avg()`, `count()`, `min()` or `max()` and a group runs inside DuckDB, so it stays fast on large tables. See Query pushdown.

Use `Prefer: count=exact` to request a total. Read the total from `Content-Range`. A count reads every row, so the proxy doesn't push the `limit` for it.

### DuckLake change feed

Each configured table exposes a read-only RPC named `dl_changes_<table>` in its target schema. PostgreSQL cuts a name at 63 bytes, so the RPC of a table with a very long name has the cut name. It accepts `start_snapshot` and an optional `end_snapshot` and returns the DuckLake change type, snapshot ID, row ID and typed row columns.

```bash
curl \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}" \
  --header "Accept-Profile: my_schema" \
  --get "${BASE_URL}/rpc/dl_changes_participants" \
  --data-urlencode "start_snapshot=12" \
  --data-urlencode "end_snapshot=15"
```

Use the schema RPC `dl_latest_snapshot` to get the current cursor before or after reading a range:

```bash
curl \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}" \
  --header "Accept-Profile: my_schema" \
  --request POST \
  "${BASE_URL}/rpc/dl_latest_snapshot"
```

Snapshot bounds are inclusive. The feed returns deleted rows as preimages. The same schema scope and row policy apply to change rows, including deleted preimages. DuckLake keeps the snapshot history for seven days, so consumers must advance their cursor within that window. Compaction preserves change history, but snapshot expiration removes history that references expired snapshots.

### Response source and cache

Read responses include:

| Header                | Values                                           |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `X-Source`            | `ducklake`, `<adapter>`, `ducklake+<adapter>`    |
| `X-DuckLake-Snapshot` | The DuckLake snapshot the response was read from |
| `X-Cache`             | `HIT`, `MISS`                                    |

`X-Source` lists the sources the request queried, not the sources that returned rows. `<adapter>` is the name of the source adapter, such as `bigquery`. A response that access control stopped has neither `X-Source` nor `X-DuckLake-Snapshot`. `X-DuckLake-Snapshot` is absent when only the source was queried. Rows from the source are always current, so they carry no snapshot.

A cache hit returns the headers of the answer it stored. Use `X-Cache` to tell a hit from a miss.

The proxy compresses a JSON answer with gzip when the request has `Accept-Encoding: gzip`. Browsers and the usual HTTP libraries send this header and decode the answer without a setting. A client that doesn't send it, such as `curl` without `--compressed`, gets the plain body. A partial answer with the status `206` isn't compressed.

#### Pin a snapshot

Send `X-DuckLake-Snapshot` to read DuckLake as of one snapshot. A pinned request reads DuckLake only and never the source:

```bash
curl \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}" \
  --header "Accept-Profile: my_schema" \
  --header "X-DuckLake-Snapshot: 42" \
  "${BASE_URL}/my_table?limit=20"
```

An unknown or expired snapshot returns `404`, and a value that's not a whole number returns `400`. DuckLake keeps the snapshot history for seven days. A table that has no published data and no fallback also returns `404`.

Use these headers for troubleshooting, not authorization.

See Security for token and access-policy setup.

---

### Try it locally

Add this entry to `/etc/hosts`, forward the gateway port and ask Keycloak for a token:

```text
127.0.0.1 data-proxy.local
```

```bash
kubectl -n istio-ingress port-forward svc/istio-ingressgateway 3111:80
token
```

`token` prints a table with the token, its type, lifetime, scope, client and realm. In Nushell, `token | get token` gives only the token. Without options, it asks the Keycloak of the local cluster for a `user` token. Use `--issuer` to ask another realm:

```bash
token --issuer https://sso.example.com/realms/prod --client-id my-client --client-secret "$SECRET"
token --issuer https://sso.example.com/realms/prod --client-id my-client --username alice --password "$PASSWORD"
```

The client secret can also come from `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET`. `--username` and `--password` switch to the password grant, and `--scope` adds scopes.

---

Source: proxy/index.md

## Proxy

The proxy stands before PostgREST in the request path. It forwards requests and caches read responses. It doesn't choose where data comes from: PostgreSQL decides that for every request.

The chart deploys the proxy as OpenResty and connects directly to Redis. Configure it under `proxy` in Helm Chart.

### Request flow

The proxy checks Redis first, calls PostgREST on a miss and stores the answer. Request sequence shows the whole read, step by step.

### Choosing the source

The table view calls one function that applies these rules in order:

1. PostgreSQL reads a request that pins a snapshot from DuckLake only.
2. A partitioned table that's not in `data_proxy.state` reads its configured source when `fallback` is true. Without fallback, the request receives a `404`.
3. A table in `data_proxy.state` reads DuckLake. A partitioned table with `fallback: true` also reads uncovered partitions from its configured source.

Row-level security runs first. A request that RLS stops reads no source and gets an empty list without `X-Source`.

An empty DuckLake result never triggers fallback. With `fallback: true`, every request also reads the configured source for partitions that DuckLake doesn't store, because PostgREST applies filters after the function returns. Keep fallback disabled when that cost isn't acceptable.

### Settings

The Helm Deployment sets the proxy settings as `PROXY_*` environment variables. See Environment Variables for each variable, its default and its meaning.

`helm/files/config/nginx.conf` lists every variable with an `env` directive, because nginx removes the other variables.

Lua code reads settings only through the table that `config.load` returns:

- `main` loads the table once at start-up, in `init_by_lua`, and passes it down.
- The load collects the text of every variable in one table. It converts and checks that table once with the `config` schema, which also sets the defaults.
- A missing required variable, a value of the wrong type or a value outside the limits stops nginx from starting. The error names the setting.
- The variable is `PROXY_` and the upper-case name of the setting.

`sync.json` sets only the cache time of each table and the paths that are never cached. The proxy checks it with a schema when it starts. The proxy checks other data that it doesn't create in the same way. This data is the entries that it reads from Redis and the claims of a bearer token.

The schema code works like this:

- The `Schema` class is in `proxy/src/proxy/schemas/schema.lua`.
- The registry is `proxy/src/proxy/schemas/main.lua` (`schemas:register(name, fields)`). When the registry module loads at start-up, it registers every file `proxy/src/proxy/schemas/definitions/<name>.lua` as the schema `<name>`.
- A definition file declares only the fields.
- Code checks data with `schemas.<name>:validate(value)`.

### Pages

- Query pushdown — what the proxy sends to PostgreSQL besides the filter.
- Cache — what the proxy stores, the cache key and the lock.
- Retries and limits — retries of a read, the load limit and the time limits.
- Table settings — how the proxy takes the table settings from the configuration.

---

Source: proxy/pushdown.md

## Query pushdown

The proxy forwards what it reads from a query to PostgreSQL, in the `X-DuckLake-Filter` header. The table view can then read less data from the sources. The parser reads comparisons and the `and`, `or` and `not` groups, and it decodes the escapes. The grammar is LPeg, in `proxy/src/proxy/parser/patterns.lua`.

| Part                | What the table view does with it                                                                                 |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `where`             | Filters the rows before it reads the sources.                                                                    |
| `columns`           | Reads only the selected columns, the order columns, and the filter columns. The other columns come back as null. |
| `limit` and `order` | Stops after the first rows. The limit includes the `offset`.                                                     |

PostgREST still applies `select`, `order`, `limit`, `offset`, embeds and content negotiation to the rows that the table view returns. A pushed part only makes that set smaller, so the answer stays the same.

The proxy sends `columns` and `limit` only when it reads every parameter of the query. A parameter that it can't read, such as a filter that its grammar doesn't accept, stops both. A `select` with an alias, a cast or an embed stops them too. A `select` with aggregates sends `columns` and never `limit`, as the next section shows. The proxy also drops `limit` for a request that needs every row:

- A request with `Prefer: count=...` or a `Range` header. The counts section shows the exception.
- A request for a single object or another media type of PostgREST.
- A `HEAD` request.

The table view pushes `order` with the limit only when every order column is a whole number, a date or a true or false value. DuckDB sorts text by bytes, and PostgreSQL sorts it by the collation, so a limit on a text order could return other rows. Columns of other types reach PostgreSQL as text, and the same rule applies to them.

A request that selects all columns of a wide table still reads all of them.

```mermaid
%% Pushdown decision
flowchart TD
  request["GET request"] --> read{"Does the proxy read<br/>every parameter?"}
  read -->|"no"| postgrest["PostgREST answers<br/>the original request"]
  read -->|"yes"| agg{"Does the select have<br/>aggregates?"}
  agg -->|"no"| table
  agg -->|"yes"| supported{"Group, functions and order<br/>are supported?"}
  supported -->|"no"| postgrest
  supported -->|"yes"| agg_call["Call table_aggregate<br/>DuckDB groups the rows"]
  agg_call --> empty{"Answer null, error<br/>or a fallback source?"}
  empty -->|"yes"| postgrest
  empty -->|"no"| answer["Send the answer<br/>and cache it"]
  subgraph table["Read the table view"]
    where["where: filter the rows"]
    columns["columns: read fewer columns"]
    limit["limit and order: stop early<br/>only for a plain read and<br/>simple order columns"]
  end
  table --> answer
  postgrest --> answer
```

### Aggregates

A `select` with aggregates, for example `select=grp,numerador:qty.sum(),total:count()`, runs in DuckDB.

1. The proxy puts the group and the aggregates in the `aggregate` field of `X-DuckLake-Filter`.
2. It calls `GET /rpc/<table>_aggregate` with the same headers and no query string.
3. The function applies the row policy and the filter, runs the `GROUP BY` in DuckDB and returns the result rows as JSON.
4. PostgreSQL orders and cuts the rows of the groups.

| Part of the select                                       | Supported                                                                                          |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Plain columns, with or without an alias (`alias:column`) | They form the group. Text, whole-number, date and true-or-false columns only.                      |
| `sum()` and `avg()` of a column                          | A numeric column, which includes decimal and floating point columns.                               |
| `min()` and `max()` of a column                          | A numeric column or a date column.                                                                 |
| `count()` and `column.count()`                           | Any column that doesn't contain JSON.                                                              |
| `order`                                                  | Columns of the group, by the name of the column, with `asc`, `desc`, `nullsfirst` and `nullslast`. |
| `limit` and `offset`                                     | Yes. They apply to the rows of the groups, after the order.                                        |

The proxy sends the original request to PostgREST in these cases:

- The `order` names an aggregate, an alias or a column outside the group.
- The group has a decimal, floating point, timestamp or JSON column.
- The select has a function other than `sum`, `avg`, `count`, `min` and `max`, a cast, an embed, a star or two values with one name.
- The request has `Prefer: count=...` or a `Range` header, asks for another media type than JSON, is a `HEAD` or isn't a read.
- The function answers `null`, doesn't exist or fails. It answers `null` when a fallback source serves a part of the table. It also answers `null` for an unsupported column type.

The proxy never sends `order` or `limit` in the filter of an aggregate.

The function gives at most `postgrest.maxRows` rows. With more rows it gives the first rows with the status `206` and `Content-Range: <first>-<last>/*`. A request with a `limit` below the cap gets exactly that many rows and no `206`. The proxy sends the `206` unchanged and doesn't store it.

A complete answer has no `Content-Range` header. It has the same `X-Source` and `X-DuckLake-Snapshot` headers as the table, and the cache stores it under the key of the original request.

### Counts

A `GET` of a table with `Prefer: count=exact` and a `limit` counts in DuckDB. The proxy calls `<table>_aggregate` with the filter and `count()`. Then it reads the page with the `limit`, pinned to the snapshot of the count. It builds `Content-Range` and `Preference-Applied`, and sends `206` unless the page has every row. Other counts, `Range`, `HEAD`, an empty page and a table with a fallback source go to PostgREST, which counts every row.

---

Source: proxy/cache.md

## Cache

This page explains what the proxy caches and how it builds the cache key. A token with another role never reads an answer that another token cached.

- The proxy stores only non-empty `GET` answers with status 200. An empty answer can mean three things: access was denied, the data isn't published yet or the access policy changed. The proxy never stores it.
- An entry stores the body with `X-Source` and `X-DuckLake-Snapshot`, so a cache hit reports what produced the answer. `X-Cache` tells a hit from a miss.
- OpenResty doesn't cache ranged, write, oversized or non-JSON responses. `/access_policy` and its subpaths are never cached. The OpenAPI document at `/` isn't cached either, because it changes when PostgREST reloads the schema after a sync run.
- The proxy reads and writes the cache through one Redis endpoint.
- After a sync run, the sync service counts up the data generation of each schema that the run planned. The answers of the other schemas stay in the cache.
- The key has the parts in the table below, and the table also has the three counters that keep the cache current.
- When an entry is missing, only one request for that key asks PostgREST. The lock section shows how.

### The cache key

| Key part | Why it's in the key |
| --- | --- |
| Method, path and query | They name the request. |
| Schema profile and representation headers | The same path can answer in another schema or format. |
| The pinned snapshot (`X-DuckLake-Snapshot`) | A pinned read must not share an entry with the latest data. |
| The scope of the user, or the user, then the schemas and the role | A token with another identity never reads an answer that another token cached. Users with the same grants have the same scope and share their answers. |
| The access policy generation | A write to `/access_policy` through the proxy raises this counter in Redis. |
| The data generation of the schema | The sync service counts it up after a run that planned the schema. The proxy reads the counter of the `Accept-Profile` schema, so a run of one schema doesn't empty the cache of another. A request without a profile reads the counter of the empty name, which every run also counts up. |
| The settings revision | `console.config()` contains it in its document. Any other change of the access policy or the rules moves `rbac.revision`. |

A trigger on `rbac.revision` queues a `reload_proxy` workflow. The sync worker asks every proxy pod to read the settings. A proxy that takes a new document stops serving the old answers immediately. Examples of such a change are a write to the access policy from the console, and a new `rbac.toml` that `configure-db` loads.

Redis keeps the counters as `policy:generation` and `cache:generation:<schema>`. The proxy reads both in one `MGET`. Upgrade the proxy before the sync workers. An older proxy ignores the data generation. It can show an answer that a run changed until the entry expires. The old keys and the new keys never meet, because the key has one more part.

### The scope

The document of `console.config()` lists a scope for each subject of the access policies. The scope is the MD5 digest of the grants of the subject in every schema: the schema, the unit type and the unit id, sorted. Two subjects with the same grants have the same scope, so the proxy puts `scope:<digest>` in the key and they share the answers. A subject that the document doesn't list gets `sub:<user>`, so the key is its own. A user name that looks like a digest never reads the entries of a scope, because of the prefixes.

The document has no scopes if a schema reads its rows by another claim than `preferred_username`, because the proxy names a subject by that claim. A change of one grant moves `rbac.revision`, so the next document has new scopes and every answer has a new key. The document grows with the number of subjects, about 60 bytes for each, and the shared dictionary `proxy_settings` has 4 MB for it.

The revision comes from the document, not from Redis. A flush of the cache, a restart of the proxy and a new proxy pod all leave it right. The proxy finds a change that happened while no proxy ran when it reads the document.

### The lock

Without a lock, a slow entry that expires sends every request for it to PostgREST at the same time. A table that reads the source is an example. The requests fill the connections of PostgREST and the limit of `proxy.maxInflight`, and the proxy then answers 503 for every route.

The proxy calls the first request for a key the leader. The other requests for the same key are followers, and they wait for the leader.

```mermaid
%% Cache lock sequence
sequenceDiagram
  participant a as Request A
  participant b as Request B (same key)
  participant n as Proxy
  participant r as Redis
  participant pr as PostgREST
  a->>n: GET
  n->>n: build the key
  n->>r: look up the key
  r-->>n: miss
  n->>n: A takes the lock
  b->>n: GET
  n->>r: look up the key
  r-->>n: miss
  n->>n: B waits (up to 30 s)
  n->>pr: A asks PostgREST
  pr-->>n: answer
  alt 200 and not empty
    n->>r: store the entry
    n->>n: A frees the lock
    n->>r: B reads the entry
    r-->>n: entry
  else nothing stored, or B timed out
    n->>pr: B asks PostgREST itself
  end
  n-->>a: answer
  n-->>b: answer
```

- A follower waits up to 30 seconds and reads the entry that the leader stored.
- The lock is `resty.lock`, which OpenResty ships, in the shared dictionary `proxy_locks`. A leader that dies frees the key after 60 seconds.
- The wait is per proxy pod. A request that waits doesn't count against `proxy.maxInflight`.
- A follower asks PostgREST itself if the leader stored nothing (for example after an error) or if the wait times out.

See Using the API for the response headers.

---

Source: proxy/limits.md

## Retries and limits

### Retries

PostgREST fails for a few seconds when PgDog loses a standby. The proxy sends a `GET` or `HEAD` again, up to two times, when PostgREST answers `502`, `503` or `504`, or doesn't answer. The first retry waits 500 ms and the second waits 1 second.

The client gets the last answer. A write is never sent again, because a second write could change the data twice.

### Load limit

The proxy counts the requests that wait for PostgREST, in one number for all the nginx workers of a pod. When `PROXY_MAX_INFLIGHT` requests already wait, a new request receives `503` with `{"error":"Proxy overloaded"}` and `Retry-After: 1` immediately.

A cached answer never waits for PostgREST, so a full database doesn't slow it down.

Measure the limit against the database, not the proxy. One PostgreSQL pod with 8 CPU cores answered about 120 selective lookups a second, and more waiting requests only made each of them slower. Set the limit near the number of requests that the database can run immediately (16 to 24). Multiply it by a small factor for the time that a request spends outside the database. Each proxy pod counts its own requests, so the total is the limit times the number of proxy pods.

The proxy waits at most 30 seconds for PostgREST. PostgREST waits at most `postgrest.dbPoolAcquisitionTimeout` seconds (3 by default) for a free database connection before it answers with an error.

---

Source: proxy/reload.md

## Table settings

The proxy needs two parts of `sync.json`: the cache lifetime of each table (`cache_ttl`) and the paths that it never caches (`noCachePaths`).

With `PROXY_CONFIG_URL` set, it takes both from PostgREST: `GET /rpc/config` with the header `Accept-Profile: console`. The function `console.config()` builds the document from the configuration tables of the console. It contains only the table names and their `cache_ttl`. All nginx workers of a pod share one copy, and a worker parses it again only when the copy changes.

The proxy needs no credentials for this call. The chart grants the anonymous role the `EXECUTE` right on that one function, and nothing else in the `console` schema. To keep the endpoint inside the cluster, the proxy refuses every request that has the profile `console` in `Accept-Profile` or `Content-Profile`. It answers 403. The proxy calls PostgREST for the configuration on its own, so this block doesn't touch the call.

The first `sync.json` comes from the file `/config/sync.json` when the file exists. The chart doesn't mount one. Before the first answer of PostgREST, the proxy uses its defaults: the lifetime of `PROXY_CACHE_TTL` and no cache for `/access_policy`.

The proxy takes a new document in three ways:

| Way | When |
| --- | --- |
| At start | Worker 0 asks PostgREST as soon as nginx starts. |
| `POST /reload` on the admin port 8081 | The sync workers call it after every change of a configuration table. The answer is `{"changed":true}`, or `changed` is `false` when the proxy already has that document. |
| A check every `PROXY_CONFIG_REFRESH_SECONDS` | Worker 0 asks again, so a proxy that missed a call still catches up. |

The Istio policy of the proxy allows `POST /reload` on port 8081 and nothing else there. The sync workers have no sidecar, so the rule can't name them. The gateway never routes to that port, so only the cluster reaches it.

A trigger on the three configuration tables queues a `reload_proxy` workflow. A burst of edits shares one waiting reload, and a change during a reload queues the next one. The worker resolves the headless Service `<release>-proxy-admin` to the address of every proxy pod and sends the request to each one. If a pod fails, DBOS repeats the step.

A document that doesn't match the schema, or an unreachable PostgREST, changes nothing. The proxy keeps the last good settings, and `POST /reload` answers 502 with the reason. `POST /reload` answers 409 when `PROXY_CONFIG_URL` isn't set, and 405 for any other method.

The admin port has no authentication, so no ingress may route it.

---

Source: database.md

## Database Schema

This page describes the PostgreSQL schemas, the roles, the application tables and the DuckLake storage. Data model has diagrams of the tables.

CloudNativePG (CNPG) creates and maintains the core roles. Init-db installs extensions, creates the internal `data_proxy` schema, creates configured application schemas and creates access policy metadata.

### Schemas

A schema is an API that PostgREST serves, a rule that the APIs share, or private. The application database `data-proxy` contains:

| Schema | Kind | Contains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rbac` | Shared rule | The table `roles` that the `configure-db` job fills from `rbac.toml`, and the functions `load()`, `can()` and `mine()`. Every other schema calls it. PostgREST doesn't serve it. |
| `console` | API, served | The views, the functions, and the three configuration tables that the web app uses. |
| `data_proxy` | Private | The `state`, `errors`, and `scope` tables of the engine, the routing and reload functions, `sees()` (which workflows a token sees), and the maintenance procedures. |
| `dbos` | Private, owned by DBOS | The workflow tables. |
| One schema for each source schema | API, served | `access_policy`, `access_log`, and the views and functions of the synced tables. |
| `public`, `duckdb` | Defaults | The goose version table, the extensions, and the objects of `pg_duckdb`. |

A source schema has a physical name, which is `<project>_<short name>`, or the short name in the project `default`. It can't have the name `console`, `rbac`, `data_proxy`, `dbos`, `public`, `duckdb` or `information_schema`, and its name can't start with `pg_`. A check on `console.schemas` refuses these names.

The `ducklake` database contains one metadata schema for each source schema, with the same name. It's a separate database because the catalog has its own owner, `ops`, and its own read-only login, `duckdb`.

DBOS stays in the application database. The console views join `dbos.workflow_status` with `data_proxy.scope` and `data_proxy.state`, and PostgreSQL can't join across databases. `console.start_sync()` and the `reload_proxy` trigger enqueue a workflow with `dbos.enqueue_workflow()`, and the trigger does it in the same transaction as the edit. A second database in the same cluster would share the write-ahead log and the disks, so it would isolate nothing. If the workflow load ever hurts the serving layer, move DBOS to its own CNPG cluster. Then let the console read workflow state through a second API.

### Shared objects

| Object | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `postgis` | BigQuery `GEOGRAPHY` support. |
| `pg_duckdb` | Executes DuckDB scans and reads SeaweedFS Parquet. |

The function `data_proxy.pre_request()` isn't an extension. It mirrors the JSON Web Token (JWT) claims into PostgreSQL session settings.

### Application schema

Each configured schema contains metadata and views:

| Object | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `<schema>.access_policy` | Active access grants. |
| `<schema>.access_log` | Append-only audit trail of grant changes. |
| `<schema>.<table>` | PostgreSQL view over the table function. |
| `<schema>.<table>_fn()` | `SECURITY DEFINER` function that checks row-level security (RLS), plans the sources, and reads them. |
| `<schema>.<table>_aggregate()` | `SECURITY DEFINER` function that applies RLS and runs the aggregate of a request inside DuckDB. It answers `null` for a request that the table function must serve. A table with a name longer than 53 bytes has none. |
| `<schema>.<table>_dl_fn(text, text, boolean, text[], text)` | Private `SECURITY DEFINER` helper that reads DuckLake at one snapshot, with the columns and the tail that the request needs. |
| `<schema>.<table>_bq_fn(text, text)` | Private `SECURITY DEFINER` helper that reads the schema source (BigQuery today) when a partitioned table sets `fallback: true`. |

Internal functions and procedures live in the application schema (`data_proxy` by default): `request_filter`, `render_ducklake_where`, `requested_snapshot`, source routing, access-log triggers and maintenance procedures. The schema isn't in `PGRST_DB_SCHEMAS`, so these objects aren't exposed as PostgREST RPC endpoints. See Proxy.

PostgreSQL doesn't contain materialized application data tables. The table views call DuckDB, which reads the catalog of its own PostgreSQL instance and scans Parquet in SeaweedFS.

### DuckLake storage

DuckLake uses one catalog per configured schema, in the `ducklake` database of the CNPG cluster:

```text
database ducklake, schema <schema>   # DuckLake catalog metadata
s3://<bucket>/ducklake/<schema>/     # DuckLake Parquet data
```

DBOS sync workers write the catalogs as the `ops` role, through the primary. Streaming replication copies them to every standby. pg_duckdb opens the catalog of its own instance read-only, as the `duckdb` role. See Serving layer.

The catalog contains DuckLake metadata, not PostgreSQL application rows. DuckLake table configuration uses `SET PARTITIONED BY` and `SET SORTED BY` for partition and RLS-related columns.

Database roles and grants describes the roles, the security and the pushdown of the predicates and the S3 access.

---

Source: grants.md

## Database roles and grants

This page describes the PostgreSQL roles, the security of the functions, the pushdown of the predicates and the S3 access. Database Schema describes the schemas.

### Roles

| Role | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `anon` | The role of a request without a token. It has no access to application data. |
| `dp_api`, `dp_policy`, `dp_console`, `dp_admin` | One role for each role of `rbac.toml`. A token switches to the role of its `role` claim. The last three roles are members of `dp_api` and share its grants. `rbac.can()` and `rbac.mine()` decide what each role may do. |
| `serving` | The login of the serving layer (`auth.servingRole`). PostgREST, the PgDog pool and the `recovery` Deployment connect with it. It's `NOINHERIT` and a member of `anon` and of every `dp_*` role. It has no rights of its own and only switches into the request role of the token. `configure-db` creates it with the password of its Secret. No token can switch to it. |
| `ops` | The owner of both databases (`cnpg.db.user`). It's the login of every internal workload: the sync workers, the recovery deployment, the chart jobs, the backup, and the autoscaler. It's a superuser. pg_duckdb turns the local file system off for every other role, and DuckDB loads its extensions and writes its persistent secrets there. It owns the `SECURITY DEFINER` functions that run DuckDB. No token can switch to it. |
| `duckdb` | The read-only login of the catalog database. pg_duckdb uses it to read the metadata schemas. |

`configure-db` creates `anon`, the `dp_*` roles and `serving` as `ops`, so a new role in `rbac.toml` needs no chart change.

The Secret of a login has the name `<release>-cnpg-<role>`: `-cnpg-ops`, `-cnpg-serving` and `-cnpg-duckdb`. After an upgrade of an install that used the old names, the chart creates the new Secrets with new generated passwords. The old names are the Secrets `-cnpg-authenticator` and `-duckdb`, and the login `postgrest`. `configure-db` creates the `serving` login and sets its password, `provision` records `pgrst.db_schemas` on it, and the PgDog users Secret carries it. The old login, the old Secrets and the old DuckDB secret files `ducklake_reader_pg` and `ducklake_reader` stay until someone deletes them.

### Security and predicate pushdown

The PostgreSQL functions are `SECURITY DEFINER` and read `access_policy` using the request claim settings. They build the allowed-row predicate and pass it into the DuckDB SQL query. This enforces RLS before the Parquet scan returns rows.

The table function builds the access policy predicate once and passes it to each source helper. See Security.

The DuckLake helper also receives the columns and the `ORDER BY` with the `LIMIT` that the proxy pushed. It writes a null for each column that the request skips, so DuckDB doesn't read it. See Query pushdown. A sync run replaces the helper and the table function of each table with the new definitions.

### S3 access

The chart creates an S3 secret from `S3_ACCESS_KEY` and `S3_SECRET_KEY`. pg_duckdb uses the configured DuckDB S3 secret to read DuckLake Parquet.

The chart projects production GCP credentials into every CNPG instance through `gcp.existingSecret`, because BigQuery fallback queries can run on read replicas.

---

---

Source: model.md

## Data model

This page shows the tables of the system. Each diagram has every column of its tables. A line joins a column to the column that it references. The crow's foot marks the table that has the reference.

A line is a foreign key, or a link that `docs/.tbls.yaml` adds where the database has no foreign key. The diagrams show no views and no functions. See Database Schema for those.

`docs:build:model` writes the diagrams from the database, and the files are in `docs/diagrams/`. Run it after a migration. See Development.


### Application database

The application database `data-proxy` has four groups of tables.

```mermaid
%% Application database tables
erDiagram

"console.schemas" }o--|| "console.projects" : ""
"console.tables" }o--|| "console.schemas" : ""
"console.rls" }o--|| "console.tables" : ""
"data_proxy.scope" }o--|| "console.schemas" : ""
"console.config_history" }o--|| "console.schemas" : ""

"rbac.revision" {
  boolean singleton
  bigint value
}
"rbac.roles" {
  text name
  text__ permissions
  text wrapped
}
"data_proxy.state" {
  text table_name
  jsonb state
}
"data_proxy.errors" {
  bigint id
  text reason
  jsonb fields
  timestamp_with_time_zone recorded_at
}
"data_proxy.scope" {
  text workflow_id
  text run_id
  text schema_name
  text table_name
}
"console.schemas" {
  text name
  text source
  jsonb settings
  text claim
  boolean encrypted
  timestamp_with_time_zone updated_at
  text updated_by
  text project
  text short_name
}
"console.tables" {
  text name
  text schema
  text strategy
  integer n
  boolean fallback
  integer cache_ttl
  jsonb partitioning
  text__ sort
  timestamp_with_time_zone updated_at
  text updated_by
}
"console.rls" {
  bigint id
  text table_name
  text column_name
  text unit_type
  timestamp_with_time_zone updated_at
  text updated_by
}
"console.config_history" {
  bigint id
  timestamp_with_time_zone changed_at
  text changed_by
  text action
  text object
  text schema_name
  text key
  jsonb old_row
  jsonb new_row
}
"console.projects" {
  text name
  timestamp_with_time_zone updated_at
  text updated_by
}
"test.access_policy" {
  text subject
  text unit_type
  text unit_id
}
"test.access_log" {
  text subject
  text unit_type
  text unit_id
  text action
  timestamp_with_time_zone changed_at
}
```

- **Configuration (`console`):** `schemas`, `tables` and `rls` store the sync configuration. A table belongs to one schema, and a row policy rule (`rls`) belongs to one table. The name of a schema can't be a reserved name. `config_history` records every change of these three tables. See Configuration and Changes.
- **Engine (`data_proxy`):** `state` has the state of each synced table as JSON. `errors` has the engine errors. `scope` links a workflow to the schemas and tables that a sync run covers. The console views use it to show a user only the sync runs of its own schemas.
- **Rules (`rbac`):** `roles` has the permissions of each role, filled from `rbac.toml`. `revision` is a single row with a counter. The proxy reads the counter to find a change of the rules.
- **Access policy (one schema for each source schema):** `access_policy` has the subjects that may read a unit, and `access_log` records each change. A trigger writes the log. See Authorization.

The `data_proxy` and `console` tables don't reference each other with foreign keys. `scope.schema_name` and `config_history.schema_name` carry the name of a schema, and nothing enforces it.

### Catalog database

The `ducklake` database has two kinds of schema.

```mermaid
%% Catalog database tables
erDiagram


"signer.keys" {
  text schema_name
  text access_key
  text secret_sealed
  timestamp_with_time_zone created_at
}
"test.ducklake_metadata" {
  varchar key
  varchar value
  varchar scope
  bigint scope_id
}
"test.ducklake_schema" {
  bigint schema_id
  uuid schema_uuid
  bigint begin_snapshot
  bigint end_snapshot
  varchar schema_name
  varchar path
  boolean path_is_relative
}
"test.ducklake_table" {
  bigint table_id
  uuid table_uuid
  bigint begin_snapshot
  bigint end_snapshot
  bigint schema_id
  varchar table_name
  varchar path
  boolean path_is_relative
}
"test.ducklake_data_file" {
  bigint data_file_id
  bigint table_id
  bigint begin_snapshot
  bigint end_snapshot
  bigint file_order
  varchar path
  boolean path_is_relative
  varchar file_format
  bigint record_count
  bigint file_size_bytes
  bigint footer_size
  bigint row_id_start
  bigint partition_id
  varchar encryption_key
  bigint mapping_id
  bigint partial_max
}
"test.ducklake_delete_file" {
  bigint delete_file_id
  bigint table_id
  bigint begin_snapshot
  bigint end_snapshot
  bigint data_file_id
  varchar path
  boolean path_is_relative
  varchar format
  bigint delete_count
  bigint file_size_bytes
  bigint footer_size
  varchar encryption_key
  bigint partial_max
}
"test.ducklake_sort_info" {
  bigint sort_id
  bigint table_id
  bigint begin_snapshot
  bigint end_snapshot
}
"test.ducklake_sort_expression" {
  bigint sort_id
  bigint table_id
  bigint sort_key_index
  varchar expression
  varchar dialect
  varchar sort_direction
  varchar null_order
}
```

- **`signer.keys`:** one row for each schema. It has the storage access key of the schema and the sealed secret. The console reads it to sign file links. See Query tab.
- **Metadata schemas:** DuckLake creates one schema for each source schema, with the name of the source schema. The diagram shows the tables that Data Proxy reads. Other tables lists the rest. The console reads `ducklake_table`, `ducklake_data_file` and `ducklake_delete_file` to list the files of a table. The sync service reads the sort tables to find the sort keys.

An empty `end_snapshot` marks a row that's still current. The code filters on it.

### Workflow tables

DBOS owns the `dbos` schema in the application database. The diagram shows the tables that the console reads. Other tables lists the rest.

```mermaid
%% DBOS workflow tables
erDiagram

"dbos.streams" }o--|| "dbos.workflow_status" : ""
"dbos.workflow_status" }o--o| "dbos.workflow_status" : ""
"dbos.workflow_status" }o--o| "dbos.queues" : ""
"dbos.workflow_status" }o--o| "dbos.workflow_schedules" : ""

  text workflow_uuid
  text status
  text name
  text authenticated_user
  text assumed_role
  text authenticated_roles
  text request
  text output
  text error

  bigint updated_at

  text application_id
  varchar_255_ class_name
  varchar_255_ config_name
  bigint recovery_attempts
  text queue_name
  bigint workflow_timeout_ms
  bigint workflow_deadline_epoch_ms
  text inputs
  bigint started_at_epoch_ms
  text deduplication_id
  integer priority
  text queue_partition_key
  text forked_from
  text owner_xid
  text parent_workflow_id
  text serialization
  bigint delay_until_epoch_ms

  boolean rate_limited
  bigint completed_at
  jsonb attributes

  bigint debounce_deadline_epoch_ms

"dbos.streams" {

  text key
  text value

}
"dbos.workflow_schedules" {
  text schedule_id
  text schedule_name
  text workflow_name
  text workflow_class_name

  text status

"dbos.queues" {
  text queue_id
  text name
  integer concurrency
  integer worker_concurrency
  integer rate_limit_max

  boolean priority_enabled
  boolean partition_queue
  double_precision polling_interval_sec
  bigint created_at

  integer partition_worker_concurrency
  integer partition_rate_limit_max
  double_precision partition_rate_limit_period_sec
}
```

- **`workflow_status`:** one row for each workflow. A sync run is a row with the name `run_sync`. Its tasks are rows with `parent_workflow_id` set to the id of the run.
- **`operation_outputs` and `streams`:** the steps and the log lines of a workflow.
- **`queues` and `workflow_schedules`:** the queues and the schedules. A workflow names its queue and its schedule.

The console views only read these tables. The console starts and controls a workflow with `dbos.enqueue_workflow()` and the `control` queue. See Control a run and a schedule. The column `data_proxy.scope.workflow_id` has the same value as `workflow_uuid`, so a view can filter the workflows by schema.

| DBOS              | `workflow_output`                       | The output of each workflow.                                          |
| DuckLake metadata | `ducklake_column_mapping`               | Links a file column to a table column when the file has no field IDs. |
| DuckLake metadata | `ducklake_column_tag`                   | The tags on a column.                                                 |
| DuckLake metadata | `ducklake_column`                       | The columns of each table, by snapshot.                               |
| DuckLake metadata | `ducklake_file_column_stats`            | The minimum and the maximum of each column in each data file.         |

## Glossary

This page defines the terms that the other pages use. Each term has one meaning on every page, except the word schema, which has three. The Tools table explains the tools that the pages name.

### Terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Access policy | The table `<schema>.access_policy`. Each row names a subject, a unit type and a unit id, and it says which rows that subject may read. |
| Adapter | The code that reads one kind of source. BigQuery is the only adapter today. |
| Batch | The contiguous changed partitions of one table that a single dump task extracts with one query and one file. `sync.dumpBatchBytes` limits its size. |
| Catalog | The DuckLake metadata of one schema. It lives in the `ducklake` database, in a metadata schema with the name of the schema. |
| Claim | A field in the JSON Web Token. The `role` claim names the role, and the `schemas` claim lists the schemas that the user may use. |
| Fallback | A table setting. With `fallback: true`, the table function reads the partitions that DuckLake doesn't store from the source. |
| Job | A Kubernetes Job. The chart runs jobs such as `provision`, and the sync worker creates one from a suspended CronJob on demand. |
| Permission | One right in `rbac.toml`, such as `read_sync`. A role has permissions. |
| Provision | The Kubernetes Job that creates the PostgreSQL schema, the access policy and the grants for each configured schema. |
| Queue | A DBOS queue that stores workflows until a worker takes them, such as `sync`, `dump`, `publish` and `control`. |
| Resume | Put a cancelled sync run back in its queue. The console action is `resume_run`. |
| Role | One of `dp_api`, `dp_policy`, `dp_console` and `dp_admin`. The database has a role with the same name. |
| Row policy | A PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS) policy. It limits which rows of a table a role may read or write. It isn't a row of the access policy. |
| Sync run | One execution of the `run_sync` workflow. A sync run has tasks. |
| Scope | The schemas and tables that a sync run covers. The table `data_proxy.scope` records it. |
| Snapshot | One version of a DuckLake catalog. Each publication commits one snapshot. |
| Source | The external system that contains the original tables. |
| Step | One recorded operation inside a workflow. |
| Task | A workflow that a sync run starts: a `dump_task` or a `publish_schema`. |
