| Workflow | A durable DBOS function that survives a restart, such as `run_sync`. |

### Tools

| Tool | Role in Data Proxy |
| --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL | The database. It stores the configuration, the access policy, the DuckLake catalogs and the DBOS state. |
| PostgREST | An HTTP server that turns PostgreSQL views and functions into a REST API. |
| PgDog | A connection pooler. It sends each read to a PostgreSQL standby and each write to the primary. |
| DuckLake | A table format. It keeps table metadata in PostgreSQL and table data in Parquet files. |
| DuckDB | A SQL engine. The `pg_duckdb` extension runs it inside PostgreSQL to read Parquet files. |
| Parquet | A file format that stores table data in columns. |
| SeaweedFS | The S3-compatible object storage that contains the Parquet files. |
| Redis | The cache of the proxy. The tests use Valkey, a compatible server. |
| OpenResty | nginx with Lua. The proxy runs on it. |
| Istio gateway | The entry point of the cluster. It checks the JWT before it forwards a request. |
| Keycloak | The identity provider of the local and test clusters. |
| goose | The tool that applies the console database migrations. |
| k6 | The tool for load tests and end-to-end checks of a cluster. |
| Hurl | The tool for the HTTP tests of the proxy. |
| devenv | The tool for the local environment, on Nix. It starts services and runs tasks. |
| prek | The tool that runs the Git hooks. |
| Terraform | The tool that manages infrastructure as code. The `data_proxy` provider lets it manage the configuration of Data Proxy. |

### Schema

The word schema has three meanings. A page uses the full phrase if the meaning isn't clear.

- **PostgreSQL schema:** a namespace in the database. PostgREST serves each source schema as a profile, which a request selects with `Accept-Profile`.
- **Project:** a group of schemas, with its own name. A schema name is unique in its project. The `projects` claim gives access to every schema of a project.
- **Physical name:** the name of a schema in the database, the API, S3 and the roles. It's `<project>_<short name>`, or the short name in the project `default`.
- **Configured schema:** an entry under `schemas` in `sync.json`. It has one source, one PostgreSQL schema and one catalog.
- **JSON schema:** a document that checks the shape of data, such as the `config` schema of the proxy.

### Acronyms

| Acronym | Expansion |
| --- | --- |
| CNPG | CloudNativePG, the operator that runs the PostgreSQL cluster. |
| CORS | cross-origin resource sharing. |
| DBOS | The library that runs the durable workflows. Its state lives in the `dbos` schema of PostgreSQL. |
| DSN | data source name, the connection string of a database. |
| JWT | JSON Web Token, the signed token that a client sends. |
| KEDA | Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling. |
| OTLP | OpenTelemetry Protocol. |
| PVC | PersistentVolumeClaim, a Kubernetes request for storage. |
| RBAC | role-based access control. |
| RLS | row-level security. |
| TTL | time to live. |

---

Source: notebooks.md

## Notebooks

The query tab of the console embeds a notebook that runs in the browser. `console/notebooks/` builds the static site of that notebook. The site runs on its own origin, so it shares no cookie with the console.

```mermaid
%% Notebook flow
sequenceDiagram
  participant u as User
  participant page as Console page
  participant nb as Notebook<br/>(own origin, in an iframe)
  participant app as Console server
  participant s3 as Object storage
  u->>page: choose tables
  page->>nb: open /?tables=people
  nb-->>page: ready
  page->>app: ask for a grant
  app-->>page: signed links, valid 5 minutes
  page->>nb: post the grant<br/>only from the console origin
  nb->>nb: register the links,<br/>create a view for each table
  nb-->>page: applied
  u->>nb: run: await query(sql)
  nb->>s3: DuckDB-WASM reads Parquet<br/>with the signed links
  s3-->>nb: rows
```

### What the site contains

The site is a static folder with no outside request. It has these parts:

- **A marimo notebook** (`notebooks/query.py`), exported with `marimo export html-wasm --offline`. Python runs in Pyodide. The notebook is in edit mode, so the user can write cells. The user presses Run once, and presses Ctrl+S before Export, Python, because marimo exports an empty file without the save. The file has the cells and no link, because a grant never enters the code. The page hides the SQL button of marimo. A SQL cell runs on the DuckDB of Pyodide, which can't see the signed links, so use `query` in a Python cell.
- **DuckDB-WASM**, with the Parquet extension on the same site. The policy of the site blocks the public repository, so the helper points `custom_extension_repository` to this site.
- **`src/helper.ts`**, in the Python worker. For each table it registers the signed links and creates a view. A data file with a delete file becomes an anti join on the row number, so a count matches the database. A new grant replaces the files, so an open notebook keeps working after the first links expire.
- **`src/bridge.ts`**, in the page. It accepts a grant only from the console that embeds the page, and it passes it to the worker. Both scripts check a grant with the valibot schema of `src/messages.ts`. They report `ready`, `applied`, `error` and a policy violation to the console.

The notebook follows the theme of the console. The console sends the message `theme` (`light` or `dark`) when the notebook is ready and each time the user switches the theme. The notebook starts in the light theme until the first message arrives.

### Query from a cell

The console opens the notebook with the tables that the user chose, as `/?tables=people&tables=orders`. The server repeats the template cell once for each table, and the name is the part of the table name after its last dot. The setup block defines one function, `query(sql, limit=100_000)`. It waits for the first grant, runs the SQL in DuckDB-WASM and returns at most `limit` rows as a Polars DataFrame. A scan of a large table stays in DuckDB-WASM, because the Python heap is the weak point of the page.

```python
await query('select * from "people" limit 15')
```

A cell needs `await`, because DuckDB-WASM runs in another worker. If the links expire, `query` tells the user to open the notebook again. If a table has no data files yet, it tells the user to sync the table. The Python package `duckdb` also runs in Pyodide, but it can't see the signed links and it doesn't apply the delete files, so use `query`.

### Build and serve

Run `nu console/notebooks/build.nu notebooks/query.py dist` to build the site. The header of `build.nu` lists the steps and the pins. The console image contains the site. The chart starts that image a second time with `node notebooks/server.ts`, as its own Deployment on its own host.

The server sends a Content Security Policy. The page can send data only to itself and to the storage host, and only the console can embed the page. `console/notebooks/csp.ts` builds the policy, and the chart builds the same string. The header of `server.ts` explains the policy and the cells.

---

Source: sql.md

## SQL Templates

SQL templates live under `sync/src/sync/templates/<target>/`. Each target is one database backend. Helm maintenance templates live under `helm/files/templates/postgres/`.

### How a request becomes SQL

SQL has three layers. Each layer has one job.

| Layer | Written in | Runs | Does |
| ----- | ---------- | ---- | ---- |
| Template | Jinja | At each sync run | Fills the identifiers and the column lists of the function of one table. |
| Static function | PL/pgSQL | At each request | Reads the filter and builds the text of the DuckDB query. It doesn't depend on a table. |
| Dynamic SQL | `format()` | At each request | Runs the text that a static function built, with `%I` and `%L`. |

Serving layer shows the request flow, and Sync layer shows the sync run that installs the functions.

Put logic in a static function and not in a template. A static function has one name, one test and one place to read.

### Template headers

Every Jinja or minijinja SQL template starts with one metadata header:

```jinja
{#
{
  "kind": "template",
  "description": "Create a table from Parquet.",
  "inputs": {
    "schema": "Destination PostgreSQL schema.",
    "table": "Destination PostgreSQL table.",
    "path": "Parquet file path."
  }
}
#}
```

Use `kind: template` and `description`. Add `inputs` when the template accepts values. Keep descriptions short. Keep metadata inside the source comment.

Document each Jinja or minijinja macro with one metadata header. Document each Helm `define` in the `_*.tpl` files of `helm/templates/` with the same structure and `kind: macro`. Each file has one area: `_helpers.tpl` (names, labels, security), `_s3.tpl`, `_redis.tpl`, `_postgres.tpl`, `_scaling.tpl`, `_proxy.tpl`, `_console.tpl` and `_jobs.tpl`.

Put the detail of a long description in a Jinja comment under the header, and keep the description under 40 words. Put one blank line before a header. Put no blank line between the header and its definition. Put one blank line after the definition. Add `name`, `description` and `returns`. Add `inputs` when needed.

Use `{# ... #}` for Jinja and minijinja. Use `{{/* ... */}}` for Go templates. Metadata must not appear in rendered output.

### Names

Use one name for each semantic role:

- PostgreSQL objects: `schema`, `table`, `view`, `function`, `policy` and `index`.
- Columns: `column` for one column and `columns` for a collection.
- Paths: `path` for one path. Use `source` and `target` for two endpoints. Use `scratch_path` for temporary storage.
- SQL roles: `user_role`, `anonymous_role` and `serving_role`.
- Predicates: `scope` for a schema predicate, `predicate` for a row or partition predicate and `claim_setting` for a session-setting name.

Match the SQL semantic to the name shape: use `table` for a SQL-safe identifier, `table_name` for a SQL literal or a prepared-statement parameter. Never use bare `name` when the object type is known.

Don't merge values with different meanings. Don't use `name` when the object type is known. Don't use shortened aliases such as `cols` or `select_cols`.

### Runtime mappings

Use the same names in Python mappings and template variables. Keep identifier, literal, type and prepared-parameter semantics in Python helpers. Use Jinja to fill names and lists, and use a static function for logic.

Keep SQLFluff context values close to the template family that uses them. Each value must be a valid example for that family.

### Macros and helpers

Use `macros.*` for Jinja and minijinja macro files. Keep Helm helpers in the `_*.tpl` files. Don't generate metadata at runtime. Don't document ordinary functions with macro metadata. Render a list with `sql_array` for SQL literals and with `name_array` for plain names.
''

---

Source: security/index.md

## Security

Data Proxy enforces access in PostgreSQL, and no layer above it calculates permissions. A token gives a role and a list of schemas. The database role decides what the caller may do. The access policy decides which rows the caller reads.

### Where to start

| Question | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Which claims must a token have? | Required JWT claims |
| What can each role do? | Roles and Permissions |
| In which order does the system check a request? | Schema and row authorization and Authorization flow |
| What does a status code mean? | Requests and Troubleshooting |
| How do I set up my identity provider? | Identity provider |
| How long does a token live, and how do I revoke access? | Tokens |

The chart also limits the pods, the network paths and the images. See Hardening.

### Configure the access model

These values must agree:

```yaml
auth:
  anonRole: anon
  userRole: dp_api
  servingRole: serving
  jwtRoleClaim: $.role

sync:
  config:
    schemas:
      test:
        claim: preferred_username
        tables:
          - name: project.dataset.participants
            strategy: full
            rls:
              - column: region_id
                unit_type: region
```

- PostgREST reads the PostgreSQL role from the JSON Web Token (JWT) `role` claim.
- The `schemas` claim of the token must contain `test`.
- The database matches the `preferred_username` claim with `access_policy.subject`.
- A row is visible only when its unit columns match an active access policy row.

---

Source: security/claims.md

## Required JWT claims

This page lists the claims that a token needs. A normal end-user token for the example of the access model has claims like these:

```json
{
  "role": "dp_api",
  "schemas": ["test"],
  "preferred_username": "test_user_1"
}
```

The `role` claim is one role of `rbac.toml`, and PostgREST switches to the database role of the same name. The role decides what the token may do. A token without `read_api` can't read any synced view. The permissions section lists all of them.

A token can also carry a `projects` claim, such as `"projects": ["sales:*"]`. It gives access to every schema of each project, including a schema that the project gets later. Use `sales` for the schemas of the project, and `sales:*` for every row of those schemas. The database expands the claim into the `schemas` claim for each request, so a token can have both claims. See Permissions.

You configure the exact identity claim per schema. If the schema uses `sub` instead of `preferred_username`, the access policy subject must match the token's `sub` value.

---

Source: security/permissions.md

## Permissions

A token has one `role` claim and a `schemas` claim. The rules live in `helm/files/config/rbac.toml`: it lists the permissions, grouped by object, and the roles with the roles that each one inherits.

The `configure-db` job loads the file into the `rbac` schema. The pre-request function copies the claims into session settings and calls `rbac.load()`, which sets the permissions of the role for the request. `rbac.can('<permission>')` answers whether the role has a permission, and `rbac.mine('<schema>')` answers whether a schema is in the `schemas` claim. Both read settings, so they work inside `SECURITY DEFINER` functions too. A name that the file doesn't list raises an error, so a typo in the code fails loudly.

| Permission | What it opens |
| --- | --- |
| `read_sync` | The views `runs`, `tasks`, `steps`, `logs`, `errors`, `queues`, `schedules`, `health`, `synced`, and `overview`. |
| `read_config` | The tables `schemas`, `tables`, and `rls`, and `sync_config()`. |
| `create_config` | Insert on the three tables. |
| `edit_config` | Update on the three tables. |
| `delete_config` | Delete on the three tables. |
| `import_config` | `import_config()`. The import also inserts, updates, and deletes rows, so the role needs the other configuration permissions too. |
| `start_sync` | `start_sync()` and `start_scope()`. |
| `control_sync` | `cancel_run()`, `resume_run()`, `retry_run()`, `pause_schedule()`, `resume_schedule()` and `set_schedule()`. Running a run again also needs `start_sync`. |
| `read_files` | `table_files()`, the Parquet files for the query tab. |
| `read_api` | The synced views of the data API. |
| `read_ducklake` | The change feed of the catalog. |
| `read_policy` | Read `<schema>.access_policy`. |
| `create_policy`, `edit_policy`, `delete_policy` | Insert, update, and delete in `<schema>.access_policy`. |

A role that edits needs the matching read permission, because an update reads the row first. The roles in `rbac.toml` include it.

The database checks a permission with a row policy or with a check at the start of the function. A role without a permission gets:

- an empty list from a view or a table
- a 403 from a write that a row policy refuses
- a 403 from a function

A delete that the row policy hides removes nothing and answers 200 with an empty list.

Every role sees only the schemas in the `schemas` claim and in the `projects` claim, and a token without them sees nothing. No role and no token reaches every schema. The `projects` claim names projects. When a request starts, `rbac.load()` expands each entry into the schemas that the project has: `<schema>` for `<project>`, and `<schema>:*` for `<project>:*`. A token with a project can add a schema in it, even though the schema doesn't exist yet. The wildcard `*` names every project. The database enforces this, not the console:

- Row-level security filters `schemas`, `tables` and `rls` by the schema of each row. A role with `create_config` writes a row only for a schema in its claim, and the claim can name a schema that doesn't exist yet.
- The views `tasks`, `logs`, `errors`, `health`, `synced` and `overview` show the rows of the schemas in the claim. A log line without a schema is hidden.
- When a sync run starts, the engine records the schemas that it covers, and the schema of each dump task, in `data_proxy.scope`. `data_proxy.sees()` tells the views which workflows a token sees. The views `runs`, `tasks` and `steps` then show only the sync runs and tasks that cover a schema of the user.
- `GET /rpc/sync_config` returns the schemas of the claim.
- Queues serve every schema. Any role with `read_sync` reads them, and no token changes a queue. A schedule belongs to one schema, and a token controls the schedules of the schemas in its claim.

`GET /rpc/permissions` returns the permissions of the role of the token, so the console can show only the controls that work. The pre-request function sets a statement timeout of 30 seconds, and the data API has 15 seconds. Database lists the schemas.

A token with `start_sync` calls `POST /rpc/start_sync` with the optional arrays `schemas` and `tables`. Empty arrays mean every schema of the token. The function enqueues `run_sync` in the `sync` queue, and a worker takes it from there.

### Request outcomes

This table lists what a client sees and why. A status can come from the gateway, the proxy, PostgREST or the database.

| Status | Cause | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `200 []` | The token has no `schemas` claim, no enabled access policy row matches its subject, or a row policy hides every row. A delete that a row policy hides also returns it. | Database |
| `400` | The claim names an unknown schema, a function gets an unknown action, or the token has an unknown role. | Database or PostgREST |
| `401` | The signature, issuer, audience or expiry of the token isn't valid. | Gateway |
| `403` | The role lacks the permission, a row policy refuses a write, or the schema or table is outside the claim (or doesn't exist). | Database |
| `404` | The sync run or the schedule doesn't exist for this token, or the schema profile is unknown. | Database or PostgREST |
| `409` | A sync run is in the wrong status for the action, or the provision job hasn't created the schema yet. | Database |
| `503` | `PROXY_MAX_INFLIGHT` requests already wait for PostgREST. | Proxy |
| `502`, `503` or `504` | PostgREST fails. The proxy retries a `GET` or `HEAD` twice and then returns the last answer. | PostgREST or proxy |

---

Source: security/roles.md

## Roles

`rbac.toml` defines four roles, and each inherits the permissions of the roles that it lists. The identity provider and the database use the same names. A token has one role.

```mermaid
%% Role inheritance
flowchart TD
  dp_api["<b>dp_api</b><br/>read_api"]
  dp_policy["<b>dp_policy</b><br/>read_policy<br/>create_policy<br/>edit_policy<br/>delete_policy"]
  dp_console["<b>dp_console</b><br/>read_sync<br/>read_config"]
  dp_admin["<b>dp_admin</b><br/>start_sync<br/>control_sync<br/>create_config<br/>edit_config<br/>delete_config<br/>import_config<br/>read_files<br/>read_ducklake"]
  dp_api -->|"inherited by"| dp_console
  dp_console -->|"inherited by"| dp_admin
  dp_policy -->|"inherited by"| dp_admin
```

The table shows the permissions that each role has, with the inherited ones. The task `docs:build:roles` writes it from `rbac.toml`.

| Permission      | `dp_api` | `dp_policy` | `dp_console` | `dp_admin` |
| --------------- | -------- | ----------- | ------------ | ---------- |
| `read_api`      | yes      |             | yes          | yes        |
| `read_ducklake` |          |             |              | yes        |
| `read_files`    |          |             |              | yes        |
| `read_sync`     |          |             | yes          | yes        |
| `start_sync`    |          |             |              | yes        |
| `control_sync`  |          |             |              | yes        |
| `read_config`   |          |             | yes          | yes        |
| `create_config` |          |             |              | yes        |
| `edit_config`   |          |             |              | yes        |
| `delete_config` |          |             |              | yes        |
| `import_config` |          |             |              | yes        |
| `read_policy`   |          | yes         |              | yes        |
| `create_policy` |          | yes         |              | yes        |
| `edit_policy`   |          | yes         |              | yes        |
| `delete_policy` |          | yes         |              | yes        |

| Role | Inherits | Adds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dp_api` | | `read_api` |
| `dp_policy` | | `read_policy`, `create_policy`, `edit_policy`, `delete_policy` |
| `dp_console` | `dp_api` | `read_sync`, `read_config` |
| `dp_admin` | `dp_console`, `dp_policy` | `start_sync`, `control_sync`, `create_config`, `edit_config`, `delete_config`, `import_config`, `read_files`, `read_ducklake` |

`dp_policy` is for an API that registers its own access policies. `dp_admin` runs schemas, and every role is limited to the schemas in its claim. A user has one role. A person who needs both console and access policy rights takes `dp_admin`.

### How the rules are tested

The Python tests in `sync/tests/unit/test_templates_roles.py` run the `create_rbac` template on the real test server with the real `rbac.toml`.

They compare `rbac.can()` for every role and permission with a reference that the test computes itself. Hypothesis tests do the same for random rules files and random names. The end-to-end suite in `k6/scenarios/` tests the console with real tokens (`console.js` and `roles.js`) on the k3d cluster. It doesn't run in CI, because it needs the cluster. Run it before you merge a change to a permission, a role, an access policy, a view or the console schema (`devenv shell -- nu scripts/cluster.nu k6 e2e`).

---

Source: security/flow.md

## Authorization flow

This page shows how a token becomes a database role and a row filter, and which PostgreSQL roles take part.

The proxy puts the role in the cache key, so a token with another role never gets an answer that another token cached.

Request sequence shows the JSON Web Token (JWT) and row-level security (RLS) flow. The gateway checks the token, PostgREST switches to the role of the token and the database applies the checks.

CloudNativePG (CNPG) manages two roles: `ops` (the owner and a superuser) and `duckdb` (the read-only catalog login). The `configure-db` job creates the rest as `ops`:

| Role                     | Purpose                                                                        |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `anon`                   | Role of a request without a token, with no application table access.           |
| `dp_api`, `dp_policy`, `dp_console`, `dp_admin` | One role for each role of `rbac.toml`. A token switches to the role of its `role` claim, and the rules decide what that role may do. The schema and row policies limit the rows. |
| `serving`                | The login of the serving layer: PostgREST, the PgDog pool and the recovery Deployment (`auth.servingRole`). It's `NOINHERIT` and can switch to `anon` and to every `dp_*` role. |

Database describes each role and why `ops` is a superuser.

Init-db creates the `data_proxy` schema and its internal functions, procedures and grants. `data_proxy` isn't in `PGRST_DB_SCHEMAS`, so these objects aren't exposed as RPC endpoints. `data_proxy.pre_request()` copies JWT claims into transaction-local PostgreSQL settings. `USAGE` on `data_proxy` doesn't grant application table access.

---

Source: security/authorization.md

## Schema and row authorization

Authorization has two independent conditions. The diagram shows the order of the checks.

```mermaid
%% Authorization checks
flowchart TD
  token["Request with a token"] --> valid{"Valid token?"}
  valid -->|"no"| refused["401 from the gateway"]
  valid -->|"yes"| role["Switch to the role<br/>of the role claim"]
  role --> schema{"Is the schema in the<br/>schemas claim?"}
  schema -->|"no"| none["200, no rows"]
  schema -->|"yes"| all{"Does the claim have * or<br/>schema:* ?"}
  all -->|"yes"| every["Every row of the table"]
  all -->|"no"| policy{"Does an access policy row<br/>match the subject and the unit?<br/>A grant * and * matches all."}
  policy -->|"yes"| unit["The rows of those units"]
  policy -->|"no"| none
```

### Schema condition

The token must list the requested schema:

```json
"schemas": ["test"]
```

The client must select the same schema:

```http
Accept-Profile: test
```

The schema name `*` stands for every schema. Use it only for a debugging account in staging. The token then reads and changes every schema, and it also reads every row, as the next section describes.

```json
"schemas": ["*"]
```

The element `<schema>:*` reaches one schema and reads every row of it. A token with it needs no access policy row for that schema, and it reaches no other schema.

```json
"schemas": ["test:*"]
```

### Row condition

For a table with this configuration:

```json
"rls": [
  {"column": "region_id", "unit_type": "region"}
]
```

an active access policy row must match the user's subject and the row's unit:

```text
subject   = JWT preferred_username (or configured claim)
OR unit_type/unit_id matches the row
```

A token whose `schemas` claim has `*`, or `<schema>:*` for the schema of the table, skips this condition and reads every row.

A subject with the grant `unit_type = '*'` and `unit_id = '*'` in the `access_policy` of the schema reads every row of the tables of that schema too. The grant covers one subject and one schema. Revoking it deletes the row, like any other grant.

An access policy row exists only while the grant is active. Revoking access deletes the row. A missing schema claim or access policy grant normally returns `200 []`. It isn't an authentication error.

### Seed access policy

Create one confidential client for the service that manages the access policy, and give its token the role `dp_policy` for the schemas that it manages. Its token looks like this:

```json
{
  "role": "dp_policy",
  "schemas": ["test"],
  "preferred_username": "test_policy"
}
```

The token reads and writes `<schema>.access_policy` for the schemas in its claim. `dp_policy` has only the four policy permissions: `read_policy`, `create_policy`, `edit_policy` and `delete_policy`. Deleting a row revokes the grant. The database records the change in `test.access_log`.

---

Source: security/requests.md

## Requests

This page shows how the system authorizes a read request, and what each result of a request means.

### Read requests

Use a normal end-user token:

```bash
curl \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${USER_TOKEN}" \
  --header "Accept-Profile: test" \
  "${BASE_URL}/participants?limit=20"
```

The proxy sends every request to PostgREST, and PgDog sends a `GET` to a standby. Rows from the source follow the same authentication and row-level security (RLS) rules as DuckLake rows. Request sequence shows the whole read.

See Proxy for the routing and cache rules. `/access_policy` is never response-cached.

### Expected results

The table maps each result of a request to its meaning.

| Result          | Meaning                                                                   |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `200` with rows | Token, schema, role, grants, and RLS checks passed.                       |
| `200 []`        | The request is valid, but the schema claim or row policy exposes no rows. |
| `401`           | The JSON Web Token (JWT) is missing, not valid, expired, or can't be used by PostgREST.    |
| `403`           | PostgreSQL/PostgREST permission or role configuration isn't valid.        |
| `404`           | The schema profile, the table, or the snapshot is unknown or unpublished. |

---

Source: security/identity.md

## Identity provider

This page shows how to set up the `role` and `schemas` claims in your identity provider. It also says what another provider needs, and how to check the roles when you deploy.

The diagram shows what happens to a token on its way to the data.

```mermaid
%% API client token
sequenceDiagram
  participant c as API client
  participant idp as Identity provider
  participant gw as Istio gateway
  participant pgrst as PostgREST
  participant db as PostgreSQL
  c->>idp: ask for a token
  idp-->>c: JWT with role, schemas<br/>and preferred_username
  c->>gw: request with Authorization: Bearer
  gw->>idp: signing keys (JWKS), cached
  gw->>gw: check signature, issuer,<br/>audience and expiry
  gw->>pgrst: request
  pgrst->>db: switch to the role claim
  db-->>pgrst: rows allowed by the policy
  pgrst-->>c: answer
```

### Set up the role claim in an identity provider

The token needs one `role` claim with the name of a role of `rbac.toml`.

In Keycloak, do these steps:

1. Create the roles `dp_api`, `dp_policy`, `dp_console` and `dp_admin` as client roles of one client.
2. Give each user or service account one of them.
3. Add a *User Client Role* mapper to the client scope. The next table gives its settings.

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Client ID | The client that defines the roles. |
| Token claim name | `role` |
| Several values | Off |
| Add to access token | On |

Add a second mapper for the `schemas` claim (a user attribute with several values) and a third for `preferred_username`. Another identity provider needs the same three claims.

A user who needs two roles takes a role that inherits both in `rbac.toml`, because a token has one.

An older Keycloak writes the single client role as the text `[dp_admin]`, even when *Multivalued* is off. PostgREST then finds no role. In that case replace the mapper with a *User Attribute* mapper: the user attribute `role`, the claim name `role` and the type String. Then give each user the attribute `role` with the name of one role. `nu scripts/kc.nu check` reports this case.

The `k3d` test realm has one client, `idp`, that's set up like this recipe:

- the client roles `dp_api` and `dp_console`
- a *User Client Role* mapper for `role`
- a *User Attribute* mapper with several values for `schemas`
- the users `idp_viewer` and `idp_console` that log in with a password

The `idp` scenario of the end-to-end suite reads their tokens and uses them on the data API and on the console. The other test clients carry a fixed `role` claim.

Use that token and the target schema profile:

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${POLICY_WRITER_TOKEN}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --header "Accept-Profile: test" \
  --header "Prefer: resolution=merge-duplicates" \
  --data '[
    {"subject": "test_user_1", "unit_type": "region", "unit_id": "region_1"}
  ]' \
  "${BASE_URL}/access_policy"
```

The access policy subject must equal the configured identity claim in the end-user JSON Web Token (JWT).

### Create the console client

`scripts/kc.nu` prints the document for the Keycloak partial import and checks a token. The header of the script has the steps. Print the document with `nu scripts/kc.nu client --host <host> > console-client.json`, import it in the realm and check a token with `nu scripts/kc.nu check <access_token> --issuer <issuer>`.

### Use another identity provider

The gateway, PostgREST and the proxy need the same three claims from any provider that issues JWTs and publishes a JWKS. Set these values, and then give each client the claims:

| Value | What it sets |
| --- | --- |
| `ingress.auth.issuer`, `ingress.auth.jwksUri`, `ingress.auth.audience` | The gateway accepts only tokens of this issuer and audience. |
| `postgrest.jwksUri` | PostgREST validates the signature with these keys. |
| `auth.jwtRoleClaim` | The claim that contains the role. The default is `$.role`. |

| Claim | Value | How to add it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `role` | One role of `rbac.toml`, as text. | Keycloak: a mapper that sets a fixed claim on a service client, or a *User Client Role* mapper for users. Auth0: an Action that sets a custom claim. `Entra ID`: an app role, with a claims mapping policy that renames it. |
| `schemas` | A list of schema names, or one name as text. | A user attribute with several values, or a fixed list on a service client. An empty list reads nothing. The name `*` stands for every schema and every row. Give it only to a debugging account. The element `<schema>:*` names one schema and reads every row of it. |
| `preferred_username` | The subject of the access policy. | The default claim of most providers. If yours doesn't set it, the access policy subject must be the `sub` value. |

The token must also carry the audience that the gateway expects. Get a token with `nu scripts/token.nu --issuer <issuer> --client-id <client> --client-secret <secret>`, and decode its payload. Check that `role`, `schemas` and `preferred_username` are there, and that `aud` and `iss` match your values. Then call `/<table>?limit=1`. A token with an unknown role gets 400 or 403, and a token without a role reads nothing.

A claim that names a role that isn't in `rbac.toml` never gains rights. PostgREST can switch only to the roles that the serving login is a member of. `verify-rbac` makes sure that this list is the list of the file.

### Check the roles at deploy time

Two checks keep `rbac.toml` and the database in step. `chart:lint:toml` checks `rbac.toml` against `rbac.schema.json`: each object has a description and an action, and each role has a name. The `configure-db` Job runs `verify-rbac` after it loads the rules. It fails in three cases. A role is missing. A request role can log in or is a superuser. The serving login belongs to a role that the file doesn't list. A role that left the file can't keep its rights without a failed upgrade.

A permission that the SQL asks for and the file lacks ends as an HTTP 500 at run time. The `roles` scenario of the end-to-end suite checks this.

---

Source: security/tokens.md

## Tokens

This page gives the lifetime of a token and the way to revoke access before the token expires.

### Token lifetime

A token is valid until it expires. If you disable a user or change a role in the identity provider, nothing changes for a token that the user already has. It keeps its rights until it expires. The next token has the new role.

The cache key includes the role, so a token with another role never reads an answer that the cache stored for the old role.

Set the access token lifetime to **5 minutes**. This is the default of Keycloak, and the `k3d` realm sets it in `accessTokenLifespan`. In Keycloak, open *Realm settings*, *Tokens* and set *Access Token Lifespan*. A client can override it under *Clients*, *Advanced*, *Advanced settings*. Other providers have the same setting under another name.

### Revoke access

Delete the grant:

```bash
curl --request DELETE \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${POLICY_WRITER_TOKEN}" \
  --header "Accept-Profile: test" \
  "${BASE_URL}/access_policy?subject=eq.test_user_1&unit_type=eq.region&unit_id=eq.region_1"
```

The database removes the row from `test.access_policy` and writes its previous state to `test.access_log` with `action = 'delete'`. To grant access again, insert the row again. You need no resync or token refresh. Every change of an access policy row makes the cached answers outdated, whether it passed the proxy or not. A trigger on the revision counter queues a reload of the proxy (Cache).

---

Source: security/troubleshooting.md

## Troubleshooting

Use this page when a request fails or returns no rows. Request outcomes lists what each status means, and the table lists what to check.

| Symptom                                       | Check                                                                                                   |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `401 Unauthorized`                            | Check the JSON Web Token (JWT) signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and `role` claim.                                    |
| `403` with `permission denied to set role`    | Check that `configure-db` completed: the `auth.servingRole` login must be a member of `anon` and of every `dp_*` role. |
| `403` with `permission denied for schema data_proxy` | Check `GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA data_proxy TO anon/user`.                                             |
| `200 []` for every table                      | Check `schemas`, the schema profile, the configured subject claim, and enabled `access_policy` rows.    |
| `404 Unknown schema profile`                  | Check `Accept-Profile`, and check that the provision job ran for the schema.                                                       |
| Access policy write fails                     | Check that the token has `edit_policy` and `read_policy`, that its `schemas` claim names the schema, and that `Accept-Profile` matches. |
| Results differ between requests               | Check `X-Source`, `X-DuckLake-Snapshot`, and `X-Cache`. Every source uses the same JWT and row-level security (RLS) rules. |
| `/access_policy` appears cached               | It must never be cached. Check nginx configuration and response headers.                                |

See Using the API, Database Schema and Proxy for related details.

---

---

Source: console/index.md

## Console

The console is the admin web app of Data Proxy. People use it to watch sync runs, change the configuration, manage the access policy and query the data. The browser never calls PostgREST. The SvelteKit server keeps the session and calls PostgREST with the token of the user. The database is the API, and it checks every permission.

| Tab | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Sync | Watch sync runs and tasks, start, cancel or resume a run, and edit a schedule. |
| Config | Edit the schemas, the tables and the rules of the sync configuration. |
| Access | Read and change the access policy, and read its access log. |
| Query | Query the synced data in a notebook in the browser. |

The code is in `console/`. `ui/` is the SvelteKit app, `notebooks/` builds the notebook site of the Query tab, and `migrations/` has the SQL of the `console` schema.

### Pages

- Application — The web app and its sign-in.
- Database views — Database views, logs and the HTTP interface.
- Control a run and a schedule — Control of sync runs and schedules.
- Configuration — Configuration tables, schemas and the configuration endpoint.
- Changes — Configuration history and import preview.
- Query tab — The query tab and its scope.

Console layer shows how the parts depend on each other.

---

Source: console/app.md

## Application

This page explains how the console app signs people in, keeps the session and shows its pages. Read it before you change `console/ui/`.

### The web app

```mermaid
%% Console sign-in
sequenceDiagram
  participant u as Browser
  participant app as Console server
  participant idp as Identity provider
  u->>app: open the console
  app-->>u: redirect to sign-in
  u->>idp: sign in
  idp-->>u: redirect with a code
  u->>app: GET /auth/callback
  app->>idp: exchange code and PKCE verifier<br/>for tokens
  app->>app: seal the tokens in a cookie
  app-->>u: the console page
```

The app signs in people with OpenID Connect: the authorization code flow with PKCE and a `state` value. The server keeps the access token and the refresh token in an encrypted cookie. The cookie is `httpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax` and host-only.

The token is too long for one cookie, so the server splits the sealed value into pieces of 3500 characters. The server refreshes the token 60 seconds before it expires, and a failed refresh sends the user back to the sign-in page. Every request that changes data must come from the origin of the console, or the server answers 403.

`GET /rpc/permissions` decides which tabs and buttons the user sees, and the database still checks every call. A token with no `role` claim shows the no-access page. The database takes it for an anonymous request, and a new sign-in would give the same token. The routes are `/sync`, `/sync/runs/<id>`, `/config`, `/access` and `/query`.

Each tab needs one permission to open, and it shows an action only if the user has its permission:

| Tab | Route | Needs | Actions need | Data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sync | `/sync` | `read_sync` | `start_sync`, `control_sync` | The views `runs`, `tasks`, `steps`, `logs`, `errors`, `overview`, `queues` and `schedules` (one schedule for each schema, with an Edit dialog for its cron). |
| Config | `/config` | `read_config` | `create_config`, `edit_config`, `delete_config`, `import_config` | The tables `schemas`, `tables` and `rls`, the history, and the import preview. |
| Access | `/access` | `read_policy` | `create_policy`, `edit_policy`, `delete_policy` | `access_policy` and `access_log` of one schema. |
| Query | `/query` | `read_files` | None | The file lists of a table and the signed links. |

The app has these routes besides the tab pages. Every route sits under the path `/console` of the API host, so `/healthz` is `/console/healthz`. Every request that changes data also needs the console origin, as described above.

| Route | Method | Sign-in | Work |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `/auth/login` | GET | No | Makes a PKCE pair and a `state`, stores them in a cookie for ten minutes, and redirects to the identity provider. The query `next` names the page to open after the sign-in. The default is `/sync`. |
| `/auth/callback` | GET | No | Checks the `state`, exchanges the code, writes the session cookie, and redirects to `next`. The cookies use the path `/console`, so the browser doesn't send them to the API. It accepts only a path on the console. It answers 400 when the answer doesn't match the request. |
| `/auth/logout` | POST | No | Deletes the session cookie. It redirects to the end-session address of the identity provider, or to `/auth/login` when the provider has none. |
| `/config/export` | GET | Yes | Downloads `sync.json`, which `console.sync_config()` builds from the rows that the user may read. |
| `/query/grant` | POST | Yes | Takes `{schema, tables}` and returns the signed links for the files of those tables. It needs `read_files` and the schema, which `console.table_files()` checks. It answers 503 when the query tab isn't set up. |
| `/sync/runs/<id>/logs` | GET | Yes | Streams the status and the new log lines of the run as server-sent events, one read each second, until the sync run finishes or the page leaves. The query `after`, or the header `Last-Event-ID` of a reconnect, limits the lines to a later time. The query `settle` keeps the stream open for 30 seconds after the status finishes, because a resume or a retry may follow. It answers 404 for an unknown run. |
| `/healthz` | GET | No | Answers `ok`. The probes of the Deployment use it. |

The code of the app is in `console/ui/src`:

- `lib/server/` contains the session, the OpenID Connect client, the PostgREST client, the catalog reader and the signer.
- `lib/types.ts` contains the types of the rows. Write the types by hand. Update them in the same commit that changes a view.

The Config page edits a row in a dialog:

- A schema has a `claim` and `encrypted`.
- A table has a strategy, `n`, `fallback`, a cache TTL (time to live) and sort columns.
- A row rule has a column and a unit type.

The page doesn't edit `partitioning`. Change it with an import of the document.

### Live data

The Sync tab and the page of a sync run reload their data at an interval that the user picks. The choices are off, 2, 5, 10, 30 and 60 seconds. The default is 5 seconds, and the choice stays in the browser. The console polls, because it reads through PostgREST and DBOS sends no notification when a workflow changes its status. The log of a run is the exception, and it streams over server-sent events.

The token of the user needs the claims that Required JWT claims lists.

---

Source: console/views.md

## Database views

The console reads the database through views and a few functions. This page lists the views, the views of the logs and of the sync runs and the HTTP interface.

### Views

The `console` schema contains the views that the console reads through PostgREST. The console migrations create and replace them. The `console` scenario of the end-to-end suite (`k6/scenarios/console.js`) tests them.

| View | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `runs` | Sync runs: status, queue, schedule, who started it, the times, the number of tasks and failed tasks, and the schemas of the token that the sync run covers. |
| `tasks` | The dump and publish workflows of a sync run. |
| `steps` | The steps of a sync run and its tasks, with the times and a `failed` flag. |
| `logs` | The log lines of a sync run and its tasks, read from the portable DBOS log stream. |
| `queues` | The queue settings and the number of enqueued, pending, and delayed workflows. |
| `schedules` | The schedules with their cron expression and status. |
| `errors` | The errors that the sync recorded, newest first. |
| `overview` | One row for each schema: its tables, how many have committed state, its last sync run, and the sync runs, failed sync runs, and errors of the last 24 hours. The dashboard reads it in one request. |

The maintenance job deletes a sync run with its tasks and logs after it finishes and `jobs.maintenance.workflowRetentionDays` days pass (90 by default). The views then no longer show it. A sync run that isn't finished stays. The job also deletes an error after the same number of days.

### Reading logs and runs

The run page streams the log. The route `/sync/runs/<id>/logs` sends server-sent events. Each second it reads `GET /runs?id=eq.<id>` for the status and `GET /logs?run_id=eq.<id>&logged_at=gte.<last>&order=logged_at.asc` for the lines. It sends each line once, using the pair of `workflow_id` and `position`.

The page has a Live logs switch, which is on while the sync run is active. Turn it off to stop the stream and the scrolling, and turn it on again to continue from the last line. The stream ends when the sync run finishes.

It reads `GET /runs?id=eq.<id>` and `GET /tasks?run_id=eq.<id>` for the status. `GET /overview` returns the dashboard in one request.

### HTTP interface

The console talks to PostgREST only. The `console` scenario in `k6/scenarios/console.js` tests this contract against the cluster.

- Send `Authorization: Bearer <JWT>` with a `role` claim (one role of `rbac.toml`) and a `schemas` claim that lists the schemas of the user. Send `Accept-Profile: console` on reads and `Content-Profile: console` on writes, because PostgREST also serves the schemas of the synced data. The access tab sends the data schema as the profile.
- Send `Prefer: return=representation` to get the written row back.
- Reads are `GET /runs`, `GET /schemas` and the other views. The configuration is `POST`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` on `/schemas`, `/tables` and `/rls`, and `GET /rpc/sync_config` reads the whole document. Queues and schedules are read-only: `GET /queues` and `GET /schedules`. The functions are `POST /rpc/start_sync`, `POST /rpc/import_config` and `GET /rpc/table_files`. `GET /rpc/permissions` tells the console which controls to show.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 200, 201 | Done, with the row or the value in the body. |
| 204 | Done, and there is nothing to return. `import_config` answers this way. |
| 400 | The value is wrong: a rule that the configuration tables enforce, a bad queue limit, a bad cron expression, or an unknown time zone. The body has the reason. |
| 401 | No token, or an anonymous one. |
| 409 | The row clashes with another row: a duplicate key, a table in two schemas, or a schema that doesn't exist. `start_sync` also answers 409 for a schema that isn't provisioned yet. |
| 403 | The token lacks the permission, or a row policy refuses the row. |

---

Source: console/runs.md

## Control a run and a schedule

A user with `control_sync` can cancel a sync run, resume it and run it again, and pause or resume a schedule or change its cron.

The functions `console.cancel_run(run)`, `console.resume_run(run)`, `console.retry_run(run)`, `console.pause_schedule(schedule_name)`, `console.resume_schedule(schedule_name)` and `console.set_schedule(schedule_name, cron)` check the permission and the schemas of the token. They're in the template `create_console_functions`.

Cancel, resume and the schedule actions enqueue a workflow in the queue `control`, and the sync worker runs it with the DBOS API. Console layer shows the sequence. A sync run accepts an action only in the right status. The diagram shows the moves, and the table lists the rules:

```mermaid
%% Run statuses
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> ENQUEUED: start_sync
  ENQUEUED --> PENDING: a worker takes it
  PENDING --> SUCCESS
  PENDING --> ERROR
  PENDING --> MAX_RECOVERY_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED: the worker is lost too many times
  ENQUEUED --> CANCELLED: cancel
  PENDING --> CANCELLED: cancel
  DELAYED --> CANCELLED: cancel
  CANCELLED --> ENQUEUED: resume
  MAX_RECOVERY_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED --> ENQUEUED: resume
  state Ended {
    SUCCESS
    ERROR
    CANCELLED
    MAX_RECOVERY_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED
  }
  Ended --> [*]: run again as a new run
```


| Action | Function | Needs | Allowed statuses | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cancel | `cancel_run` | `control_sync` | `PENDING`, `ENQUEUED`, `DELAYED` | Stops the sync run at the next step. A dump stops at its next partition. |
| Resume | `resume_run` | `control_sync` | `CANCELLED`, `MAX_RECOVERY_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED` | Puts the sync run back in the `sync` queue, so the concurrency of that queue still applies. |
| Run again | `retry_run` | `control_sync` and `start_sync` | `SUCCESS`, `ERROR`, `CANCELLED`, `MAX_RECOVERY_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED` | Starts a new sync run through `start_sync`, for the schemas of the old sync run that the token reaches. |

| Case | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| The token lacks `control_sync` | 403 |
| The sync run is in another status | 409 |
| The token doesn't see the sync run | 404 |

### Schedules

Each schema has one schedule, named `sync-<schema>`. It starts a sync run for that schema only, at the cron of the schedule. A new schema gets the cron of `SYNC_SCHEDULE` (`0 2 * * *`). The workflow `reconcile_schedules` makes the schedules match the schemas. It runs in its own queue, `schedules`, one at a time.

It runs at the start of a worker, and after each insert or delete in `console.schemas`. It also deletes the schedule of a removed schema, and the old global schedule `sync`.

The Sync tab lists the schedules of the schemas in the claim. Its Edit dialog changes the cron, which has 5 fields, or 6 with the seconds first. The times are UTC. The schedule keeps its paused state, its context and its queue. There is no delete button, because every schema keeps one schedule. Pause the schedule to stop its runs.

A schedule doesn't backfill. A run whose time passes while no sync worker runs is skipped, so start it by hand from the Sync tab.

A schedule action needs the schema of the schedule in the `schemas` claim. A token without that schema gets 404, as for a sync run. A bad cron returns 400, and the worker never sees it.

The setting `LISTEN_QUEUES` limits the queues that one worker listens to. It contains queue names separated by commas, and an empty value means every queue. The test stack runs a second worker with `LISTEN_QUEUES=control,schedules`. The browser tests therefore run the control workflows and the schedule reconcile, and never a sync run.

---

Source: console/configuration.md

## Configuration

This page lists the configuration tables that the console edits. It also says what happens when you remove a table or a schema, and which endpoint gives the configuration to the engine and the proxy.

### Configuration tables

The sync configuration is data in three tables of the `console` schema. The console migrations create them, and the end-to-end suite tests the rules.

| Table | Contains |
| --- | --- |
| `projects` | One row per project: `name`. A project has schemas. |
| `schemas` | One row per synced schema: `project`, `short_name`, `name`, `source`, `settings`, `claim`, `encrypted`. |
| `tables` | One row per source table: `name`, its `schema`, `strategy`, `n`, `fallback`, `cache_ttl`, `partitioning`, `sort`. |
| `rls` | One row per rule: the `table_name`, the `column_name`, and the `unit_type`. |

Every row records `updated_at` and `updated_by`. The database sets both. The name comes from the `preferred_username` claim of the token, then from `sub`.

Constraints replace a validation step:

- A project name uses lowercase letters and digits. The project `default` always exists. A project with schemas can't be deleted.
- A schema has one project. Its `name` is the physical name that the sync, the proxy, S3 and the roles use: `<project>_<short_name>`, or `<short_name>` in `default`. The database builds it from the project and the short name.
- A physical name uses lowercase letters, digits and underscores, and it starts with a letter. It has at most 56 characters, so that the role name `schema_<name>` fits in 63. Two schemas can't share one.
- A schema can't change its project or its short name. Delete it and add it again to rename it.
- A table name is unique in the whole configuration, and unique in its schema by its last part.
- `n` and `fallback` need the `partitioned` strategy, and `n` must be positive.
- A table needs a schema that exists, and an `rls` rule needs a schema with a `claim`.
- A schema can't lose its `claim` while one of its tables has a rule.

The engine checks the rules of a source, such as the form of a table name, when a sync run starts.

Two read-only views compare the configuration with the system. `health` shows, for each schema, whether the PostgreSQL schema, its `access_policy` and its views exist. `synced` shows, for each table, whether a sync committed its state, with the signature and the number of partitions.

### Remove a table or a schema

Deleting a row in `tables` or `schemas` destroys the data of that table or schema, so `delete_config` is a destructive permission. The database asks for no confirmation, and the console asks the user first. A sync run for a schema that an editor removes during the run fails.

**A table.** A trigger on `tables` queues the workflow `cleanup_tables` when none waits. The sync worker runs it. For each schema, the workflow drops the DuckLake tables that the configuration no longer lists and deletes their data files in S3. It also deletes the state and the errors of those tables. The daily `maintenance` Job drops the views. Every step can run again, and DuckLake maintenance deletes the orphan files of a stopped run.

**A schema.** A trigger on `schemas` queues the workflow `provision_schemas` when none waits. The queue runs one workflow at a time, so a change during a sync run gets the next sync run. The sync worker creates a Job from the suspended `provision` CronJob (Initialization). The Job makes the database match the configuration. Every sync run does the same at its start, so a lost event heals.

- **Add:** the Job creates the PostgreSQL schema with `access_policy` and `access_log`, adds it to `pgrst.db_schemas` and tells PostgREST to reload. It takes seconds.
- **Remove:** the Job stops serving the schema and purges the files in S3. It drops the metadata schema in the catalog database. It deletes the state, the errors and the scope of its tables. It drops the schema of the database last, so the next sync run finds an unfinished removal. Every step can run again.

### The configuration endpoint

`GET /rpc/sync_config` returns the whole configuration in the shape of `sync.json`. A token with `read_config` gets the schemas of its claim. The engine and the proxy read this one document.

`console.sync_config()` builds it from the tables. It omits every default value. There is no `claim` without a claim, no `rls` without rules and no `fallback` unless it's true. The tables are sorted by name, and the rules keep their order.

A new setup can load an existing file. A token with `import_config`, `edit_config` and `delete_config` calls `POST /rpc/import_config` with `{"document": <sync.json>}`. The function inserts or updates the schemas and tables of the document, and it replaces the rules of each table in the document. It never deletes a schema or a table, and it never moves a table to another schema. The call is one transaction, so a row the constraints refuse leaves nothing behind. The scenario "The exported document imports again" in `console/ui/tests/features/config.feature` exports the document, previews it with no change and applies it.

One limit: the export drops a `null` value inside the `settings` of a source, because the export removes every `null` of the document.

The proxy reads a smaller document, `console.config()`: the table names and their `cache_ttl`. The chart grants it to the anonymous role, and the proxy refuses the `console` profile from outside, so only the cluster can call it.

A trigger on `schemas`, `tables` and `rls` queues a `reload_proxy` workflow after every statement. A change queues a reload only when none waits. A burst of edits therefore shares one reload. A change during a sync run queues the next one, and an editor never sees an error from it. The sync worker then sends a reload request to every proxy pod (Table settings).

---

Source: console/changes.md

## Changes

This page explains how the console records each change of the configuration, and how it previews an import before it applies it.

### History of the configuration

`console.config_history` records every insert, update and delete in `schemas`, `tables` and `rls`. A row contains the time, the user name, the schema, the key and the old and the new row. The trigger `record_change` writes it, and nobody else can.

A token with `read_config` reads the rows of the schemas in its claim, and the Config tab shows them.

The history doesn't record a rule that the database deletes together with its table. The history row of the table delete already shows the change.

### Import preview

`console.import_preview(document)` runs `import_config` in a sub-transaction, reads the rows that the history trigger wrote and rolls the import back.

It returns one row for each schema, table and rule with the action `insert`, `update`, `delete` or `unchanged`. A token needs `import_config`.

The Config tab shows the preview before it imports. The import applies only after you choose Apply import.

---

Source: console/query.md

## Query tab

This page explains how the Query tab gives a user a notebook for the synced data. It also says how the grant of signed links works and what limits the links to one schema.

### The notebook

A role with `read_files` queries the synced data in a notebook in the browser. The notebook is a marimo export that runs Python (Pyodide) and DuckDB compiled to WebAssembly. The files stay in object storage, and the browser reads them directly.

The notebook runs on its own origin, `notebooks.<domain>`, which is a different site from the console, and the console page embeds it in an `iframe`. The notebook has no token and no cookie of the console. The page opens it with the chosen tables in the address, and the notebook shows one cell for each table (Notebooks).

### How a grant works

The grant that the console server builds for one schema has four steps, which the diagram shows:

```mermaid
%% Query tab grant
sequenceDiagram
  participant u as Browser
  participant app as Console server
  participant api as PostgREST
  participant db as Catalog database
  participant s3 as Object storage
  u->>app: choose a table
  app->>api: 1. authorize: table_files
  api-->>app: allowed, or 403 and 409
  app->>db: 2. list the data and delete files<br/>as console_signer
  db-->>app: file paths
  app->>app: 3. sign a GET link for each path<br/>valid for 5 minutes
  app-->>u: grant with the signed links
  u->>s3: 4. read Parquet with a signed link
```

1. **Authorize.** The server calls `GET /rpc/table_files?schema_name=<schema>&table_name=<source table>` with the token of the user. `console.table_files` needs `read_files` and checks the schemas of the token.
   - It answers 403 for a schema or a table outside the schemas, for a name that doesn't exist and for a token without the permission.
   - It answers 409 for a schema with encrypted files, because the browser has no key.
2. **List.** The server connects to the catalog database with the `console_signer` login and runs `SET LOCAL ROLE schema_<name>` for the schema that step 1 authorized. That role reads the metadata of its schema only. The server reads the data files and the delete files of each table at the latest snapshot.
3. **Sign.** The server signs a `GET` link for each listed path, valid for 5 minutes. PostgREST can't sign links, so the database never contains storage credentials.
   - The credential is the identity of that schema. It's a user in the storage with a policy that allows `s3:GetObject` on the folder of the schema and nothing else.
   - The console makes the identity on the first query of the schema, through the IAM API of the storage, with an admin credential (`S3_ADMIN_ACCESS_KEY`, `S3_ADMIN_SECRET_KEY`).
   - The storage shows the secret of a key only once, so the console seals it and stores it in `signer.keys` in the catalog database.
   - An advisory lock keeps two replicas from making two keys.
   - Without the admin credential, every schema signs with one read-only credential. A storage that can't limit a credential to a prefix, such as GCS, does the same.
4. **Send.** The page sends `{ schema, tables, expiresAt }` to the notebook with `postMessage` and the exact origin of the notebook. It sends a new grant every 4 minutes. The notebook builds one view for each table. A data file with a delete file becomes an anti join that removes the deleted rows, so the counts match the database.

### What scopes the links

Three layers scope the links to one schema:

| Layer | What it checks | What it stops |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Application database | `read_files`, the schema in the `schemas` claim, that the table exists, and that the schema isn't encrypted. It verifies the token. | A user who asks for a schema outside the claim. |
| Catalog role | The role `schema_<name>` reads the metadata of its schema only. | The console server that lists the files of another schema by mistake. |
| Signed links | A link works for one object and one signature. A credential limited to the prefix of a schema can't sign a key outside it. | A path that isn't in the list, a changed key, and a link for another file. |

The layers protect against a partial bug, such as a wrong table name or a path that a user supplies. They don't protect against a stolen console server, which stores the catalog login and the signing credentials. Only the application database verifies the token. The server must therefore call `table_files` first, and use the schema that it authorizes for the other two layers.

Row-level security doesn't apply to the files. A user with `read_files` reads every row of the tables of their schemas, and only `dp_admin` has `read_files`.

Every link is a `GET`. A `HEAD` request on a link signed for `GET` answers 403, and so does a changed signature. With one read-only credential, the first two layers are the only scope.

### Objects behind the grant

- `provision` creates the role `schema_<name>` with the schema and drops it with the schema. The role has no login. It reads the metadata schema of its schema, now and for the tables that DuckLake creates later.
- `configure-db` creates the `console_signer` login without inheritance, with its password in the Secret `<release>-signer`. The login is a member of every `schema_<name>` role and must switch into one.
- `configure-db` also creates `signer.keys` in the catalog database. Only that login reads and writes it, and the drop of a schema deletes its row.
- The step `cleanup_s3_credentials` deletes the identity `sig_<schema>` of a schema that left the configuration. It runs in `provision_schemas` and `cleanup_tables`, only when `S3_IDENTITIES` is `true`. The chart sets that with `console.storage.perSchemaIdentities`.

### Storage setup

The bucket needs a cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rule for the notebook origin. The rule allows `GET`, `HEAD` and the `Range` header, and it exposes `Content-Length`, `Content-Range`, `ETag` and `Accept-Ranges`. Without `Content-Range`, DuckDB fails with the message No magic bytes found. Set `s3.bootstrap.corsOrigins`, and the bootstrap Job sets the rule through the S3 API. It skips a GCS endpoint, which needs its own command.

The notebook origin sends a Content Security Policy that allows only its own files and the storage host. Notebooks describes the build of the site.

---

Source: dev/index.md

## Development

This section helps you set up the repository, run the checks and find your way in the code. Tests says how to run each suite. CI describes the pipeline and the release. Production deploys says how a release reaches production. Provider releases and Provider development cover the provider. Style has the rules for the code and the docs.

### Code map

```mermaid
%% Code map
flowchart LR
  proxy["<b>proxy/</b><br/>OpenResty and Lua.<br/>The request path."] ~~~ sync["<b>sync/</b><br/>Python and DBOS.<br/>Source to DuckLake."] ~~~ console["<b>console/</b><br/>SvelteKit app, notebook<br/>site and SQL migrations."]
  helm["<b>helm/</b><br/>The chart, the job scripts<br/>and the SQL templates."] ~~~ k6["<b>k6/</b><br/>Load and end-to-end tests."] ~~~ nix["<b>nix/ and */devenv.nix</b><br/>Profiles, processes<br/>and tasks."]
  scripts["<b>scripts/</b><br/>Nushell commands for<br/>developers and CI."] ~~~ k3d["<b>k3d/</b><br/>The local cluster."] ~~~ docs["<b>docs/</b><br/>This wiki."]
  terraform["<b>terraform/</b><br/>Go. The Terraform<br/>provider of Data Proxy."]
```

### Set up the local cluster

Install k3d, Podman, `kubectl`, Helm and the Google Cloud CLI. The Podman network needs DNS, and the shell that runs k3d needs the Docker-compatible socket variables of Podman.

```bash
devenv --profile default shell
gcloud auth application-default login
cluster up
```

`cluster up` stops before Helmfile when the application-default credentials are missing. It writes the credentials of the cluster to the ignored `k3d/.kubeconfig` and doesn't change your kubeconfig. It installs KEDA, k6, Istio, SeaweedFS, Keycloak, PostgreSQL with `pg_duckdb`, Valkey, PostgREST and Data Proxy.

| Command | Work |
| --- | --- |
| `cluster sync` | Applies the current local image tag. |
| `cluster sync --build` | Builds and pushes new local images, then applies them. |
| `cluster down` | Stops the cluster. Run `cluster down` and `cluster up` again when the Helm install fails. |
| `cluster` | Lists every command. |

`sync/` is one flat Python project. Its `pyproject.toml` has the settings of `ruff`, `pyrefly`, `complexipy`, `vulture` and `pytest`. `uv sync` prepares `sync/.venv`.

### How devenv sets up the repository

The root `devenv.yaml` imports the folders `proxy/`, `sync/`, `console/` and `helm/`. Each folder has a `devenv.nix` with the profiles of its component. Run a profile with `devenv --profile <name> <command>`, where the command is `shell`, `up`, `test` or `tasks run <task>`.

| Profile | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `default` | Everything that a developer needs: the three stacks, the docs and the cluster scripts. |
| `repo` | Every lint and unit task. The CI job `repo` runs it. |
| `sync-unit`, `proxy-unit`, `console-unit` | The lint and unit tasks of one component. |
| `sync`, `proxy`, `console` | One component with its test services, for `devenv test` and `devenv up`. |
| `integration` | The three `:int` tasks, which start the service profiles. |
| `chart` | Helm, `cog` and the `ci` script. |
| `terraform` | Go and `golangci-lint` for `terraform/`. `terraform-acc` adds OpenTofu. |
| `nix` | The checks of the profile sizes and of the commands in the docs. |
| `base`, `python` | The parts that the other profiles share, in `nix/profiles/shared.nix`. |

A profile fetches every package that its tasks and processes name, so keep each one small. `nix:lint:closure` fails when a profile grows over its limit in `nix/profiles/nix.nix`. The processes of the test stack are in `nix/stack/`, the helpers in `nix/utils/` and the ports, addresses and test logins in `nix/data.nix`. Task names follow `<component>:<verb>:<target>`, and devenv rejects a name that doesn't.

A task skips its work when its input files didn't change since the last green run. To force a run, change an input or delete `.devenv/profiles/<profile>/state/tasks.db`.

### Run the checks

```bash
devenv --profile repo tasks run repo:lint repo:test:unit
```

| Task | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| `sync:lint:py`, `sync:lint:sql` | Python and SQL: `ruff`, `pyrefly`, `complexipy`, `vulture`, `sqlfluff` and `goose validate`. |
| `proxy:lint:lua` | Lua: StyLua, luacheck and the LuaLS type check. |
| `console:lint:ui`, `nb:lint:ts` | The app and the notebooks: `svelte-check`, ESLint and Prettier. |
| `chart:lint:helm`, `chart:lint:toml` | The chart and `rbac.toml`. |
| `ci:lint:wf`, `ctr:lint:files`, `nu:lint:scripts` | Workflows, container files and Nushell scripts. |
| `tf:lint:go`, `tf:test:unit` | The provider: `gofmt`, `golangci-lint` and `go test`. |
| `docs:lint:code` | The style rules that a pattern can check, and the last 50 commit subjects. |
| `docs:lint:style`, `docs:lint:links`, `docs:lint:nav`, `docs:lint:llms` | The style page, the links, the page order and `llms.txt`. |
| `nix:lint:closure`, `nix:lint:cmd` | The profile sizes and the `devenv` commands in the docs. |

The git hooks run when you commit. `eslint`, `prettier`, `lx-fmt`, `ruff` and `ruff-format` fix files, so stage the result and commit again. `ripsecrets` blocks a secret, and `vale` checks the prose of the docs. CI doesn't run Vale. Run `vale <file>` for a quick check.

Before a release, run the checks that CI can't run. `cluster k6 e2e` tests the whole system. `cluster k6 load` tests the latency gates and KEDA. `cluster upgrade --from <previous chart version>` tests the upgrade path, after the first release.

### Run the console locally

```bash
devenv --profile console up
```

Add `-d` to run in the background, wait with `devenv processes wait` and stop with `devenv down`. Open `http://console.localhost:13001/console`, or run `devenv --profile console tasks run console:open:browser`. Sign in as `admin` (role `dp_admin`, schema `test`) with the password `admin`. The tests also use six users with the password `web-test`:

- `web_admin`: role `dp_admin`, schema `test`.
- `web_viewer`: role `dp_console`.
- `web_api`: role `dp_api`.
- `web_policy`: role `dp_policy`.
- `web_other`: role `dp_admin`, schema `other`.
- `web_root`: role `dp_admin`, every schema.

No sync worker runs, so a sync run that you start stays `ENQUEUED`. A worker for the queues `control` and `schedules` runs, so cancel, resume and the schedule actions work.

### Write the docs

`devenv --profile default up docs` writes the page footers and the sidebar, then serves the wiki. devenv prints the address. The port is 18200, or the next free port when 18200 is busy. The page order is in `docs/.nav.json`.

The diagrams of Data model come from the database. Run `devenv --profile repo tasks run docs:build:model`. The task starts the databases, writes `docs/diagrams/` and the page, and stops the databases. Commit both after a migration.

`llms.txt` has every page except Style as plain text for an LLM. After a docs change, run `devenv --profile repo tasks run docs:build:llms` and commit the file.

### Database migrations and the local API

The header of `scripts/migrate.nu` explains the migrations. Run `migrate up`, `migrate status` or `migrate down` in the console shell with `PG_DATABASE_URL` set. Using the API shows how to get a token and call the local API.

---

Source: dev/tests.md

## Tests

Each component has two test tasks. `<component>:test:unit` needs no service. `<component>:test:int` starts the services that it needs. The rules for a test are in Style.

| Component | `:unit` (no service) | `:int` (services) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sync` | `pytest tests/unit -m "not postgres"` | `pytest tests/integration` and `pytest tests/unit -m postgres`, with PostgreSQL and SeaweedFS |
| `proxy` | The Lua specs | The Hurl files, with OpenResty, Valkey and a mock PostgREST |
| `console` | Vitest | The browser tests, with PostgreSQL, SeaweedFS, Keycloak, PostgREST and the console |
| `chart`, `nu` | The Helm chart tests and the Nushell tests | None |

### Run the suites

```bash
devenv --profile repo tasks run repo:test:unit                      # every :unit task
devenv --profile integration tasks run proxy:test:int               # one suite
devenv --profile integration tasks run sync:test:int console:test:int
```

Run one suite at a time on one machine. The suites share `.devenv/test-state`, and two runs can pick the same port. CI runs each suite on its own runner.

devenv skips a task when none of its input files changed since the last green run, and a skipped task takes under a second. A failed run leaves no state, so the task runs again. A change in `sync/src` runs the sync suite and the console suite, because the console tests seed their data with the sync code. To force a run, change an input or delete `.devenv/profiles/integration/state/tasks.db`. Every input is a file or a glob over files, because devenv compares a folder by its metadata, and a fresh checkout changes every folder. `utils.mkInputs` throws for a folder, and `utils.mkGlobs` throws for a file with an unlisted extension.

### The test stack

Each `:int` task runs `devenv test` for a profile. devenv starts the processes, waits for their `ready` checks and setup tasks and runs the tests.

| Profile | Processes |
| --- | --- |
| `sync` | PostgreSQL in Podman (the image of `Containerfile.pg`), SeaweedFS |
| `proxy` | Four OpenResty instances with a mock PostgREST each, and Valkey. The proxies start one after another, because each `lx exec` rewrites `proxy/lux.lock`. |
| `console` | The `sync` processes, Keycloak (the test image of `Containerfile.kc`), PostgREST, the console with its gateway, and a worker for the `control` queue |

Every process asks devenv for its port with `ports.<name>.allocate`. A port keeps its base number when it's free and moves up when it's busy. The setup passes the real number to the tests in environment variables. The base numbers are in `nix/stack/`. PostgreSQL starts empty on every run. `devenv --profile sync tasks run s3:clean:data` empties the object store.

Install Podman, or install Docker and set `CONTAINER_RUNTIME=docker`. The first PostgreSQL build is slow, and the engine keeps the layers. The image installs the `ducklake` extension while it builds, and an old layer fails the DuckLake tests. Refresh it with `podman build --no-cache`. To add a test container, declare a process with `utils.mkProcess { command = utils.podmanRun { ... }; }`, as `nix/stack/postgres.nix` does.

### Sync tests

The suite runs with `pytest-xdist` on up to four workers. Each worker clones its own database from `test_template`. A setup that every worker runs takes a file lock (`one_worker_at_a_time` in `sync/tests/helpers/core.py`). A new test uses only its own schema, so it runs on any worker.

- **Unit tests** check one function or template with every input. The template tests are in `sync/tests/unit/test_templates_*.py`, one file for each family: `duckdb`, `routing`, `filter`, `serving`, `access`, `maintenance` and `roles`. All but `duckdb` run on the real test server. The `rbac` tests also use Hypothesis, with 300 examples (`RBAC_EXAMPLES` sets another number).
- **Console SQL tests** build the console from the real migrations and templates with the fixture `console_api`. They cover the functions, the views, the import and the migrations on older data. `proxy/tests/unit/fixtures/console_config.json` is the document that `console.config()` writes, and a pytest case and the Lua specs both check it.
- **Integration tests** (`sync/tests/integration/`) check behavior across units. `test_pipeline.py` runs the body of `run_sync` with its real steps, a fake source and the real PostgreSQL, S3 and DuckLake.

These tests don't cover the API schemas, the database roles or what a token may do. The end-to-end suite covers those.

### Browser and proxy tests

`devenv --profile console test` runs the `playwright-bdd` features in `console/ui/tests/features/`: 94 scenarios in about 30 seconds, after about 25 seconds for the processes. The header of `console/ui/playwright.config.ts` explains the projects and the tags. Set `PLAYWRIGHT_GREP` to run some scenarios.

The proxy unit specs run with `nu scripts/lux.nu test`. The Hurl files in `proxy/tests/integration/` run through `devenv --profile proxy test` against the four proxies.

### End-to-end and load tests

The k6 suites need the k3d cluster, so CI doesn't run them. Run `cluster k6 e2e` before you merge a change to a permission, a role, an access policy or a view. The headers of `k6/e2e.js` and `k6/load.js` describe the scenarios, the log events, the traffic and the gates.

| Command | Work |
| --- | --- |
| `cluster k6 e2e` | Validates the deployed release. `--build` builds fresh images first, and `--scenarios a,b` runs a subset. |
| `cluster k6 smoke` | One virtual user for 40 seconds. |
| `cluster k6 load` | Ramps to `K6_PEAK_RATE` and has it. `--capacity` widens the gates. |

### Coverage

Each suite prints the lines that no test runs. There is no minimum. Read the report to find a branch of your own code that no test reaches.

| Suite | Command |
| --- | --- |
| `sync` | `PYTEST_ADDOPTS='--cov=sync --cov-branch --cov-report=term-missing:skip-covered' devenv --profile sync test` |
| Console | `pnpm --dir console/ui coverage` |
| Proxy | `nu scripts/lux.nu coverage` |

---

Source: dev/ci.md

## CI and releases

The workflow `.github/workflows/ci.yaml` checks, tests, builds and releases. A second workflow, `sast.yaml`, runs the security scan. The scripts are in `scripts/ci.nu`. Run `ci` in the `chart` shell to call them.

### Triggers

The pipeline runs on a push to `main`, on a pull request and on a manual start. A push or a pull request starts it only when it changes a path of the list `ci_paths`. The list has the component folders, `terraform/`, `nix/`, `k3d/`, `k6/`, `scripts/`, the workflows, the container files and the linter and devenv files. A change in `docs/` doesn't start it. A new run of a branch waits for the run before it, so two releases never overlap.
