A manual start has three inputs. `force_checks` runs every check and test without the saved task state. `force_full` does the same, builds every image and starts the release job, which still needs a release-level commit and a chart or image change. `provider_version` sets the version of the provider release.

### Jobs

```mermaid
%% CI jobs
flowchart LR
  push["Push, pull request<br/>or manual start"]
  subgraph checks["Parallel jobs"]
    changes["changes<br/>which images and chart changed"]
    repo["repo<br/>lint and unit tests"]
    sync["test-sync"]
    console["test-console"]
    proxy["test-proxy"]
    terraform["test-terraform"]
    sizes["profile-sizes"]
  end
  subgraph main["Only on main"]
    build["build-images<br/>fill the layer cache"] --> pushimg["push-images<br/>push and sign"] --> helm["helm<br/>publish the chart"]
    provider["terraform<br/>release the provider"]
  end
  push --> changes
  push --> repo
  push --> sync
  push --> console
  push --> proxy
  push --> terraform
  push --> sizes
  changes --> build
  repo -->|"tests pass"| pushimg
  sync --> pushimg
  console --> pushimg
  proxy --> pushimg
  repo --> provider
  terraform --> provider
```

| Job | Work |
| --- | --- |
| `changes` | Runs `ci changes`. It writes which images need a build and whether the chart needs a release. |
| `repo` | Runs `repo:lint` and `repo:test:unit`. |
| `test-sync`, `test-console`, `test-proxy` | Run the `:int` task of the component in the `integration` profile. A task runs only if one of its inputs changed. |
| `test-terraform` | Runs `tf:test:int`. Only `terraform` waits for it. |
| `profile-sizes` | Runs `nix:lint:closure` and `nix:lint:cmd`. No other job waits for it. |
| `build-images` | Builds each changed image and pushes nothing. It fills the layer cache while the tests run. |
| `push-images` | Waits for every test job. It builds each image again from the cache, pushes it and signs it, so no image of an untested commit reaches the registry. |
| `helm` | Releases the chart when the chart or an image changed. |
| `terraform` | Runs the action `terraform-release` on main after `repo` and `test-terraform` pass. The provider tag is `terraform-v*`. See Provider releases. |
| `cache-branch`, `cache-pr` | Delete the caches of a deleted branch and of a closed pull request. They're the only jobs that run on those events. |

Each job restores the task state of the last green run of `main` before it runs, and only a run on `main` saves it. Caches keep the uv cache, the pnpm store and the Nix fetcher files between runs, keyed by the lock files.

### Images

`ci changes` matches the files that changed since the last `helm-v*` tag against the table `IMAGES` in `scripts/lib.nu`. A push to `main` compares with the last tag. A pull request compares with its base. Each image goes to `ghcr.io/<repository>-<name>` with the short commit hash and `latest` as tags. The PostgreSQL image adds the prefix `18-` to the hash.

| Image | Rebuilds when this changes |
| --- | --- |
| `data-proxy-sync` | `sync/src/`, `sync/pyproject.toml`, `sync/uv.lock`, `console/migrations/` |
| `data-proxy-proxy` | `proxy/src/`, `proxy/lux.toml`, `proxy/lux.lock` |
| `data-proxy-console` | `console/ui/`, `console/notebooks/` |
| `data-proxy-jobs`, `data-proxy-postgres` | The Containerfile of the image |

### Chart releases

CI releases the Helm chart from Conventional Commits with `cog`. `cog` reads the commit subjects since the last `helm-v*` tag. A type with `!` makes a major version, `feat` a minor version and `fix` a patch version. Other types make no release.

| Command | Work |
| --- | --- |
| `ci version` | Prints the next version, or says that no release is due. It changes nothing. |
| `ci guard` | Skips the release when no chart file and no image path changed since the last tag, or when every release commit changed only the provider or the docs. |
| `ci images resolve`, `ci images pin` | Find the newest tag of each image and write the tags in `helm/values.yaml`, so a release never uses `latest`. |
| `ci release bump` | Runs `cog bump`. It sets the chart version, writes `CHANGELOG.md`, commits and tags. |
| `ci chart package`, `ci chart publish` | Package the chart and push it to the OCI registry. |
| `ci release push <tag>`, `ci release notes <tag>` | Push the commit and the tag in one push, and write the release notes. |

A commit that changes only `terraform/`, `docs/` or `llms.txt` never releases the chart, even as a `feat` or a `fix`. A later release still counts it in the version and the changelog.

The chart is published before the push. A failed publish leaves no tag, so run the workflow again. A failed push leaves a published chart and no tag. The next run publishes the same version again. `GITHUB_TOKEN` can't push to `main`. The job pushes with the deploy key `bot` (the secret `RELEASE_DEPLOY_KEY` of the environment `release`), which `protect-main` lists as a bypass.

Staging follows every chart. Production follows the chart tag `prod`, which a reviewer moves. See Production deploys.

`ci.nu` reads `CI_REPOSITORY`, `CI_REGISTRY`, `CI_REGISTRY_USER`, `CI_REGISTRY_TOKEN`, `CI_BOT_NAME`, `CI_BOT_EMAIL` and `CI_OUTPUT_FILE`, and it uses the GitHub Actions values when they're missing.

### Security scan

`sast.yaml` calls the shared action `prefeitura-rio/actions/sast`, which sends the code to SonarQube and the findings to DefectDojo. It needs the variables `SONARQUBE_URL` and `DEFECTDOJO_URL` and the secrets `SONARQUBE_TOKEN`, `DEFECTDOJO_TOKEN`, `TS_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` and `TS_OAUTH_SECRET`. `sonar-project.properties` excludes the tooling and the tests.

The run on `main` fails at the SonarQube quality gate. The log doesn't name the condition, so read the project dashboard on the SonarQube server. Checkov reports five `CKV_SECRET_6` findings although `.checkov.yaml` skips that check, so the action may not read the file.

The rule set `protect-main` protects `main`. It requires a pull request, one approval and the checks `Lint and unit tests`, `Sync integration tests`, `Console integration tests` and `Proxy integration tests`. Only the repository admin role and deploy keys bypass it.

---

Source: dev/promote.md

## Production deploys

Staging deploys every release. Production runs one chart version that a person approves.

### How the versions move

- The staging HelmRelease follows the range `2.x`, so Flux deploys each new chart within five minutes.
- The production HelmRelease follows the chart tag `prod` in `ghcr.io/prefeitura-rio/charts/data-proxy`. The tag points to one version, and production stays on it until the tag moves.

Staging runs 2.11.0, and then CI releases 2.12.0 and 2.13.0. Staging now runs 2.13.0, and production still runs 2.11.0. After an approval, production runs 2.13.0. A chart has every change before it, so 2.13.0 includes 2.12.0.

### Approve a deploy

The workflow `promote.yaml` runs after each CI run on `main`. It compares the newest chart with the version of the tag `prod`. When they differ, it starts the job `Promote to production` in the environment `production`, and the job waits for a reviewer. The job name shows the version that production runs and the version to promote.

1. Open the run in GitHub Actions and choose Review deployments.
2. Check that staging is healthy with the version that you promote.
3. Approve. The job moves the tag `prod` and writes `prod: 2.11.0 to 2.13.0` in its summary.
4. Flux deploys the chart to production within five minutes.

A newer run with a chart to promote cancels the job that waits. The environment `production` has one waiting job at a time, for the newest chart. An approval of an old run does nothing when a newer chart exists.

### Roll back or choose a version

Start `promote.yaml` by hand with the input `version`, such as `2.11.0`. The job needs the same approval. A rollback leaves staging alone. A CI run on `main` that has a chart to promote cancels a rollback that waits. Approve the rollback before the next merge, or start it again.

### Commands

| Command | Work |
| --- | --- |
| `ci chart prod` | Prints the version that production runs. |
| `ci chart next` | Writes the version to promote, the version of production and whether they differ. |
| `ci chart promote <version>` | Moves the tag `prod` to a released version. `--if-latest` skips an old version. |

### Settings

The reviewers are in the GitHub settings of the repository, under Environments and `production`. The infra repository has the production HelmRelease. It reads the tag with an `OCIRepository` whose `ref.tag` is `prod`. CI and releases describes the chart release that comes before a promotion.

---

Source: dev/provider.md

## Provider releases

The Terraform provider has its own versions and its own releases. A chart release doesn't release the provider, and a provider release doesn't change the chart or production.

### How a release happens

CI runs on every push to `main`. When `repo` and `test-terraform` pass, the job `terraform` of CI runs the action `terraform-release` on the same commit. The action decides whether a release is due. The job doesn't wait for the chart release. A failed provider release turns the run red, so the chart stays out of staging.

1. `ci terraform next` reads the commits that changed `terraform/` since the last tag `terraform-v<version>`.
2. A `feat` or a breaking commit raises the minor version, and a `fix` raises the patch. Other types give no release. The major version stays 0 until a person sets it.
3. `ci terraform release` builds the provider for Linux, macOS and Windows, packs each binary in a zip archive, and signs the checksums with the GPG key.
4. It creates the GitHub Release `terraform-v<version>` with the archives, the checksum file and its signature. The notes list the commit subjects under `terraform/`.
5. `ci terraform registry` writes the registry files from every release and uploads them to a bucket.

A tag that exists already makes the job fail, so a version never changes after its release. To release a version by hand, start CI with the input `provider_version`.

### The registry

The registry is a set of static JSON files, as the [registry protocol](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/internet-documentation/provider-registry-protocol) describes. The release workflow writes them to a public bucket. The ingress of Data Proxy sends `/.well-known/terraform.json` and `/v1/providers/` to that bucket, so the host of the API also serves the registry. The archives stay in GitHub Releases, and the JSON files point to them.

The provider and the scripts have no host name. Every name comes from a variable.

| Variable | Where | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TERRAFORM_REGISTRY_HOST` | GitHub repository variable | The host that serves the registry. The provider reports `<host>/<namespace>/data-proxy` as its address. |
| `TERRAFORM_REGISTRY_NAMESPACE` | GitHub repository variable | The namespace in the address and in the registry paths. |
| `TERRAFORM_REGISTRY_BUCKET` | GitHub repository variable | The bucket that stores the registry files. |
| `GCP_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_PROVIDER`, `GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` | GitHub repository variables | The identity that writes the bucket. |
| `GPG_PRIVATE_KEY`, `GPG_PASSPHRASE` | GitHub secrets | The key that signs the checksums. |
| `ingress.registry.bucket` | Chart value | The bucket that the ingress serves. An empty value adds no route. |

Terraform and OpenTofu refuse a provider from a registry unless a GPG key signs its checksums. The workflow gets the public key from the private key, so the secrets are the only key input.

### Set up the registry

1. Create a GPG key without an expiry date, and add its private key and its passphrase as the secrets `GPG_PRIVATE_KEY` and `GPG_PASSPHRASE`.
2. In the infra repository, set the variable `terraform_registry` of the GCP module with the repository that publishes. Apply the module. It creates the bucket, the service account and the identity pool.
3. Set `terraform_registry_enabled` of the k8s module, and apply it. It adds the route values for the ingress and the Istio objects for the storage host.
4. Copy the outputs of the GCP module into the GitHub variables of the table above. The workflow does nothing while `TERRAFORM_REGISTRY_HOST` is empty.

The route needs a chart version that has `ingress.registry`. Staging gets each chart first, and production waits for an approval.

### Use a release

```hcl
terraform {
  required_providers {
    data-proxy = {
      source = "registry.example.com/example/data-proxy"
    }
  }
}
```

Replace the source with `<host>/<namespace>/data-proxy` of your registry. A local name has no underscore, and Terraform reads the provider of `data_proxy_table` from the part before the first underscore. So each resource needs `provider = data-proxy`. `terraform init` downloads the archive and checks the signature and the checksum.

### Roll back and rotate

- A bad release stays in the registry. Fix it with a new `fix` commit. Or delete the GitHub Release and run `ci terraform registry` again, which drops the version from the files.
- To rotate the key, add the new key and rerun `ci terraform registry`. A release that the old key signed fails to install with the new key, so keep the old key until you release again.

### Commands

| Command | Work |
| --- | --- |
| `ci terraform next` | Writes `release` and `version` from the commits since the last provider tag. |
| `ci terraform release <version>` | Builds, signs and publishes the GitHub Release. |
| `ci terraform registry` | Writes the registry files from the releases and uploads them to the bucket. |

CI and releases describes the chart release.

---

Source: dev/provider-development.md

## Provider development

This page says how to build, run and test the Terraform provider in `terraform/`. Terraform provider describes what it does, and Provider releases describes how it ships.

### Build and test

Run the commands in `terraform/`. The module has its own `go.mod`, so the commands don't build the rest of the repository.

```bash
cd terraform
go build ./...
go vet ./...
go test ./...
```

### Local development

Terraform downloads a provider from the registry. To test your local binary, add a `dev_overrides` block to the command-line configuration file `~/.terraformrc`. The block tells Terraform to load the provider from a folder on your machine.

1. Build the binary with the name that Terraform expects. `terraform/bin/` is in `.gitignore`.

   ```bash
   cd terraform
   go build -o bin/terraform-provider-data-proxy .
   ```

2. Add the block to `~/.terraformrc`. Write the absolute path of `terraform/bin` in your clone.

   ```hcl
   provider_installation {
     dev_overrides {
       "registry.example.com/example/data-proxy" = "/home/you/data-proxy/terraform/bin"
     }
     direct {}
   }
   ```

3. Run `terraform validate` or `terraform plan` in a folder with a configuration that uses the provider. Don't run `terraform init` for this provider. Terraform prints a warning that says the override is active.

The `direct {}` block keeps the normal download for every other provider. Build the binary again after each change. Terraform loads the new binary on the next command. To use the file only in one shell, set `TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE` to its path. Remove the block when you want the registry version again.

#### Acceptance tests

An acceptance test runs the provider through Terraform against a real API. It's a `TestAcc` function in `terraform/internal/provider/`. It runs only when `TF_ACC` is set, so `go test ./...` compiles it and skips it.

```bash
devenv --profile terraform tasks run tf:test:int
```

The task runs `devenv --profile terraform-acc test`. That profile starts the console stack: PostgreSQL, SeaweedFS, Keycloak, PostgREST and the console. It sets `TF_ACC=1` and the `DATA_PROXY_*` variables. The provider calls the local PostgREST. It gets its token from the local Keycloak with the test client `terraform`. That client has the role `dp_admin` and the `schemas` claim `*`. The stack needs Podman, as the tests page says.

To run one test, start the console stack and set the variables yourself. PostgREST listens on port 13000 and Keycloak on port 18180 when the ports are free. Run `go test` in the `terraform-acc` shell, because the tests call OpenTofu.

```bash
devenv --profile console up -d
devenv processes wait
export TF_ACC=1 DATA_PROXY_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:13000 DATA_PROXY_CLIENT_ID=terraform DATA_PROXY_CLIENT_SECRET=test-secret
export DATA_PROXY_TOKEN_URL=http://localhost:18180/realms/dev/protocol/openid-connect/token
devenv --profile terraform shell -- go -C terraform test -count=1 -run TestAccPermissionsDataSource ./...
```

A new acceptance test uses the helpers in `acceptance_test.go`. Give `testAccPreCheck` to `PreCheck` and `testAccProviderFactories` to `ProtoV6ProviderFactories`. Name each object with `testAccName`, which returns `tfacc` and 10 random letters and digits. Register `testAccCleanup` for each object, so a failed step leaves no row behind. Register a parent before its children, because the cleanups run in reverse order.

The client `terraform` has the `schemas` claim `*`, so a test can add projects and schemas. The stack runs no sync worker, so a schema never gets provisioned. Set `timeouts { create = "0s" }` on a schema to skip the wait. The schema `test` is provisioned at start, so use it for an access policy.

---

Source: operations/index.md

## Operations

These pages are for the people who deploy and run Data Proxy. Start with the Helm chart, and then read the page for your task.

| Task | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Install the chart and choose the images | Helm Chart |
| Understand the first start of the database | Initialization |
| Expose the API, the console and the notebooks | Ingress |
| See which pods run and how they scale | Topology and KEDA Scaling |
| Harden pods, network and images | Hardening |
| Set an environment variable | Environment Variables, Proxy variables and Console variables |
| Tune the memory and the spill of the sync workers | DuckDB Memory and Spill |
| Make lookups on one value read fewer files | Lookup Layout |
| Watch the system | Metrics |
| Back up and restore the access policy | Backups |

Source: operations/helm.md

## Helm Chart

The Helm chart deploys Data Proxy: the CloudNativePG (CNPG) cluster, PgDog, PostgREST, the proxy, the sync workers, the console and the notebooks.

### Objects

The chart creates these main objects. Each name starts with the release name.

| Object | Kind | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The release name | CNPG `Cluster` | The PostgreSQL primary and standbys. |
| `-proxy`, `-postgrest`, `-pgdog` | Deployment | The serving layer. KEDA scales the proxy and PostgREST. |
| `-sync` | Deployment | The sync workers. KEDA scales them. |
| `-recovery` | Deployment | Recovers the DBOS workflows that a dead sync pod left behind. |
| `-console`, `-notebooks` | Deployment | The console and the notebook site. |
| `-swagger-ui` | Deployment | The Swagger UI of the API. |
| `-swagger-ui-schemas` | ConfigMap | The schema list of the Swagger UI. A sync worker keeps it current. |
| `-configure-db`, `-migrate-db`, `-provision` | Job | The install Jobs of Initialization. `configure-db` and `provision` also have a suspended CronJob of the same name. |
| `-s3-bootstrap` | Job | Creates the S3 bucket or waits for it. |
| `-backup`, `-maintenance` | CronJob | The access policy backup and the database maintenance. Maintenance also deletes the DBOS workflows that finished, and the errors that the sync recorded, more than `jobs.maintenance.workflowRetentionDays` days ago (90 by default). |
| `-duckdb` | PersistentVolumeClaim | The shared volume of the DuckDB secrets. |

### Prerequisites

Install [KEDA](https://keda.sh/docs/latest/deploy/). Install Istio when `ingress.enabled` is `true`. Install the CloudNativePG operator 1.26 or newer, because the cluster uses `probes.readiness.type` and `maximumLag`. The k3d stack tests chart 0.29.1 of the operator, which is operator 1.30.1.

### Install

```bash
helm install data-proxy \
  oci://ghcr.io/prefeitura-rio/charts/data-proxy \
  --version <chart-version> \
  --values my-values.yaml
```

See `helm/values.yaml` for all values.

### Chart tests

```bash
devenv --profile default tasks run chart:test:unit
```

The task runs Helm lint, Helm unit tests and Kubeconform.

### Images

The chart pins repository images in `helm/values.yaml`. Released chart values don't use `latest` for Data Proxy images.

### Proxy

Configure the OpenResty caching proxy under `proxy`. Values include `cacheTtl`, `cacheRedisDb`, `maxCacheBodyBytes`, `maxInflight`, `configUrl` and `configRefreshSeconds`.

The chart passes these values to the proxy Deployment as `PROXY_*` environment variables. The proxy connects to Redis directly. See Proxy for request flow and cache behavior.

### Serving values

These values tune the serving layer. The defaults are in `helm/values.yaml`. The columns of the tables are the value, its default and what it does.

#### PostgREST

| Value | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `postgrest.maxRows` | `1000` | The most rows that PostgREST returns for one request. The sync worker gets it as `AGGREGATE_MAX_ROWS`, so an aggregate function gives at most as many rows. |
| `postgrest.aggregatesEnabled` | `true` | Allows `avg()`, `count()`, `max()`, `min()` and `sum()` in `select`. |
| `postgrest.dbPool` | `24` | The backend connections that each PostgREST pod opens. |
| `postgrest.dbPoolAcquisitionTimeout` | `3` | Seconds that a request waits for a backend connection before it fails. |
| `postgrest.dbPoolMaxIdleTime` | `300` | Seconds before PostgREST closes an idle backend connection. |
| `postgrest.preStopSleepSeconds` | `5` | Seconds that a stopping pod waits before it closes its port. The mesh needs this time to stop sending requests. |
| `postgrest.jwksUri` | empty | The address of the JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) that checks the JSON Web Token (JWT) signature. |
| `postgrest.jwtSecret` | empty | A shared HS256 secret. When set, it replaces `jwksUri`. |
| `postgrest.proxyUri` | empty | The public address that PostgREST and the Swagger UI show in the API description. |

#### PgDog and Redis

| Value | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pgdog.poolSize` | `24` | The connections that one PgDog pod opens to the primary, and as many to the standbys. Keep `pgdog.replicas` × `poolSize` well below `max_connections`. |
| `cnpg.duckdb.maxMemory` | `1GB` | The memory of each DuckDB backend of PostgreSQL. One heavy read took about 1.4 GiB, and six of them stopped a standby with a 6Gi limit. In the worst case, `pgdog.poolSize` × 1.4 GiB must fit `cnpg.resources.limits.memory`. |
| `redis.host`, `redis.port` | required, `6379` | The Redis address that the proxy uses for its cache. A host name with no dot gets the namespace of the release, because nginx doesn't use the search domains of the pod. |
| `redis.writeKey`, `redis.passwordKey` | `REDIS_WRITE`, `REDIS_PASSWORD` | The key names in the Secret `redis.existingSecret` that the sync workers read. |
| `redis.writerAddress`, `redis.writerHost`, `redis.writerPort` | `redis-writer:6379`, `redis-writer`, `6379` | The address that the chart writes into the Redis Secret. It makes the Secret only when `redis.existingSecret` is empty. |

#### Proxy, mesh and service account

| Value | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `proxy.largeClientHeaderBuffers` | `4 64k` | The number and size of the buffers for a large request header, as in the nginx directive `large_client_header_buffers`. |
| `ingress.sidecarInject` | `true` | Adds the Istio sidecar label to the console and notebooks pods. |
| `serviceAccount.create`, `serviceAccount.name` | `true`, `data-proxy` | Makes the ServiceAccount of the sync pods, or names an existing one. |
| `serviceAccount.annotations` | empty | Annotations for the ServiceAccount, such as the Workload Identity annotation for BigQuery. |

### Versioning

Images and the chart have separate versions. Each push to `main` that changes an image publishes it with the short commit hash as the tag, for example `data-proxy-sync:caa0da9`. The PostgreSQL image adds the prefix `18-`.

A chart release pins the newest tag of each image in `helm/values.yaml`. A released chart doesn't use `latest` for a repository image.

The chart version comes from the Conventional Commits since the previous release. A `feat` raises the minor version, a `fix` raises the patch version and a `!` raises the major version. Don't change `helm/Chart.yaml` by hand. See Chart releases.

---

---

Source: operations/initialization.md

## Initialization

The chart sets up the database storage, runs the initialization Jobs and waits until the database is ready.

### Database storage

CloudNativePG (CNPG) creates one retained PostgreSQL PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) per instance. Configure the size under `cnpg.storage.size`. Kubernetes doesn't support PVC size reduction. Remove retained PVCs only as a separate destructive operation.

SeaweedFS stores Parquet data in its own configured storage. The PostgreSQL database uses pg_duckdb to read Parquet. pg_duckdb is an extension, not a separate database service.

### Database initialization and readiness

Three Jobs prepare the database, and each one waits for what it needs.

```mermaid
%% Install Jobs sequence
sequenceDiagram
  participant h as Helm install or upgrade
  participant cfg as configure-db Job
  participant mig as migrate-db Job
  participant prov as provision Job
  participant pg as PostgreSQL primary
  participant pgr as PostgREST
  h->>cfg: start
  cfg->>pg: wait for the writer
  cfg->>pg: roles, rbac, state tables, functions
  cfg->>pg: DuckDB secrets and grants
  h->>mig: start
  mig->>pg: wait for the state tables
  mig->>pg: dbos migrate
  mig->>pg: goose up (console schema)
  h->>prov: start
  prov->>pg: wait for the console tables
  prov->>pg: console functions and triggers
  prov->>pg: fill an empty configuration
  prov->>pg: schemas, access policies, grants
  prov->>pg: set pgrst.db_schemas
  opt the schema list changed
    pg->>pgr: NOTIFY after the standbys replay
  end
```

| Job | Waits for | Work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `configure-db` | Its CNPG writer. | Runs idempotent SQL with `ON_ERROR_STOP=1`, as `ops`. CNPG owns two roles, `ops` and `duckdb`. The Job owns the system objects (see below). It also writes the persistent DuckDB secrets, which only a superuser may write. |
| `migrate-db` | The last of the state tables. | Runs in the sync image. It runs `dbos migrate` and `goose up`, and it owns the `console` schema of the console. The image contains `goose` and the files of `console/migrations`. |
| `provision` | The `console` tables. | Runs on every install and upgrade. See below. |

The system objects of `configure-db` are:

- the request roles: `anon`, the `dp_*` roles of `rbac.toml` and the `serving` login
- the `rbac` schema
- the state, error and scope tables of the engine
- the pre-request function and its grants
- the functions that reload PostgREST
- the maintenance procedures

`provision` also exists as a suspended CronJob, `<release>-provision`, that a Job comes from when a schema changes (see Run a Job on demand). On install and upgrade, it does these steps:

- It first installs the functions and triggers of the console, which need the tables and views of the migrations.
- It fills an empty configuration once from `sync.config`. Afterward the console controls the configuration.
- It grants the baseline role (`auth.userRole`, which every `dp_*` role is a member of) its rights on the `console` schema. The rights are wide, and each view, row policy and function asks for the permission of the token.
- For each schema in `console.schemas`, it creates the PostgreSQL schema and its access policy, with row policies that ask for `read_policy` and `edit_policy`.
- It grants the anonymous role the right to call `console.config()`, the one function that the proxy reads.
- It sets `pgrst.db_schemas` on the `serving` login to the schemas plus `console`, in that order, because the first schema is the default profile of PostgREST.
- It tells PostgREST to reload only when that list changes. The database waits until every standby replayed the change, then sends a `NOTIFY` on the `pgrst` channel.

PostgREST serves a schema that an editor adds within seconds. The job drops a schema that an editor removes: the files first, then the catalog, then the schema of the database. See Console.

The header of `scripts/migrate.nu` explains what belongs to the chart and what belongs to the migrations.

### Run a Job on demand

`configure-db` and `provision` each exist twice. One is a Job named by the release revision, which Helm runs on every install and upgrade. The other is a suspended CronJob, `<release>-configure-db` and `<release>-provision`.

A suspended CronJob never runs on a clock. It contains the pod definition, and both objects get it from one helper, so they can't differ. Something that needs the work creates a Job from the CronJob:

| Context | Who creates the Job | What runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Install and upgrade | Helm | The per-revision Jobs, with every schema (`PROVISION_ALL=true`). |
| An editor adds or removes a schema in the console | The sync worker. A trigger on `console.schemas` queues the workflow `provision_schemas`. | `provision`: what's pending and what's removed. |
| The start of every sync run | The sync worker, with the same call | `provision`. A lost event or a drift heals here. |
| An operator, after a change of `rbac.toml` or a failed run | A person | `configure-db` or `provision`. |

The one-line command for a person:

```bash
kubectl -n data-proxy create job --from=cronjob/<release>-provision provision-by-hand
kubectl -n data-proxy create job --from=cronjob/<release>-configure-db configure-db-by-hand
```

The sync ServiceAccount may read the CronJobs and create Jobs in its namespace, and nothing more.

The PostgREST Deployment uses an HTTP readiness probe on `/`. It isn't Ready until PostgREST is serving its configured schema.

---

Source: operations/ingress.md

## Ingress

The chart exposes the console, the notebooks and the API through the Istio gateway.

```mermaid
%% Ingress paths
flowchart LR
  client["Client"]
  subgraph gateway["Istio gateway"]
    vs["VirtualService"]
  end
  jwt["JWT check<br/>ingress.auth.enabled"]
  subgraph api["API host"]
    proxy["Proxy to PostgREST<br/>/ and the tables"]
    docs["Swagger UI<br/>/docs"]
    console["Console<br/>/console"]
  end
  subgraph nb["Notebook host"]
    site["Notebook site"]
  end
  client --> vs
  vs -->|"/ and /docs"| jwt
  jwt --> proxy
  jwt --> docs
  vs -->|"/console<br/>signs in with OIDC"| console
  vs -->|"other host,<br/>other origin"| site
```

### Console and notebooks

`console.enabled` and `notebooks.enabled` add the web console and the static site of the notebooks. Each one has a Deployment and a Service.

The console answers on the `/console` path of `ingress.host`, the host of the API. The notebooks have their own host. A notebook is code that a user can edit, so it must never share an origin with the console.

Both use the image `console.image`, and the notebooks Deployment starts it with another command.

| Value | Contains |
| --- | --- |
| `ingress.host`, `ingress.scheme` | The public origin of the API, the docs and the console. |
| `console.oidc.issuer`, `console.oidc.clientId`, `console.oidc.clientSecret` | The confidential client of the identity provider. `console.oidc.existingSecret` names a Secret with `OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET` and `COOKIE_SECRET` instead. |
| `console.storage.endpoint` | The storage endpoint that the signed links use. The browser must reach it. The notebook policy allows only this host. |
| `console.storage.existingSecret` | A Secret with `accessKey`, `secretKey`, and optionally `schemaCredentials` with a JSON object of credentials limited to one schema. Without it, the console signs with the read-only credential of the chart. |
| `notebooks.host` | The public host of the notebooks. It uses `ingress.scheme`. |
| `console.resources`, `notebooks.resources` | The resource requests and limits of the two Deployments. |
| `s3.bootstrap.corsOrigins` | The origins that the cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rule of the bucket allows. Set it to the notebook origin. The bootstrap Job sets the rule through the S3 API, and it skips a GCS endpoint. |
| `console.storage.perSchemaIdentities`, `console.storage.adminSecret`, `console.storage.iamEndpoint` | One storage identity for each schema, made by the console with the admin credential of `adminSecret` or of the S3 secret of the chart. SeaweedFS needs the flag `-s3.iam.readOnly=false` (`seaweedfs.allInOne.extraArgs`). |
| `auth.signerRole` | The login that the console uses to read the catalog. |

The chart makes a read-only identity next to the admin identity of the S3 secret, in the keys `S3_READER_ACCESS_KEY` and `S3_READER_SECRET_KEY`, and in `seaweedfs_s3_config`. `configure-db` creates the signer login, and its password is in the Secret `<release>-signer`.

### Istio ingress

Set `ingress.enabled` to create the VirtualService. Set `ingress.auth.enabled` to create JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication and authorization resources. Create the configured Gateway before installing the chart.

The values `ingress.retries.attempts`, `perTryTimeout` and `retryOn` set the retries of the gateway. Don't put `503` in `retryOn`. The proxy answers `503` with `Retry-After` when it sheds a request, because too many requests wait for PostgREST. A retry sends the same request again and adds load to a system that's already full. The proxy already retries PostgREST itself, so use `reset,connect-failure`.

---

Source: operations/topology.md

## Topology

This page shows what the chart deploys, how the pods connect and how each workload scales. Read it to understand a failure or to size a release. The chart always deploys the same pieces:

| Part       | Role                                                                                                                             |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| PostgreSQL | One CloudNativePG (CNPG) Cluster with a primary and at least one standby. `cnpg.autoscaling` adds standbys under load. CNPG promotes a standby on failure. |
| PgDog      | A pooler in front of PostgreSQL. It sends read-only transactions to the standbys and every other transaction to the primary. It runs `pgdog.replicas` pods (two by default), and no scaler. |
| PostgREST  | One Deployment that connects to PgDog. `postgrest.autoscaling` scales it.                                                        |
| Proxy      | Sends every request to PostgREST.                                                                                                |

```mermaid
%% Deployment topology
flowchart TD
  gateway["Istio gateway"]
  s3[("Object storage<br/>SeaweedFS")]
  redis[("Redis cache")]
  subgraph release["Helm release"]
    proxy["Proxy<br/>KEDA: 1 to 6"]
    postgrest["PostgREST<br/>KEDA: 1 to 6"]
    pgdog["PgDog<br/>2 pods, no scaler"]
    ro["Service -ro"]
    rw["Service -rw"]
    sync["Sync workers<br/>KEDA: 3 to 15"]
    console["Console and notebooks"]
    subgraph cnpg["CNPG: KEDA 2 to 6"]
      primary["Primary"]
      standbys["Standbys"]
      secrets[("DuckDB secrets<br/>shared volume")]
      primary -->|"WAL replication"| standbys
      primary -->|"writes"| secrets
      standbys -->|"reads"| secrets
    end
    proxy --> postgrest
    postgrest -->|"queries"| pgdog
    postgrest -->|"LISTEN connection"| rw
    pgdog -->|"read-only transactions"| ro
    pgdog -->|"other transactions"| rw
    ro --> standbys
    rw --> primary
    sync -->|"DBOS state and catalog"| rw
    console -->|"views and actions"| postgrest
  end
  gateway --> proxy
  gateway --> console
  proxy -->|"cache"| redis
  sync -->|"write Parquet"| s3
  cnpg -->|"pg_duckdb reads Parquet"| s3
```

PostgREST starts a read-only transaction for each `GET`, and a read/write transaction for each write and each function call. PgDog reads that option from the `BEGIN`. A `GET` goes to a standby, and a write goes to the primary. With one instance, or while no standby can serve, PgDog reads from the primary.

PgDog pools transactions, so many PostgREST connections share a few PostgreSQL backends. The pool uses the `serving` login from the `<release>-pgdog-users` Secret.

PgDog finds the standbys through the `-ro` Service of the cluster, so it sees them as one host. Kubernetes picks the standby for each new connection. PgDog closes a server connection after about one hour, so a new standby takes its share within that time.

The lag of a standby works like this:

- CNPG takes a standby that's more than `cnpg.maxReplicaLag` behind out of the `-ro` Service until it catches up.
- After a pod change, CNPG updates the standbys first, then switches the primary to a standby (`cnpg.primaryUpdateMethod`).
- A standby that stops answering leaves the Service within about six seconds.
- PgDog reads the log position of each database every second. It bans a standby that's more than 16 MiB behind (`ban_replica_lag_bytes`) until the standby catches up. An idle primary has lag 0.
- A pool that can't connect, or that keeps a read waiting for more than 20 seconds (`checkout_timeout`), gets no requests for 10 seconds. The next read goes to the primary.

The PostgREST connection address lists PgDog first and the `-rw` Service second. PostgREST asks for a read/write session for its `LISTEN` connection. PgDog never gives one, so the listener connects to the primary. A `NOTIFY` on the primary then reaches PostgREST.

A read that follows a write can reach a standby that hasn't replayed it. The lag stays below `cnpg.maxReplicaLag`, and it's normally a few milliseconds. A caller that needs the new row reads it from the answer of the write (`Prefer: return=representation`).

Only the primary keeps state. A scaled-down standby loses its volume.

Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling (KEDA) sets the count of every workload except PgDog. Helm sets only `pgdog.replicas`, because each extra PgDog pod opens its own pools and adds connections to PostgreSQL. Helm never sets `replicas` or `instances` on any other workload, so an upgrade can't conflict with a scaler.

Default scaling:

| Workload | Default trigger | Minimum | Maximum | Wait before scale-down |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cluster (CNPG instances) | Active PostgREST sessions per instance. The target comes from the CPU limit and the DuckDB threads. | 2 | 6 | 300 s |
| PostgREST | CPU at 70% and memory at 90% of the request. | 1 | 6 | 300 s |
| Proxy | CPU at 70% of the request. | 1 | 6 | 300 s |
| Sync workers | The count of active DBOS workflows. See KEDA Scaling. | 3 | 15 | 60 s |
| PgDog | None. Helm sets `pgdog.replicas`. | 2 | 2 | Not applicable |
| Redis | None, unless you supply custom triggers. | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable |

Set `triggers` in an `autoscaling` block to replace a default. KEDA can't scale a CNPG resource on CPU, because the resource has no pod selector.

Notes for the cluster:

- Every instance has the same `cnpg.resources`.
- The chart raises the instance floor to 2 (one primary and one standby). Raise it more with `cnpg.autoscaling.minReplicaCount`.
- Replication is asynchronous, so a changed access policy can reach a standby a moment later. To make `access_policy` writes wait for a standby, set `cnpg.postgresql.synchronous` (for example `{method: any, number: 1, dataDurability: preferred}`) after the cluster has scaled up. CNPG rejects it on one instance, so it can't be a default. A trigger then uses `remote_apply` for access policy writes only.
- The DuckDB secrets (the S3 secret `s3`, and the catalog secrets `ducklake_catalog_pg` and `ducklake_catalog`) are files in `/duckdb/secrets` on the shared `<release>-duckdb` volume. The chart creates the volume when `ducklake.secrets.storage.storageClass` is set. Set it before you serve data, because the console adds schemas after the install and the chart can't know them. Every instance mounts that folder at `~/.duckdb/stored_secrets`, and only the primary writes it. The catalogs aren't on this volume: they live in the `ducklake` database, and every standby gets its own copy through replication. After the first upgrade that adds a secret, run `helm upgrade` once more so `configure-db` writes it to the volume.
- Each PostgreSQL backend starts its own DuckDB and attaches the catalog on its first aggregate, which takes about 160 ms. PgDog keeps a server connection for one hour, so a backend then serves many requests at 10 to 15 ms each.
- DuckDB reads the S3 secret once for each PostgreSQL backend. When the S3 keys change, `helm upgrade` rolls PgDog and the PostgREST pods, so every backend reloads the secret.

Redis has no autoscaler. The proxy needs `redis.host`, and the chart fails to render without it. Helm Chart lists the Redis values.

---

Source: operations/hardening.md

## Hardening

This page describes how the chart limits what a pod, a network peer and an image can do. Each default is a value that you can override.

### Pods

Every container drops all Linux capabilities, forbids privilege escalation and uses the default seccomp profile. Every pod must run as a non-root user. The chart sets a numeric user for each container, because Kubernetes can't check a user that has only a name.

| Component | User | Read-only root file system | Reason for a difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Console, notebooks | 1000 | Yes | |
| PostgREST, PgDog | 1000 | Yes | |
| Proxy | 10001 | Yes | nginx writes the file with its process number and its temporary files to `/tmp`, an `emptyDir` volume. |
| Sync worker | 10001 | No | DuckDB and Python write to the home folder. |
| Jobs image | 1000 | No | Nushell writes its history and its settings to the home folder. |
| Swagger UI | root | No | nginx writes its settings and its cache, and then it runs the workers as its own user. The container keeps only the capabilities that this needs. |

The values `securityContext.pod` and `securityContext.container` have the defaults. The values `securityContext.components.<name>` replace a default for one component. An init container of a pod uses the settings of its own image, so a `wait-for-postgres` step runs as the user of the Jobs image.

### Network policies

The chart doesn't render a network policy by default. Set `networkPolicy.enabled` to `true` to limit the traffic that comes into the pods. Your network plugin must enforce policies. The policies don't limit the traffic that leaves a pod.

| Pods | Port | Allowed sources |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Proxy | 8080 | The Istio ingress gateway |
| Proxy | 8081 (admin) | The sync workers |
| PostgREST | 3000 | The proxy and the console |
| PostgREST | metrics port | The monitoring namespace |
| PgDog | 6432 | PostgREST |
| PgDog | 9090 (metrics) | The monitoring namespace |
| Swagger UI, console, notebooks | The port of the pod | The Istio ingress gateway |

Three values set the sources:

- `networkPolicy.gatewayNamespace` is the namespace of the gateway pods. The default is `istio-ingress`.
- `networkPolicy.monitoringNamespace` is the namespace that reads the metrics. An empty value opens no metrics port.
- `networkPolicy.extraPeers` is a list of more peers for the proxy and PostgREST. Add the pods of a load test here.

Redis and the database are outside the chart. Limit them in the repository that deploys them.

### Console headers

The console sends a content security policy on each page. The policy allows only scripts, styles, images and connections of the console itself. SvelteKit adds a hash or a nonce for its own inline script.

The hook of the console adds two sources that only the settings know. The notebook address joins `frame-src`, and the address of the identity provider joins `form-action`, because the sign-out form leads there. The hook also sets `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy: same-origin` and `Cache-Control: no-store`. A route that sets its own `Cache-Control` keeps it.

Every browser scenario fails if the browser reports a refusal under the policy.

### Images

The chart pins PostgREST, PgDog and Swagger UI by tag and digest. Each `Containerfile` pins its base images the same way. The digest decides which image runs, and the tag tells you the version.

To update an image, read the digest of the new tag from its registry, and change the tag and the digest in one commit.

CI signs each image that it pushes with a keyless cosign signature. It also attaches a provenance record and a software bill of materials. To check a signature, run:

```bash
cosign verify ghcr.io/prefeitura-rio/data-proxy-sync:<tag> \
  --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/prefeitura-rio/data-proxy/.github/workflows/ci.yaml@.*' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
```

---

Source: operations/environment.md

## Environment Variables

Application defaults apply outside Helm. Helm sets the same values through the chart templates. The Default column contains the default of the application. A row names the chart value where the chart sets another one. The worker doesn't print a password or a key. It stops at start if a required variable is missing.

### Connections

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PG_DATABASE_URL` | required | PostgreSQL data source name (DSN) for the target database. |
| `REDIS_WRITE` | `redis://localhost:6379/0` | Redis address for cache writes. |
| `DBOS_SYSTEM_DATABASE_URL` | required | DBOS system database address. |
| `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` | unset | BigQuery credentials file. Omit with Workload Identity. |

`schemas.<schema>.source` contains only non-secret source configuration. Put BigQuery and future source credentials in environment variables or Kubernetes Secrets.

### S3 and DuckLake

These variables set the object store and the DuckLake catalogs.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `S3_BUCKET` | `test-bucket` | SeaweedFS/S3 bucket for scratch and DuckLake data. |
| `S3_ENDPOINT` | `localhost:8333` | S3 endpoint host and port. |
| `S3_REGION` | `us-east-1` | S3 region name. |
| `S3_USE_SSL` | `false` | Use TLS for S3. |
| `S3_ACCESS_KEY` | required | S3 access key. |
| `S3_SECRET_KEY` | required | S3 secret key. |
| `S3_SCRATCH_PREFIX` | `tmp` | The folder of the temporary extraction Parquet files. The sync worker deletes everything under it when a run ends, so each install that shares a bucket needs its own. The chart sets it with `s3.scratchPrefix`. |
| `S3_IDENTITIES` | `false` | Delete the S3 identities of schemas that the console no longer lists (the step `cleanup_s3_credentials`). The chart turns it on with `console.storage.perSchemaIdentities`. |
| `DUCKLAKE_CATALOG_URL` | required | Connection URI of the catalog database, with the `ops` role. The chart builds it from the password Secret of `ops`. Each schema writes to its own metadata schema. |
| `DUCKLAKE_CATALOG_PATH` | `ducklake` | S3 prefix for the per-schema Parquet data. |
| `DUCKLAKE_TARGET_FILE_SIZE` | `512MB` | Target Parquet file size for DuckLake writes. |
| `DUCKLAKE_SNAPSHOT_EXPIRATION` | `7d` | Age at which old snapshots are expired and files become eligible for cleanup. |
| `DUCKLAKE_COMMIT_MAX_ATTEMPTS` | `60` | How many times the commit and the maintenance of a schema retry while the catalog is locked. |
| `DUCKLAKE_COMMIT_RETRY_SECONDS` | `1.0` | Seconds between two of those retries. |
| `DUCKLAKE_MAX_COMPACTED_FILES` | `10` | Maximum compacted files per table in one maintenance call. |
| `DUCKLAKE_REWRITE_DELETE_THRESHOLD` | `0.95` | Minimum deleted fraction for rewriting a data file. |

### DBOS

These variables set the DBOS application and its system database.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DBOS_APPLICATION_NAME` | `data-proxy-sync` | DBOS application name. |
| `DBOS_APPLICATION_VERSION` | `0.1.0` | DBOS application version. |
| `DBOS_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `300` | Seconds that a worker waits for its running workflows after SIGTERM. The chart gives the pod 30 more seconds. |
| `DBOS_SYSTEM_SCHEMA` | `dbos` | DBOS metadata schema. |
| `DBOS_APP_SCHEMA` | `data_proxy` | Application state schema. |

### Sync queues and schedule

These variables set the first values of the DBOS queues and of the sync schedule, and the limits of a sync run.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SYNC_SCHEDULE` | `0 2 * * *` | The cron of the DBOS schedule that a new schema gets. The schedule is named `sync-<schema>`. The console changes the cron of a schedule later. |
| `SYNC_QUEUE_CONCURRENCY` | `1` | Initial sync workflow concurrency. |
| `LISTEN_QUEUES` | empty | Queue names, separated by commas, that this worker listens to. Empty means every queue. An unknown name stops the worker. |
| `SYNC_RUN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `3600` | Maximum duration of one sync run. |
| `MAX_REMOVALS` | `10` | Most tables, or most S3 identities, that one step removes. A larger removal fails and names what it would delete. |
| `SYNC_STEP_MAX_ATTEMPTS` | `3` | Retry attempts for transient steps. |
| `DUMP_QUEUE_WORKER_CONCURRENCY` | `2` | Initial dump worker concurrency. |
| `DUCKDB_MEMORY_LIMIT` | `1GB` | Memory of each DuckDB connection of a sync worker. DuckDB spills to the disk beyond it. |
| `DUCKDB_THREADS` | `2` | Threads of each DuckDB connection. |
| `DUCKDB_TEMP_DIRECTORY` | `/tmp/duckdb` | Parent folder of the spill of the DuckDB connections. Each connection spills to a folder of its own in it, and removes the folder when it closes. |
| `DUMP_QUEUE_RATE_LIMIT` | `0` | Initial dump tasks per minute. `0` turns the limit off. |
| `DUMP_BATCH_BYTES` | `268435456` | Logical size of the source data of one dump task. The planner joins contiguous changed partitions into one query and one file up to this size. |
| `DUMP_QUEUE_MAX_ATTEMPTS` | `3` | Dump workflow retry attempts. |

The engine creates the queues and the schedule when they don't exist, and never overwrites them. These values are only the first ones, because a restart keeps the stored values. The console shows the queues and the schedules and doesn't edit them. See Control a run and a schedule for what a schedule allows.

### Observability

These variables set the log level and the OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) endpoints for the logs, the traces and the metrics of the sync workers.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | `INFO` | Log level of the sync workers: `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARNING`, `ERROR` or `CRITICAL`. |
| `OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT` | unset | OTLP logs endpoint. |
| `OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT` | unset | OTLP traces endpoint. |
| `OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT` | unset | OTLP metrics endpoint. |

See Proxy variables for the variables of the roles and of the OpenResty proxy.

Source: operations/proxy.md

## Proxy variables

These variables set the roles of the serving layer, the link from the sync workers to the proxy and the settings of the OpenResty proxy. Environment Variables has the variables of the other components.

### Auth and proxy

These variables set the PostgreSQL roles of the serving layer and the settings that connect the sync workers to the proxy and the provision job.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTH_ANON_ROLE` | `anon` | Unauthenticated PostgreSQL role. |
| `AUTH_USER_ROLE` | `dp_api` | The baseline PostgreSQL role. Every role of `rbac.toml` is a member of it. The chart sets it with `auth.userRole`. |
| `AUTH_SERVING_ROLE` | `serving` | The login of the serving layer: PostgREST, PgDog and the recovery Deployment. |
| `PROXY_CACHE_REDIS_DB` | `1` | Redis database for cached proxy responses. |
| `PROXY_ADMIN_URL` | unset | Address of the reload endpoint of the proxy, for example `http://data-proxy-proxy-admin:8081/reload`. The sync workers resolve its host to every proxy pod and send each one a reload request. Unset: nobody is notified. The chart sets it. |
| `SWAGGER_SCHEMAS_CONFIGMAP` | unset | Name of the ConfigMap with the schema list of the Swagger UI page. A sync worker writes the schemas of the console into it. The chart sets it when `swaggerUi.enabled` is true. Unset, the worker skips the step. |
| `PROVISION_CRONJOB` | unset | Name of the suspended `provision` CronJob. A sync worker makes a Job from it when a schema changes and at the start of every sync run. The chart sets it. Unset, the worker skips the step. |
| `PROVISION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `600` | How long the worker waits for the provision Job. |

### OpenResty proxy

The Helm chart sets these variables on the proxy Deployment. The Lua code reads them through `config.load` in `proxy/src/proxy/config.lua`. The proxy loads all settings once at start-up.

It collects the text of the variables in one table. Then it converts and checks that table once with the `config` schema (`proxy/src/proxy/schemas/definitions/config.lua`). A variable that isn't set uses the default of its setting.

A missing required variable, a value of the wrong type or a value outside the limits stops nginx from starting. The error names the setting. A variable name is `PROXY_` and the upper-case name of the setting. `helm/files/config/nginx.conf` lists every variable with an `env` directive, because nginx removes the other variables.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PROXY_CACHE_TTL` | `300` | Default cache lifetime in seconds, `0` or more. A table in `sync.json` can set its own `cache_ttl`. |
| `PROXY_MAX_BODY` | `262144` | Largest response body in bytes that the proxy stores. `0` means no limit. |
| `PROXY_REDIS_HOST` | required | Redis host for the cache. The operator provides one stable endpoint. Give nginx a name with a dot, such as `valkey.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`, because its resolver doesn't use the search domains. The chart adds the namespace to a name with no dot. |
| `PROXY_REDIS_PORT` | `6379` | Redis port for the cache, from `1` to `65535`. |
| `PROXY_REDIS_DATABASE` | `1` | Redis database for cached responses, `0` or more. |
| `PROXY_REDIS_PASSWORD` | unset | Redis password. Omit it for no login. |
| `PROXY_POSTGREST` | required | Base address of the PostgREST service. |
| `PROXY_MAX_INFLIGHT` | `0` | Most requests that wait for PostgREST at the same time in one proxy pod. More get a `503` with `Retry-After`. `0` means no limit. The chart sets `32`. |
| `PROXY_CONFIG_URL` | unset | Address of the configuration function of PostgREST, for example `http://postgrest:3000/rpc/config`. The proxy sends the profile `console` with it. When it's set, the proxy takes its table settings from there. The chart sets it. |
| `PROXY_CONFIG_REFRESH_SECONDS` | `60` | Seconds between two checks of PostgREST for a new document. The check is a safety net: the sync workers also call the reload endpoint immediately after a change. |

Source: operations/console.md

## Console variables

The console server reads these variables. The chart sets them from its values. See Console and notebooks for the values.

| Variable | Contains |
| --- | --- |
| `OIDC_ISSUER` | The address of the identity provider. |
| `OIDC_CLIENT_ID`, `OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET` | A confidential client with the redirect URI `<origin>/console/auth/callback`. |
| `COOKIE_SECRET` | The secret that seals the cookie. |
| `KEYS_SECRET` | Optional. The secret that seals the storage keys of the schemas. Without it, the console derives one from `COOKIE_SECRET`. A new value, or a new `COOKIE_SECRET` while this one is unset, makes the console create new keys at the next grant. The chart reads it from the key `KEYS_SECRET` of the console Secret. |
| `POSTGREST_URL` | The address of PostgREST. |
| `ORIGIN` | The public origin of the API host, with no path. The server compares the `Origin` header of every change with it. The server sets the `Secure` flag on its cookies when it starts with `https`. |
| `PROTOCOL_HEADER` | The header that contains the scheme to the Node adapter, `x-forwarded-proto` behind the gateway. Without it, the adapter assumes `https` and refuses every form post from an `http` site. |
| `NOTEBOOK_ORIGIN`, `CATALOG_URL`, `S3_ENDPOINT`, `S3_BUCKET`, `S3_ACCESS_KEY`, `S3_SECRET_KEY` | The query tab. Without them, the tab says that it isn't set up. `S3_REGION` is optional. `NOTEBOOK_ORIGIN` must be another origin than `ORIGIN`, and the console answers every request with an error when both match. |
| `GRANT_TTL_SECONDS` | Optional. The lifetime of the signed links in seconds. The default is 300. The page renews a grant at 80% of it. |
| `S3_ADMIN_ACCESS_KEY`, `S3_ADMIN_SECRET_KEY`, `S3_IAM_ENDPOINT` | Optional. They turn on one storage identity for each schema. The IAM endpoint is the storage endpoint by default. |

---

Source: operations/keda.md

## KEDA Scaling

Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling (KEDA) scales the DBOS sync Deployment from the DBOS system database. The sync workers share the `data-proxy-duckdb` PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC). They publish through one `publish` queue that's partitioned by schema, so each schema runs one publish task at a time.

```mermaid
%% Scaling triggers
flowchart LR
  subgraph keda["KEDA"]
    sync_trigger["Count of active DBOS workflows<br/>every 30 seconds"]
    cpu["CPU 70% and memory 90%"]
    cpu_proxy["CPU 70%"]
    sessions["Active PostgREST sessions<br/>for each instance"]
  end
  subgraph targets["Scaled workloads"]
    sync["Sync workers<br/>3 to 15 pods"]
    postgrest["PostgREST<br/>1 to 6 pods"]
    proxy["Proxy<br/>1 to 6 pods"]
    cnpg["CNPG instances<br/>2 to 6"]
  end
  pgdog["PgDog<br/>fixed: pgdog.replicas"]
  style pgdog stroke-dasharray: 3
  sync_trigger --> sync
  cpu --> postgrest
  cpu_proxy --> proxy
  sessions --> cnpg
```

KEDA also scales PostgREST, the proxy and the CloudNativePG (CNPG) standbys. Topology describes how.

```yaml
triggers:
  - type: postgresql
    metadata:
      connectionFromEnv: DBOS_SYSTEM_DATABASE_URL
      query: "SELECT ceil(COUNT(*)::decimal / 16) FROM dbos.workflow_status WHERE application_name = 'data-proxy-sync' AND status IN ('PENDING', 'ENQUEUED', 'DELAYED', 'RUNNING');
      targetQueryValue: "1.1"
      activationTargetQueryValue: "5"
```

`connectionFromEnv` reads `DBOS_SYSTEM_DATABASE_URL`. The query counts pending, queued, delayed and running DBOS workflows for the sync application.

### Orchestrator and dump workers

These Helm values set the scale and the concurrency of the sync workers. The table gives the default of each value.

| Value | Helm default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sync.autoscaling.minReplicaCount` | `3` | Minimum active sync replicas. |
| `sync.autoscaling.maxReplicaCount` | `15` | Maximum sync replicas. |
| `sync.autoscaling.pollingInterval` | `30` | Seconds between KEDA checks. |
| `sync.autoscaling.cooldownPeriod` | `60` | Seconds before scale-down. |
| `sync.autoscaling.targetQueryValue` | `"1.1"` | Target query value. |
| `sync.autoscaling.activationTargetQueryValue` | `"5"` | Activation threshold. |
| `sync.dumpQueueWorkerConcurrency` | `2` | Dump concurrency per sync process. |
| `ducklake.secrets.storage` | see values | Shared volume of the DuckDB secrets. |
| `sync.dumpBatchBytes` | `268435456` | Logical size of the source data of one dump task. |
| `sync.dumpStepMaxAttempts` | `3` | Dump workflow retry attempts. |

### Dump concurrency

A worker takes small batches: two dumps at a time. KEDA adds pods when more dumps wait. Each dump and each publish opens a DuckDB connection, so the concurrency sets how much memory a pod needs. For the memory and spill values, see DuckDB Memory and Spill.

The queue stores its limits when it starts for the first time, and a restart keeps them. A change of `sync.dumpQueueWorkerConcurrency` therefore changes only a new installation. To change an installed queue, update the row in the system database. The workers read the row again within seconds, so they need no restart.

```sql
UPDATE dbos.queues SET worker_concurrency = 2 WHERE name = 'dump';
```

### Dump batches

A BigQuery table can have thousands of small partitions. One query for each partition makes a run slow, because the delay of a query is longer than the work. The planner joins contiguous changed partitions into one task with one query and one file, until the batch has `sync.dumpBatchBytes` of logical data. An unchanged partition ends a batch, so a batch never reaches rows that the run keeps. A batch is the unit of a failure: if its dump fails, every partition of the batch fails together. The dump queue runs the batches of one table at the same time.

The planner orders partitions by their integer id, so a range with a negative start batches in key order. A partition with no reported size forms a batch of its own, because the planner can't tell how large it is.

An out-of-memory error in the commit step points first to the partitioning of the DuckLake table. See DuckLake partitioning and encryption.

### Catalogs

The DBOS sync workers write the catalogs in the `ducklake` database, through the primary. PostgreSQL replication copies them to every standby.

Publishing remains parallel across schemas because each schema has a separate metadata schema in the catalog database. Publishing remains sequential within one schema because its DBOS queue has global concurrency one.

### Disruption budgets

The chart keeps one pod of PgDog available during a node drain. It does the same for PostgREST and the proxy when their `autoscaling.minReplicaCount` is 2 or more. A budget on a workload that can run as one pod would block every drain.

### Configuration

This example shows the Helm values that set the schedule, the retries and the KEDA scaling of the sync workers.

```yaml
sync:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  dumpStepMaxAttempts: 3
  dumpQueueWorkerConcurrency: 2
  # DBOS workers use the shared data-proxy-duckdb PVC.
  autoscaling:
    minReplicaCount: 3
    maxReplicaCount: 15
    pollingInterval: 30
    cooldownPeriod: 60
    targetQueryValue: "1.1"
    activationTargetQueryValue: "5"
```

DBOS deduplicates the scheduled workflow across orchestrator replicas. The sync Deployment never scales below `minReplicaCount`, so a new schedule always reaches a worker. The chart doesn't set `idleReplicaCount`, because KEDA supports only `0` for it and any other value makes KEDA and the HPA fight.

---

---

Source: operations/duckdb.md

## DuckDB Memory and Spill

These values tune the memory and the spill of the sync workers. The defaults are in `helm/values.yaml`. KEDA Scaling describes the scale of the workers.

| Value | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sync.duckdb.memoryLimit` | `1GB` | The memory of each DuckDB connection of a sync worker. DuckDB spills to the disk beyond it. |
| `sync.duckdb.threads` | `2` | The threads of each DuckDB connection. |
| `sync.duckdb.tempDirectory` | `/tmp/duckdb` | The folder where DuckDB spills beyond `memoryLimit`. Each connection makes a folder of its own in it. |
| `sync.duckdb.tempVolume.enabled` | `false` | Mounts a volume at `tempDirectory`. When it's off, the spill uses the filesystem of the container, which is the disk of the node. |
| `sync.duckdb.tempVolume.type` | `ephemeral` | `ephemeral` makes a claim for each pod and deletes it with the pod. `emptyDir` uses the disk of the node. |
| `sync.duckdb.tempVolume.size` | `50Gi` | The size of the claim, or the size limit of the `emptyDir`. |
| `sync.duckdb.tempVolume.storageClassName` | empty | The StorageClass of the claim. Empty uses the default StorageClass. |

### Memory

A DuckDB connection takes 80% of the memory of the pod and every thread of the node. A pod has one connection for each dump task and one for each publish. Without a limit, the connections of one pod fill the pod and Kubernetes kills it (`OOMKilled`).

`sync.duckdb.memoryLimit` limits each connection. Each connection has its own spill folder, because two connections in one folder overwrite the files of each other and DuckDB crashes. Keep `memoryLimit` times (`sync.dumpQueueWorkerConcurrency` + 2) below `sync.resources.limits.memory`. The 2 stands for a publish and a maintenance run. Four connections of 1 GB (two dumps, a publish and a maintenance run) use 4 GB of the 6 GiB of a pod.

A row group is in memory while DuckDB writes it. The default of 122880 rows needs more than 3 GB for a table with wide JSON columns. The dump writes row groups of 10000 rows. The publish writes row groups of 122880 rows and stops a row group at 32 MB. The limit in bytes, not the rows, bounds the memory of wide tables. The two widest tables took 1.1 GB with it, and they ran out of memory at 1 GB without it. A narrow table keeps the large row groups, which DuckDB reads about twice as fast as groups of 10000 rows.

### Spill volume

Without a volume, the spill folder is on the filesystem of the container, which is the disk of the node. A large spill can fill that disk, and then Kubernetes evicts the pod.

Set `sync.duckdb.tempVolume.enabled` to give the folder a disk of its own. Use `type: ephemeral` with a fast `storageClassName` for a large spill: the chart makes a claim for each pod and deletes it with the pod. Use `type: emptyDir` to cap the use of the node disk with `size`.

A disk-backed volume belongs to root. The chart sets `fsGroup` on the sync pod to the group of the sync user, so the sync can write to the volume.

Don't mount a bucket through FUSE as the spill folder. Each connection writes and reads small blocks at random, and a bucket mount is slow for that access. Each connection also needs a folder of its own.

---

Source: operations/lookups.md

## Lookup Layout

These settings change how a DuckLake table is laid out in the bucket, so a lookup on one value reads fewer files. A table with no setting works, and the settings help a large table. Use them in the table configuration. The memory values are on the page DuckDB Memory and Spill.

### Partition key of an integer range table

An integer range table doesn't need a partition key for a table of a few gigabytes. The batches of a run are contiguous key ranges, so the minimum and maximum of each file already skip most files. A test with 2.75 million rows (2.4 GB) at a DuckDB memory limit of 2 GB gave these results.

| Layout | Files | Insert time | Peak memory | Files read by a lookup on one value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No key | 4 | 23 s | 1.2 GB | 1 |
| `bucket` with 8 | 8 | 26 s | 2.3 GB | 1 |
| `bucket` with 16 | 16 | 38 s | 2.5 GB | 1 |
| `SET SORTED BY` the column | none | none | out of memory | none |

A `bucket` key reads every bucket for a range query, because it spreads neighbouring values. Set a `bucket` transform in the table configuration only when the table has hundreds of files and its queries look up one value.

Never use the `identity` transform on a column with a different value in each row. DuckLake makes one partition for each value, and the commit runs out of memory.

### Sort columns of an integer range table

A sort on the key gives each file tight row groups, so a lookup on one value reads one row group. DuckLake sorts the rows of one insert in memory. A sorted table therefore gets one insert for each batch file, and a sort keeps one batch and not the whole table. The same test as above, with the table sorted by the key, gave these results.

| Commit | Files | Time | Peak memory | Row groups read by a lookup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No sort | 4 | 20 s | 1.2 GB | 3.8 |
| Sorted, one insert for each batch, 2 GB limit | 10 | 12 s | 1.3 GB | 1.0 |
| Sorted, one insert for all batches, 2 GB limit | none | none | out of memory | none |
| Sorted, one insert for all batches, 4 GB limit | 5 | 31 s | 4.2 GB | 1.0 |

A sort in the extraction query alone, with no sort on the table, gave 1.9 row groups for a lookup. Set the sort columns of a table in its configuration. Use the console import with `"ducklake": {"sort": ["cnpj_particao"]}`, or the `sort` list of the `ducklake` block of the Terraform resource. A change of the sort or of the partitioning makes the next sync rebuild the table.

The commit of a table runs its delete and its inserts in one DuckLake transaction. A failed insert leaves the table as it was.

---

Source: operations/metrics.md

## Metrics

Sync workers send their metrics through OpenTelemetry when `OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT` is set. They use the OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP).

### Worker metrics

The sync workers export these Prometheus metrics. The table gives the labels and the meaning of each metric.

| Metric                 | Labels                      | Meaning                                                       |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dump_tasks_total`     | `table`, `schema`, `status` | Dump tasks. Status: `success` or `error`.                     |
| `publish_tables_total` | `schema`, `status`          | Published tables. Status: `success` or `error`.               |
| `seed_runs_total`      | `schema`, `status`          | Seed runs. Current status: `success`.                         |
| `sync_runs_total`      | `status`                    | Sync runs. Status: `success` or `failure`.                    |

### Proxy logs

The proxy writes one text log line per request, for example `Proxy request completed: method=GET path=/people status=200 source=cache duration_ms=3 bytes=120`.

| Field         | Meaning                                      |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `method`      | HTTP method.                                 |
| `path`        | Request path.                                |
| `status`      | HTTP status.                                 |
| `source`      | `cache`, the `X-Source` value from PostgREST (`ducklake`, or `ducklake+<configured-fallback>`), `postgrest` when PostgREST sent none, or `none` when it was unreachable. |
| `duration_ms` | Request duration in milliseconds.            |
| `bytes`       | Response size.                               |

A request with `source=cache` was a cache hit. A repeated request that always shows another source means that the cache doesn't store the answer.

The cache is optional, so a Redis failure doesn't fail a request. The proxy writes the warning `Redis cache <connection|read|write> failed: <reason>` at most once every 30 seconds in each worker. Alert on this warning: without it, every request goes to PostgREST.

Use API response headers for client troubleshooting. Use logs for request analysis. See Using the API.

### PostgREST metrics

PostgREST serves Prometheus metrics at `/metrics` on its admin port, 3001 by default. The pod has the `prometheus.io/*` scrape annotations. Set `postgrest.metrics.enabled` to `false` to turn the admin port off.

The port is open to the pods in the cluster, and `/schema_cache` on it shows the schema structure.

| Metric                          | Meaning                                                                               |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pgrst_db_pool_waiting`         | Requests that wait for a database connection. A value above 0 means that the pool is full. |
| `pgrst_db_pool_available`       | Free connections in the pool.                                                         |
| `pgrst_db_pool_timeouts_total`  | Requests that gave up after `dbPoolAcquisitionTimeout` seconds. A rising value means that clients get errors. |

Alert when `pgrst_db_pool_waiting` stays above 0, and when the timeouts counter rises. Both point to a database that needs more capacity, or to a request mix that's too demanding.

### Load profile limits

The load test gates a run on latency bounds for the cache and for bounded DuckLake reads. It reports the heavy, selective, pinned and fallback routes. The header of `k6/load.js` lists the bounds, the traffic mix and the flags. Load tests shows the commands.

### Capacity diagnosis

Check these signals during a load run. Compare pool waits with DuckLake and configured-fallback latency in the same PostgREST instance.

```sql
SELECT state, wait_event_type, wait_event, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE usename = 'serving'
GROUP BY state, wait_event_type, wait_event
ORDER BY count(*) DESC;
```

```sql
SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time::numeric / 1000, 1) AS total_seconds,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS mean_ms,
       left(regexp_replace(query, E'\\s+', ' ', 'g'), 160) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

One PostgREST and one PgDog serve both DuckLake and configured fallback reads. The proxy logs separate cache hits, DuckLake reads and configured fallback reads. A rising `duration_ms` p95 for DuckLake reads with low PostgreSQL execution time indicates pool wait or request queueing. A rising fallback trend indicates external-source latency. Keep the local k3d result as a comparison only: the load generator and services share one host.

### Scraping

CloudNativePG (CNPG) exposes metrics on port 9187. SigNoz should scrape the CNPG pod metrics endpoint through its OpenTelemetry Collector. Select CNPG pods by their cluster labels and scrape the named `metrics` port.

The external Redis platform runs the Redis exporter and its metrics endpoint. The data-proxy chart doesn't deploy Redis metrics resources or Prometheus Operator resources.

PostgREST and nginx use Metrics Server for their default CPU and memory autoscalers. Istio exposes their traffic metrics for custom Prometheus-based Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling (KEDA) triggers.

### Queries

These PromQL queries count the dump tasks and the published tables of the sync workers.

```promql
sum by (table, status) (dump_tasks_total)
```

```promql
sum by (schema) (publish_tables_total{status="success"})
  / sum by (schema) (publish_tables_total)
```
