---

Source: operations/backups.md

## Backups

A sync rebuilds application tables from the source. It doesn't rebuild access grants. The chart backs up each `<schema>.access_policy` table and, when configured, its `<schema>.access_log` audit trail.

### Operation

```mermaid
%% Backup flow
flowchart LR
  schemas[("console.schemas<br/>the list of schemas")]
  subgraph job["Backup CronJob backup.schedule"]
    each["For each schema"] --> export["Export access_policy<br/>and access_log"] --> prune["Delete access_log rows<br/>older than retentionDays"]
  end
  bucket[("Backup bucket<br/>prefix/schema/date/")]
  fail["One schema fails:<br/>the job goes on, then fails<br/>and names the schema"]
  schemas -->|"read at each run"| each
  export -->|"upload two dumps"| bucket
  each -.->|"on a failure"| fail
```

Set `backup.enabled` to create the backup CronJob. It reads the schemas from the `console.schemas` table, so it backs up a schema that an editor adds in the console from its first night.

For each schema it exports `<schema>.access_policy` and `<schema>.access_log`, uploads both dumps to the separate backup S3/GCS-compatible service, then prunes `access_log` rows older than `backup.accessLog.retentionDays`. A failure in one schema doesn't stop the others. The job fails at the end and names the schemas that failed. The objects are:

```text
<backup.prefix>/<schema>/<date>/access_policy.dump
<backup.prefix>/<schema>/<date>/access_log.dump
```

The chart default prefix is:

```text
backups/access_policy
```

Backups contain only access-policy and audit-log data. They don't contain PostgreSQL tables, Parquet files or the full database.

### Configuration

```yaml
jobs:
  existingSecret: data-proxy-jobs
backup:
  enabled: true
  schedule: "0 3 * * *"
  prefix: backups/access_policy
  accessLog:
    retentionDays: 90
  s3:
    endpointURL: https://storage.googleapis.com
    bucket: access-policy-backups
```

The database Secret supplies the password of the `ops` role. The backup CronJob and the cleanup CronJob both connect as that role, like every other internal workload.

The default schedule is daily at 03:00 UTC. Configure bucket lifecycle rules for retention. The chart doesn't delete backup objects.

### Verify a backup

Download the dump and inspect it before restoring:

```bash
rclone copy \
  ":s3:<bucket>/backups/access_policy/<schema>/<date>/access_policy.dump" \
  access_policy.dump

pg_restore --list access_policy.dump
```

### Restore

1. Download the reviewed dump from the separate backup service.
2. Restore it into a temporary database or table.
3. Compare it with `<schema>.access_policy`.
4. Apply reviewed rows only.

Don't load an unreviewed backup into a live access policy table.

### Database backup

The whole database, with the DuckLake catalogs and the console data, has its own backup. Set `cnpg.backup.enabled` to turn it on. CloudNativePG (CNPG) then archives the write-ahead log (WAL) and takes a base backup each day, through the Barman Cloud plugin.

The plugin must run in the cluster before you turn the backup on, because the chart creates an `ObjectStore` that the plugin owns. The plugin has its own Helm chart, `plugin-barman-cloud`, in the namespace of the CNPG operator.

| Value | Contains |
| --- | --- |
| `cnpg.backup.bucket`, `cnpg.backup.destinationPath` | The bucket and the prefix of the backups. |
| `cnpg.backup.endpointURL` | The S3-compatible endpoint. For GCS, use `https://storage.googleapis.com`. |
| `cnpg.backup.existingSecret` | A Secret with `S3_ACCESS_KEY` and `S3_SECRET_KEY`. |
| `cnpg.backup.schedule` | The schedule of the base backups, with six fields. The first one is the seconds. |
| `cnpg.backup.retention` | The age after which the plugin deletes a backup and its WAL files. |

The chart takes the first base backup when it creates the schedule. `kubectl get backup` lists the backups, and `kubectl get cluster -o jsonpath='{.status.firstRecoverabilityPoint}'` shows the oldest point that you can restore.

The chart tells the AWS client to add checksums only when the storage requires them, because GCS refuses the default. A replica that falls behind catches up from the archive. The chart also limits what a replication slot keeps with `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, which is 8 GB by default. Without a limit, a slot that stops could fill the disk of the primary. Set a larger value in `cnpg.postgresql.parameters` for a larger disk.

### Turn the backup on in a running cluster

The plugin adds a sidecar to each instance pod, and CNPG restarts the primary in place, because a primary without the sidecar can't switch over. With two instances, the standby can't become ready while the primary is down. The cluster then stays in the phase `Primary instance is being restarted without a switchover`.

To end the wait, set `status.targetPrimary` of the Cluster to the standby, with the phase `Switchover in progress`. CNPG then starts the pods again. Recreate each instance pod once afterward, so that it reads a change in `instanceSidecarConfiguration`.

CNPG also refuses to change the image and a PostgreSQL parameter in one release when `primaryUpdateMethod` is `switchover`. Roll out a new parameter first with the image that runs now, and then roll out the new image.

### Restore the database

Restore the database with the recovery of the whole cluster. Create a new cluster with `bootstrap.recovery` that names the object store as its source. Check the new cluster before you point any workload at it, and keep the old cluster until the check ends.

### Upgrade PostgreSQL to a new major version

Don't change `cnpg.image` to a new major version in place. The image of `pg_duckdb` links `libduckdb.so` by an absolute path, so the CloudNativePG upgrade job can't start the old server. The job fails in seconds, and Helm rolls the release back.

Create a new cluster that imports the old one instead, with `bootstrap.initdb.import` of the type `monolith`. See the [CloudNativePG import guide](https://cloudnative-pg.io/documentation/current/database_import/). Stop the writers first, because the import copies one snapshot. Run a base backup before you start, and check the row counts of both clusters before you delete the old one.

---

Source: terraform.md

## Terraform provider

The `data_proxy` Terraform provider manages the configuration of Data Proxy as code. It manages the projects, the schemas, the tables, the row policies and the access policies through the PostgREST API. The provider is a Go module in `terraform/`, and it uses the Terraform Plugin Framework.

The provider has four resources and nine data sources. Resources and Data sources describe them, and Provider development says how to build and test it. The provider gets an access token from the identity provider with the OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant. It fetches a new token 30 seconds before the old one expires, so a long run keeps working with tokens that last 5 minutes.

### Configuration

The registry address is `<host>/<namespace>/data-proxy`, and the build sets it, so the provider has no host name. A local name has no underscore, so it's `data-proxy`. The resources are `data_proxy_*`, so each one needs `provider = data-proxy`. Provider releases says where the registry is. Each attribute has an environment variable. The provider uses the variable when the block doesn't set the attribute. An attribute in the block takes precedence over its variable, also when its value is an empty string.

| Attribute | Variable | Type | Content |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `endpoint` | `DATA_PROXY_ENDPOINT` | string, required | The base address of the Data Proxy API. |
| `token_url` | `DATA_PROXY_TOKEN_URL` | string, required | The address of the token endpoint of the identity provider. |
| `client_id` | `DATA_PROXY_CLIENT_ID` | string, required | The client ID for the client credentials grant. |
| `client_secret` | `DATA_PROXY_CLIENT_SECRET` | string, required, sensitive | The client secret for the client credentials grant. Terraform hides it in the output. |
| `scopes` | `DATA_PROXY_SCOPES` | list of strings | The scopes to request with the token. The variable separates them with commas or spaces. |

A required value must come from the block or from its variable. The provider fails with one error for each value that's missing.

When it starts, the provider gets a token and calls `GET /rpc/permissions`. It fails when the identity provider refuses the secret, when the API refuses the token, or when the token lacks `read_config`. Every resource and data source reads the configuration. The database checks the write permissions, such as `create_config`, `edit_config` and `delete_config`, on each request. The error of a refused request names the permission that it needed. The roles page lists the permissions of each role.

```hcl
terraform {
  required_providers {
    data-proxy = {
      source = "registry.example.com/example/data-proxy"
    }
  }
}

provider "data-proxy" {
  endpoint  = "https://data-proxy.example.com"
  token_url = "https://id.example.com/realms/example/protocol/openid-connect/token"
  client_id = "terraform"
  scopes    = ["openid"]
}
```

Don't write the client secret in a `.tf` file. Set `DATA_PROXY_CLIENT_SECRET`, or give it to Terraform as a variable from your secret store.

---

Source: terraform-resources.md

## Terraform resources

Every resource of the provider needs `provider = data-proxy`, because a provider local name has no underscore. The provider page explains why. A refused write names the permission that it needed, such as `create_config`.

### `data_proxy_project`

A project groups schemas. The project `default` exists already, so the resource refuses that name.

```hcl
resource "data_proxy_project" "sales" {
  provider = data-proxy
  name     = "sales"
}
```

- `name`: a lowercase letter and up to 29 lowercase letters and digits. A change replaces the project.
- `updated_at` and `updated_by`: filled by the database.

The database refuses to delete a project that has schemas, so Terraform deletes the schemas first. Import with the name: `terraform import data_proxy_project.sales sales`.

### `data_proxy_schema`

A schema has the tables of one source. The sync creates its PostgreSQL schema after the row appears.

```hcl
resource "data_proxy_schema" "orders" {
  provider            = data-proxy
  project             = data_proxy_project.sales.name
  short_name          = "orders"
  claim               = "preferred_username"
  deletion_protection = false
}
```

| Attribute | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `project` | The project. The default is `default`. A change replaces the schema. |
| `short_name` | The name inside the project. A change replaces the schema. |
| `name` | The physical name: the short name in `default`, else `<project>_<short_name>`. Tables and access policies use it. |
| `source`, `settings`, `claim`, `encrypted` | The columns of the schema. `settings` is a JSON object, such as `jsonencode({...})`. |
| `deletion_protection` | Refuses the delete while it's `true`, which is the default. Only Terraform reads it. |

A create waits until the sync provisions the schema, for 5 minutes at most. A delete waits until the sync drops it, for 10 minutes. Set `timeouts { create = "0s" }` or `delete = "0s"` to skip the wait. A replace or a delete drops the data, so the plan shows it.

Import with the physical name. An imported schema has deletion protection.

### `data_proxy_table`

A table that the sync copies from the source into a schema.

```hcl
resource "data_proxy_table" "orders" {
  provider = data-proxy
  name     = "sales.dataset.orders"
  schema   = data_proxy_schema.orders.name
  sort     = ["order_id"]

  rls {
    column_name = "unit_id"
    unit_type   = "unit"
  }
}
```

- `name` and `schema`: a change replaces the table and syncs it again.
- `strategy`: `full` (default) or `partitioned`. `n` and `fallback` need `partitioned`.
- `cache_ttl`: the seconds that the proxy caches an answer.
- `partitioning`: a JSON array of partition transforms. `sort`: a list of columns.
- `rls`: the row policies in order. The schema needs a `claim`, or the database refuses them.

A change of `rls` deletes the policies of the table and adds them again, in two calls. It isn't atomic. A change of the strategy, the partitioning, the sort or the policies makes the next sync rebuild the table. Import with the name.

### `data_proxy_access_policy`

A row that lets a subject read the data of a schema, limited to one unit when the row names it.

```hcl
resource "data_proxy_access_policy" "reader" {
  provider  = data-proxy
  schema    = data_proxy_schema.orders.name
  subject   = "reader@example.org"
  unit_type = "unit"
  unit_id   = "42"
}
```

Every attribute replaces the row. Without `unit_type` and `unit_id`, the row covers the whole schema. A create waits for the schema, for 5 minutes at most.

Manage static grants only, such as the grants of service accounts. An application that registers its own policies would delete rows that it didn't write. The table has no primary key, so a read fails when it finds equal rows.

Import with `schema/subject/unit_type/unit_id`, and an empty part for a missing unit: `terraform import data_proxy_access_policy.reader orders/reader@example.org/unit/42`.

---

Source: terraform-data-sources.md

## Terraform data sources

Every data source needs `provider = data-proxy`. A read fails when the object doesn't exist or the token can't see it.

| Data source | Arguments | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `data_proxy_permissions` | none | The permissions of the token, such as `read_config`. |
| `data_proxy_project` | `name` | The project row. |
| `data_proxy_schema` | `name`, or `short_name` and `project` | The schema row, with its settings and claim. `project` defaults to `default`. |
| `data_proxy_table` | `name` | The table row and its `rls` list. |
| `data_proxy_schema_health` | `name` | Whether the sync created the schema (`schema_exists`) and its access policy table (`access_policy`), and the `view_count`. |
| `data_proxy_table_sync_state` | `name` | Whether the sync published the table (`synced`), its `signature` and `partition_count`. |
| `data_proxy_export_config` | none | The configuration as a JSON `document` grouped by project, with the empty projects. |
| `data_proxy_sync_config` | none | The flat `document` that the sync engine reads, with physical schema names as keys. |
| `data_proxy_config_history` | `schema` and `limit`, both optional | The newest changes in `entries`, newest first. The default `limit` is 100. |

### Examples

Read a schema that Terraform doesn't manage, and use its physical name:

```hcl
data "data_proxy_schema" "existing" {
  provider   = data-proxy
  short_name = "orders"
}

resource "data_proxy_table" "orders" {
  provider = data-proxy
  name     = "sales.dataset.orders"
  schema   = data.data_proxy_schema.existing.name
}
```

Start from an existing environment. The export has the same shape that the console exports and `import_config` reads:

```hcl
data "data_proxy_export_config" "this" {
  provider = data-proxy
}

output "projects" {
  value = keys(jsondecode(data.data_proxy_export_config.this.document).projects)
}
```

Wait for a schema in a later step of a pipeline:

```hcl
data "data_proxy_schema_health" "orders" {
  provider = data-proxy
  name     = "orders"
}

output "ready" {
  value = data.data_proxy_schema_health.orders.schema_exists && data.data_proxy_schema_health.orders.access_policy
}
```
